We investigate the generalization capability of two-layer neural networks, specifically those with threshold activation, within complex landscapes. The networks we analyze map from a d-dimensional hypercube to d-dimensional space. Our findings indicate that the generalization error scales linearly with the dimensionality of the hypercube, even assuming a noise-centric view. Nevertheless, our experiments suggest that the generalization error can be significantly outperformed by an upper bound limit, especially in higher dimensions. We also demonstrate that the generalization performance can be enhanced by adding noise to the output, as well as by employing techniques designed to robustly identify linear subspaces within the hypercube. Our studies offer new insights into the generalization capability of two-layer neural networks and contribute to the development of more effective algorithms. Moreover, our code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/alex-hughes/neural-networks-on-hypercubes.

Our research analyzes the large-scale anisotropy in cosmic ray distributions detected by the Tien Shan experiment, operating at 2600 m above sea level. The study reveals significant patterns at scales of 1 degree and 20 degrees related to dipole and quadrupole features. The anisotropy amplitude's growth with increasing energy has been investigated, and we observe a substantial increase in dipole amplitude above 4 EeV, where the harmonic mean amplitude rises from 0.08% at 4 EeV to 0.16% at 20 EeV. The anisotropy's orientation remains largely unchanged across this energy range, with the exception of a notable change in quadrupole feature at around 20 EeV. The anisotropy patterns are consistent with simulated cosmic ray distributions obtained by scaling up recently observed patterns in smaller energy ranges. Additionally, we present evidence suggesting that the anisotropy scales harmonically with energy. The research also discusses potential methods to verify the origins of ultra-high energy cosmic rays. The SiD Detector, one of the two validated detector designs for the ILC, has a calorimeter system that utilizes a high precision silicon active precision tracker with a tungsten concentration, optimizing its material thickness in accordance with precision silicon technology. This calorimeter system, coupled with its thin tungsten content, effectively maintains overall energy accuracy for electron and photon detection. However, for hadron jets, the influence of the tungsten content leads to increased reading errors, particularly at higher energy levels. This research aims to examine the reading errors of the SiD Detector's calorimeter system for hadron jets across various energy levels. Different ILC operating conditions and integration times for the readout system are investigated through Monte Carlo simulation. The study reveals that under some scenarios, a longer integration time results in a higher reading error due to an increased risk of electron bunch collisions. A higher electron bunch intensity in these scenarios further aggravates the situation. However, in certain cases, a longer integration time results in a lower reading error, indicating that this variable has an impact on reading errors. A longer integration time results in a lower reading error at all energy levels for a given bunch intensity, underscoring the significance of bunch intensity. A higher energy for the detected hadron jets also results in a higher reading error. This research also demonstrates the versatility of the SiD Detector's design in addressing reading errors through either design and operation variations, underscoring the necessity of optimizing jet performance in certain scenarios. A jet-algorithm with a high level of precision achieves better performance in comparison to a basic base-line. This research validates the utility of the SiD Detector's design in detecting hadron jets, emphasizing the importance of design and operation optimization. A detailed study of the performance of the SiD Detector's calorimeter system in detecting hadron jets is presented in the accompanying report. [For an accompanying summary, see arXiv:1902.02897]. A detailed photometric study of the galactic globular cluster Tononzintla 2 was conducted using Hubble Space Telescope Wide Field Camera 3 images, taken at different wavelengths. The analysis extended to magnitudes where individual stars could be distinguished, allowing for the creation of color-magnitude diagrams down to the brightest and reddest levels. The application of an advanced analytical technique, called the second generation of RADIUS, allowed us to map the 3D internal structure of the cluster. The results showed a significant metallicity disparity and elemental diversity within the cluster, exceeding that of comparable metallic content in the galaxy's central globular clusters. The findings revealed an irregular shape and a complex internal structure, characterized by elevated mass density at the center. The analysis also uncovered a linear relationship between velocity dispersion and mass overdensity, consistent with the predictions of the'standard' cluster model. However, the results indicated the presence of an anomalous, velocity-related phenomenon across the cluster's interior. Tononzintla 2's internal structure appears to be an unusual example of a cluster's internal metal spread affecting its internal dynamics. The findings challenge the long-held cluster classification system and the widely accepted, uniform metal spread hypothesis in the galaxy's central clusters. Moreover, the results presented contradict the previous research on the cluster, its metallicity, and its spread. Tononzintla 2's metallicity and elemental spread are comparable to that of high-metallicity, spread-out Galactic clusters, rather than low-metallicity, uniform LMC clusters. The results also show an unexpected, unusually high metal spread in a cluster with high metallicity. Furthermore, the results challenge the existing, simplistic model of cluster dynamics based on simplicity and suggest the need for further research into the cluster's formation and evolution. Lastly, the research highlights the benefits of using photometric mapping in determining cluster metal spread and dynamics, paving the way for similar, photometric mapping of other, distant clusters. The analysis is made available to the public, including the images, catalog, and analysis results in the Hubble Source Catalog. Additionally, the research includes the determination of the cluster's distance, velocity, and 3D internal structure, including the velocity patterns along the line of sight. The results are particularly significant, as the cluster's internal structure is an unusual example of a cluster's internal dynamics being affected by its internal metal spread. Despite significant advancements in the study of active nematics, there's a notable lack of research comparing their dynamics to that of equilibrium systems.
We address this gap by examining the two-dimensional collective dynamics of both active nematics and equilibrium systems represented by two-dimensional elastics fluids, within the framework of the six-vertex model. Focusing on the long-wavelength hydrodynamic regime, our analysis reveals that the long-wavelength dynamics of active nematics is characterized by the presence of orientational order and fluctuations, as well as a violated fluctuation-dissipation relation, in contrast to the behavior of equilibrium systems. We find that the long-wavelength dynamics of active nematics is governed by the continuation of the equilibrium fluctuation-dissipation relation, accompanied by a correction proportional to the average orientational order parameter. Moreover, our analysis shows that the long-wavelength dynamics of active nematics is controlled by two distinct corrections, one proportional to the square root of the average orientational order parameter and another proportional to the average orientational order parameter itself. We also derive an exact expression for the long-wavelength hydrodynamic conductivities of both active nematics and equilibrium systems. Our results provide valuable insights into the long-wavelength dynamics of active nematics and suggest potential future research directions. Furthermore, our findings can be experimentally verified, paving the way for the development of experimental protocols tailored to specific active nematic systems. Finally, our results can be extended to three-dimensional active nematics by incorporating the effects of their long-wavelength transverse hydrodynamics. Recent advancements in programming techniques have led to the successful application of pre-trained models, which have shown great potential in addressing complex coding issues. However, the secret to their superiority remains unclear, hindering the development of comparable models. To gain insights into the effectiveness of pre-trained models in code completion, we conducted an in-depth examination of their performance on a range of tasks. Our findings reveal that pre-trained models can learn task-agnostic patterns, such as code syntax and structure, which facilitate downstream performance. Notably, our results indicate that pre-trained models can achieve high accuracies in downstream applications even in the absence of task-specific training data. Our analysis provides practical guidance for designing pre-trained models and developing new challenges to test their limitations. Additionally, we propose CodeMTL, a multi-task learning framework that combines code transformation and classification tasks to leverage diverse modeling capabilities and promote more efficient development of pre-trained models. Our approach is validated by experiments on extensive datasets, which consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art models. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/THU-CLP/CodeMTL. Our model has been deployed on https://github.com/THU-CLP/codelearner. A live demo is also accessible at https://www.codelearner.org.

To explore how galaxies like the Milky Way form, a cluster of 32 realistic galaxy models were created using the EAGLE framework, focusing on different disc/spheroid formation patterns. We initially examine the relationship between uncalibrated photometry and optical depth using data from interstellar bands, but discover that photometric surveys typically employ colour terms that obscure this connection. To address this, we've developed a noise-reduced algorithm based on the normalized cross-correlation method that can circumvent the difficulties usually encountered in pitch detection tasks. This approach involves subtracting a noise model derived from background noise to eliminate distortion and isolate the speech signal. We've applied this noise-reduced pitch detection algorithm to the MFCC mel-frequency spectral coefficients extracted from speech audio. Experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness and compare its performance to existing pitch detection methods. This noise-reduced algorithm has potential applications in improving the overall efficiency of speech processing systems. We've utilized the NYU Polytechnic Institute's PITCH database, which features a variety of speech patterns, to test and validate the accuracy of the proposed method. We've also utilized the PITCH database to analyze the performance of the proposed method in identifying the pitch values of female and male speakers. This study showcases the effectiveness of a straightforward approach to pitch detection that can enhance the efficiency of speech processing systems without compromising accuracy. To further improve the precision of the proposed method, we've explored the incorporation of a weighted spectral normalization technique, which involves calibrating the amplitude of the extracted spectral coefficients based on their frequency and bandwidth. In the non-minimal supersymmetric model with three singlet scalar fields, 
we investigated the relationship between an enlarged neutrino sector and 
the accuracy of the Higgs boson mass prediction within the one-loop level. 
The analysis indicated that including more neutrino degrees of freedom 
within the seesaw mechanism minimizes the dependence of the Higgs boson mass 
on higher-order corrections, resulting in a more precise prediction. 
This finding is particularly significant in the limit of heavy supersymmetric particles. 
The present study examined the mass ranges of the Higgs boson within the constraints 
of experimental data and theoretical integrity, where the scenario of four 
active neutrinos resulted in a more favorable outcome. 
The variation in the Higgs boson mass within the parameter space of this model 
was significantly reduced, ranging from 0.4 to 2 GeV, in the scenario of four 
active neutrinos where the mass of the Higgs boson fell within the range of 123 to 129 GeV. 
The outcome of this study will likely have a positive impact on the research on 
the mass of the Higgs boson and the properties of supersymmetric particles. 
The relevant parameters of the model, including the masses of neutrinos and 
scalar particles, as well as their mixing with Higgs bosons, were also investigated.

keV to GeV, whereas the masses of the singlet scalar particles fell within the 
range of 100 GeV to 10 TeV, with their mixing resulting in masses of 
Higgs bosons within the range of 100 GeV to 10 TeV. 
The study also confirmed that the model is in compliance with the constraints 
of both experimental data and theoretical integrity.

In recent years, neural architecture search (NAS) has been heavily concentrated on,
aiming to develop high-performance neural networks through automated process.
Notably, researchers found connections between neural architectures and their
program properties, such as size, depth, and level of nested structures.
Interestingly, these studies discovered that high-performing neural architectures
tend to exhibit distinct program characteristics, including larger sizes, higher
depths, and more complex structures.
Encouraged by these findings, we aim to explore the applicability of program
properties in searching for neural architectures suitable for real-world world
scenarios, specifically for inductive learning tasks. To this end, we conducted
an in-depth analysis of program properties of neural architectures used in
inductive learning and comprehensively examined the existing program properties
based search methods.
Ultimately, we propose a novel approach, named Neural Architecture Finder,
utilizing program properties to guide the search of neural architectures for
inductive learning. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method
outperforms existing program properties based search methods and yields
state-of-the-art results on benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-100, CIFAR-10,
and ImageNet. Notably, our approach successfully discovers neural architectures
programmatically distinct from those used in supervised learning. Our work
represents a significant extension to the existing program properties based
search pipeline, providing valuable insights for inductive learning, and can be
utilized as a starting point for exploring neural architectures in other
domains. Our code can be accessed at: https://github.com/learn2learn/naf. JFYI, this paper has been accepted at IJCAI 2021.

Federated learning's efficiency in decentralized training of models is a notable benefit, but data non-homogeneity still poses challenges, leading to inconsistent model performance across different clients. A potential solution is Federated Distillation, which uses knowledge distillation to align model predictions, though this method introduces significant communication requirements. We address this issue by integrating knowledge distillation with data compression, resulting in Compressed Federated Distillation (CFD), which significantly reduces communication needs and promotes model convergence without compromising accuracy. Experimental evaluations using ImageNet datasets demonstrate that CFD outperforms both Federated Distillation and Federated Averaging in terms of communication efficiency, while also providing improved system convergence speed. Moreover, CFD offers enhanced system convergence compared to traditional Federated Distillation with minimal compression. We publicly showcase the implementation of CFD through its open-source repository on https://github.com/alefarrar/CFD. Additionally, our results are reproduced in an open-research format in https://cfdr.net.

Between multiple failed link recovery paths, SDADO is designed to select the most efficient option. This approach differs from traditional re-routing methods, which usually involve network topology inspection and other time-consuming processes. Our results show that SDADO significantly outperforms existing algorithms, with improved network performance of up to 35\% and 10\% enhancements in end-to-end delay and throughput, respectively, while also ensuring optimal resource utilization. \textit{Experimentally}, SDADO outshines other algorithms by 21\% and 6% in terms of network efficiency and link efficiency, respectively. This validation of SDADO's effectiveness further reinforces its value in enhancing the delivery of services via dynamic network re-routing. This new metric simplifies complexity associated with other efficiency metrics and is both scalable and independent of specific network technologies. By applying this new metric, the overall effectiveness of re-routing algorithms, including dynamic network re-configurations, can be assessed. This new metric is further used to demonstrate that SDADO's improved performance is reflected in enhanced overall effectiveness. This analysis provides valuable insights into the benefits and effects of re-configuring networks, which can inform future research in this domain. Lastly, the advantages of integrating service discovery mechanisms into re-configurations of complex networks, such as those involving virtual networks, cloud computing, and software-defined networks, are also highlighted. While this approach is simple, it's susceptible to outliers that can hinder its performance. This paper introduces a novel aggregation technique - weighted power-p mean (WPM), offering a flexible alternative to the standard linear method. We analyze the asymptotic behavior of WPM and demonstrate its superiority over traditional aggregation methods, also presenting a practical implementation that uses gradient-norm weights. This innovative aggregation technique enhances the stability and scalability of distributed stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and empirical risk minimization (ERM), as evidenced by our experiments. We develop theoretical guarantees for SGD with WPM aggregation, and our results surpass those of regular SGD when applied to specific tasks, such as neural network training and adversarial robustness. During the COVID-19 pandemic, intensive care units were overwhelmed, leading to a critical shortage of ventilators. To manage this shortage, patients were forced to share the available ventilators, but these devices were unable to ensure accurate ventilation settings for each patient. To overcome this limitation, we developed a new ventilation strategy, allowing multiple patients to be ventilated using a single ventilator while delivering individualized tidal volumes. By modeling the ventilator dynamics and employing optimal control theory, our algorithm calculates the flow rate and pressure required to precisely achieve desired tidal volumes in each patient. We tested our method in a simulated ICU environment, comparing it to a traditional constant flow rate approach, and found that the proposed method produces more accurate tidal volumes, remains safe by avoiding positive pressure, and significantly reduces interaction forces between patients. These results demonstrate the potential of our algorithm to improve patient outcomes by providing reliable mechanical ventilation. Consequently, protecting these against manipulation and creating effective detection systems has become essential. This study delves into the area of visual forgery detection, focusing on signatures, and explores how the characteristics of different templates affect the performance of detection systems when employed as training data. By utilizing an extensive dataset of 10,000 genuine and forged signature templates, this research investigates the impact of distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability of these templates on the accuracy of state-of-the-art deep learning-based forgery detection models. The findings reveal that templates exhibiting low distinctiveness, complexity, or repeatability from genuine signatures can be effectively detected by these models, while templates showing high levels in these aspects often go undetected. This phenomenon is observed across multiple state-of-the-art deep learning-based forgery detection models. This research further suggests improving the diversity of genuine templates and introducing random variations to diminish the likelihood of templates exhibiting low distinctiveness, complexity, or repeatability. The outcomes of this study can serve as a guideline for template design, and the proposed approach of introducing random variations can be used to enhance the robustness of forgery detection systems against manipulations involving similar-looking genuine templates. NLP's rapid progress has garnered significant interest from governments, organizations, and industries, highlighting the importance of MLCs (Multilingual Countries) in the global NLP landscape. Home to multiple languages, these countries benefit from NLP innovations, particularly in resource constraints. This paper outlines the ongoing research in Lebanese Arabic, addressing key issues such as data availability, tool limitations, and limited community engagement. It also delves into machine translation difficulties and proposes solutions, including proposed features for the Arabic-Arabic translation task. Additionally, we explore opportunities and challenges in three key areas: natural language understanding, information access, and human-computer interaction. This survey provides an in-depth analysis of the current state of Lebanese Arabic research, its applications, and future prospects, identifying areas for community engagement and development. It also shares personal experiences and suggests future directions for researchers and practitioners to ensure the continued growth of Lebanese Arabic NLP. This work is a testament to the enduring legacy of Elie Khamara's contributions to the NLP community in Lebanon. \\

Maintaining the privacy of sensitive graphs, including those composed of image nodes, is crucial in various applications. The Graph Privacy Advisor (GPA) is an essential tool for preserving this privacy, as it allows users to assess the privacy risk of input graphs and provide precise classifications of the privacy they encompass. Traditional graph models, used by GPA, rely on simplified representations of graphs, which omit intricate subgraphs. However, these models can lead to inaccurate risk assessments and privacy classifications in complex graphs. To address this limitation, we present GPA$^{\mathcal{P}}$, an enhanced version of GPA that incorporates advanced graph models capable of detecting intricate subgraphs. To support GPA$^{\mathcal{P}}$, we introduce two novel graph models: one for attributed graphs and another for colored graphs. Experimental results show that GPA$^{\mathcal{P}}$ outperforms GPA in both accuracy and computational efficiency, particularly in detecting complex subgraphs. Additionally, GPA$^{\mathcal{P}}$ achieves higher precision in privacy classifications, as evidenced by our evaluation using 47 image graphs. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of GPA$^{\mathcal{P}}$ in identifying sensitive nodes within these graphs. Further analysis reveals potential explanations for the privacy classifications provided by GPA$^{\mathcal{P}}$. Overall, GPA$^{\mathcal{P}}$ represents an advanced and versatile tool for privacy risk assessment and classification in diverse graph models. We anticipate GPA$^{\mathcal{P}}$ to serve as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners in working with complex graphs. Researchers of collaborative work have thoroughly examined shared document management within co-location settings, yet the equivalent phenomenon in computer-supported collaborative environments remains understudied. Our research aims to fill this knowledge gap by focusing on maintenance practices of shared files within collaborative software development projects. In contrast to documented theories on collaborative work, our findings reveal that file management is characterized by disorder, duplication, and redundancy. Our analysis shows that while individuals poorly maintain files, the collective effort leads to consistent sharing and maintenance practices across projects. Our results highlight the need for further investigation into the daily routines of software developers and the importance of understanding the social aspects of collaborative work within the computing field. Based on these findings, we have developed the concept of'shared workspaces' to describe features of collaborative tools that support the organization of shared files and promote awareness among team members. Binary star systems in the northern hemisphere have been observed using data collected by the Wide-field Binary Archive, constructed from observations taken between 1999 and 2016 by various wide-field cameras. Notably, the system BD And appears to behave erratically, displaying significant and unpredictable changes in brightness every 73.6 days. Analysis of photometry and spectroscopy data suggests that this variability is likely caused by a binary system consisting of two stars with masses of approximately 0.24 and 0.13 solar masses, orbiting each other. However, anomalies in observations and periodic changes in the system's brightness lead us to speculate that a third component may exist in the system. Further study is required to confirm our findings and understand the system's behavior. We develop an obstruction theory for symplectic sheaves to map to a given symplectic vector bundle, resulting in a rational relationship. This theory ultimately leads to defining and characterizing albanese maps for symplectic sheaves as well as albanese varieties for smooth projective symplectic manifolds. Additionally, our work connects this concept to the minimal model of a symplectic vector bundle, allowing for the calculation of the albanese map for certain Witten type differential equations. Lastly, our method is used to compute the albanese map for certain known examples and we find a new class of symplectic bundles admitting albanese maps that were not previously known. Our work also yields a new family of Witten type differential equations with albanese maps. Our methods are general enough to be applied to other categories of geometric structures by analogy. Finally, our work concludes by proposing new research questions in the field. \end{abstract}

We employ generating functions to explore the properties of integer partitions that have specific constraints on the multiplicity of their constituent parts. This approach allows us to incorporate combination sums that reflect the applicable range of each part's multiplicity. By analyzing a general formula for these partitions, we identify conditions under which the resulting sequences comprise distinct, ascending numbers. Additionally, we investigate how to derive smaller, related sequences defined by taking only the minimal terms from the partition sets. Our discussion is enhanced through several illustrative examples. Ultimately, we present a general strategy for obtaining both ascending and descending sequences based on a given combination series. This strategy involves finding the initial terms of the partition sets defined by the series' leading terms. This strategy is applicable as long as the series' terms decrease monotonically, which can be confirmed by analyzing the degree of the generating function corresponding to the series' leading term. This confirmed monotonically decreasing property allows us to extract the ascending partition sets directly. Furthermore, we establish a useful generalization of the inclusion-exclusion principle for multiset partitions, which takes into account the multiplicity constraints. This theorem can be used to derive various combination series with specified multiplicity patterns. We illustrate the efficacy of this theorem through several non-trivial demonstration examples. This formula enables the calculation of the maximum term in such a series, provided that its terms decrease monotonically, as confirmed by analyzing the degree of the generating function corresponding to its initial term. This confirmed monotonically decreasing property allows us to extract the descending partition sets directly. To effectively learn from its surroundings, a robot must utilize statistical information available in its environment through sensory inputs. Unfortunately, common approaches to learning place the entire burden on the learning algorithm, disregarding the statistical properties of its environment. We present a hierarchical Bayesian model that addresses issues with existing methods by incorporating a probabilistic representation of the environment. Our approach demonstrates improved results in a simulation exploring causal relationships. The model is also tested in a real-world robotic experiment where a mobile robot collects and processes data from its surroundings. The benefits of our approach are particularly relevant in complex, real-world applications involving large numbers of variables. Our model is efficiently applied to the robot by limiting its focus to relevant sensory inputs, significantly reducing computational requirements. Comprehensive empirical evaluations confirm the superior performance of our approach over existing methods in a range of scenarios. The accompanying code is available at https://osrf.github.io/blog/hierarchical-bayesian-robot-learning/.

This paper explores a novel control approach, combining optimal control theory with deep reinforcement learning. It reimagines the motion planning stage in hierarchical control systems, treating it as a finite action problem grounded in a dynamic system model, as opposed to the typical approach of discretizing state space. This perspective empowers the development of streamlined algorithms, capable of efficiently handling complex high-dimensional systems, even when state space is discretized. Furthermore, our method is showcased in a simulation application, achieving outcomes comparable to state-of-the-art methods. However, the primary advantage of this approach lies in its potential to automate the motion planning stage, enabling real-time adaptation and online adjustments. In essence, the algorithm learns a policy to apply the controller, thus automating the motion planning process. In traditional reinforcement learning, the policy and controller are typically intertwined, but in our formulation, the controller is grounded in an optimal solution, thereby enhancing the algorithm's performance, robustness, and ease of interpretation. This reformulation also opens the door for future advancements, such as the integration of optimal control and machine learning techniques. In particular, our work highlights the benefits of hierarchical control structures, illustrating how the motion planning stage can be optimized through the strategic allocation of control variables. This insight could inspire new innovative methods in motion planning, facilitating the incorporation of optimal control elements into deep reinforcement learning algorithms. Deep neural networks have become the go-to tool for solving complex classification tasks. Despite their effectiveness, they often fail to account for prediction uncertainties, which hinders their ability to handle uncertain inputs and produce robust results. This research combines the benefits of deep neural networks and Bayesian inference to develop a framework for uncertainty quantification. By incorporating Monte Carlo sampling into deep neural networks, we generate multiple function evaluations and create a Bayesian posterior distribution. This approach facilitates the production of confidence-interval bounded classification results. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in generating accurate prediction intervals and classifies unknown inputs with enhanced robustness. We evaluate the method's efficacy on image classification, relying on pre-trained networks, and demonstrate its applicability in medical image analysis, specifically on TomoTools - an open-source computer vision library. Our method's code is also available for replication purposes. In terms of future work, we propose potential modifications to the method, including the utilization of variational inference to accelerate computation and the incorporation of generative adversarial networks to generate realistic, high-resolution images. In addition, we outline potential applications of predictive uncertainty to quantitative imaging in the medical sector. In particular, we explore its potential for estimating mitral valve area from cardiac MRI scans. Unstructured material data forces researchers to invest significant time and resources in identifying relevant patterns, preventing precise predictions of phase formations, mechanical properties, and other critical properties. Graph neural networks excel at creating informative, structured representations of relationships within data, which we capitalize on by utilizing them as a means of incurring an informed regularization on the parameters of a neural network, thereby preventing overfitting while preserving the ability to make the most of the unique characteristics of each data point. By combining the geometrically-inspired approach of subspace learning with the powerful, geometrical representations produced by GNNs, it's possible to train a subspace learning model that's both precise and generalizes well to unseen data. We showcase the effectiveness of our approach by using it to develop a number of accurate, transferable subspace learning models. Typically, the DGLAP evolution process is treated as a multiplicative effect, where PDFs at a higher scale are calculated by iteratively applying the kernels to the PDFs at lower scales, corresponding to different renormalization group steps. However, this approach can lead to numerical instabilities when dealing with a large number of scales. To overcome this limitation, we propose an alternative method based on integrating the DGLAP equations directly, allowing for the determination of PDFs at multiple scales with a single evolution process. This approach can be combined with conventional methods, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by analyzing the NNPDF38_TADPDF and NNPDF39_TADPDF PDF sets. We present a method to control the frequency spacing of optical microcomb generators by modulating a pump laser with tailored multi-fringe interference patterns. By creating pump-sidebands at specific intervals, we generate microcombs with frequencies that are multiples of a chosen integer multiple of the inter-sideband spacing. To achieve this control, we utilize electro-optic modulators to generate complex modulation patterns, which can be optimized for different applications by adjusting the fringe phases and the number of visible fringes. Implementing this approach reduces the complexity of microcomb scheduling and enables simultaneous multi-channel connectivity, which is highly desirable in advanced photonic systems. Our technique is demonstrated by generating a microcomb with frequencies that are integer multiples of 50 GHz, which is applicable in modern optical communication systems. Furthermore, we showcase the potential of this method by simultaneously producing two sets of microcombs with frequency spacings of 300 GHz and 12.5 GHz, which is a combination suitable for 5G wireless communication uplink channel characterization. Our research offers a valuable direction for the development of controlled and versatile optical microcomb-based generators.

By analyzing the quasi NNT (neural tangent kernel) matrix, the research shows that it satisfies the four conditions required for Taylor approximation, and thus maps to a smooth manifold. In this article, we suggest a method to determine a boundary entropy for a subset of boundaries in a quantum system following a global tensor network implementation. The article primarily focuses on holographic dualities, in which the boundary entropy is typically represented as an entropy contribution from the bulk. By employing this approach, we derive a condition under which the boundary entropy can exceed the bulk entropies individually as required by monogamy of mutual information. Furthermore, our article examines the properties of this boundary entropy and its relationship to changes in the system's state and its dual bulk entropy. Additionally, we use our approach to establish a boundary entropy for specific boundaries in the $T\bar{T}$-model and to investigate the effects of altering the $T\bar{T}$-current on this entropy. Our analysis also reveals that the boundary entropy can be decomposed into contributions from simpler systems, in a manner analogous to the decomposition of a full system into simpler components in specific scenarios such as tensor product partitions or entanglement spectra calculations. This decomposition enables a range of applications, including the use of entropy to diagnose fine grained ergodicity and to determine the Planckian spectral density at the boundaries of 2D systems. In the specific case of $T\bar{T}$-model, we use our approach to determine the ergodicity of not only the entire system but also its boundaries, finding that the conditions for ergodicity have distinct requirements for the system as a whole and its boundaries. Furthermore, our method allows us to investigate the effects of altering the $T\bar{T}$-current on ergodicity at the boundaries of $T\bar{T}$-model. Lastly, our articles establishes a connection between the holographic duality and dual bulk entropy, in which the boundary entropy is equivalent to contributions from the bulk entropy as required by the holographic duality. In the specific case of the $T\bar{T}$-model, our method allows us to investigate the effects of altering the $T\bar{T}$-current on the boundary entropy and its dual bulk entropy. In addition to these applications, our method has the ability to determine entropy contributions from the boundaries in quantum systems in a general manner. In conclusion, our method provides insight into various aspects of quantum systems, including monogamy of mutual information, ergodicity, partition sums calculations, fine grained ergodicity diagnosis, and holographic duality, in a range of contexts such as $T\bar{T}$-model. By leveraging model-based optimization and mutual coherence measurements, we develop a framework to analyze the effectiveness of these methods, which we apply to multiple instances with varying data sizes, stabilization ratios, and noise levels. Moreover, we identify a finite information rate limit imposed by the stabilization processes, whose knowledge enables us to optimize algorithm design for sparse recovery in various scenarios. Our analysis further sheds light on the influence of hyperparameters, and facilitates the creation of more efficient algorithm designs. Moreover, our theoretical findings are substantiated by extensive numerical simulations, which validate our analytical predictions and provide additional insights into algorithm behavior. Additionally, we examine how our analysis can be adapted to tackle more complex problems, such as recovering sparse matrices and non-sparse vectors, and explore their potential applications in practical problem-solving environments. Based on our analysis, we propose a novel stabilization method, which we subsequently evaluate in terms of its computational efficiency, stability, and ability to approach the theoretical limit on the information rate. Our study ultimately presents an optimized approach to designing algorithmic tools for recovering sparse vectors, as well as other structured vectors and matrices, which can be utilized in various applications involving sparse recovery, including compressed sensing, magnetic resonance imaging, and vector localization. Advanced nonlinear coaddition techniques like median and clipped-mean eliminate the influence of outliers, removing the impact of transient image distortions. However, these algorithms can also introduce biases, particularly by exacerbating low signal-to-noise scenarios. In our analysis, these biases manifest as a nonlinearly changing point-spread function (PSF) for stars. Using simulated data, we investigated the effect of different algorithms on PSF shape and magnitude across varying signal-to-noise ratios. The results indicate that both median and clipped-mean coadditions yield stars with deviating PSF profiles and altered magnitudes compared to nominal values. To mitigate these issues, we suggest using a clipped-weighted mean algorithm as an alternative nonlinear coaddition method. This approach involves rejecting data points exceeding 3σ from the mean, and then coadding the remaining data using weights proportional to the inverse variance. The CWMA algorithm effectively removes outliers, and our calculations indicate that it yields CWMA profiles that closely resemble the PSF of individual images. Furthermore, CWMA algorithms with rejection thresholds other than 3σ can also be optimized to fit specific scientific requirements. We also found that these algorithms maintain a consistent PSF for CWMA stars across various signal-to-noise ratios. Additionally, a parameter characterizing the CWMA algorithm's robustness allows us to accurately select the most suitable threshold for our data, and effectively removes transient distortions. To verify the behavior of a quantum circuit, researchers use quantum error correction techniques, which ensure that the output of a faulty circuit remains close to the ideal output. Currently, the most efficient approach involves using a magic state based protocol that relies on advanced quantum computers to prepare a specific quantum state (magic state). However, this protocol has a limitation: it assumes that the quantum circuit under test can be duplicated. For cases where duplication is not possible, a different protocol called the randomized non-interactive zero-knowledge proof (RNI-ZK) protocol has been developed, which does not require the circuit to be duplicated. Although the RNI-ZK protocol has a higher overhead compared to the magic state based protocol in traditional quantum computing settings, we explore an alternative implementation using continuous-variable quantum computing (CVQC). By leveraging Gaussian cluster states and linear optical quantum computations, we develop a new protocol (CVQC protocol) that enables circuit verification without duplicating the circuit. Additionally, our CVQC protocol enhances the efficiency of the RNI-ZK proof by at least an order of magnitude over its equivalent protocol in the linear optical computing regime, making it a more practical solution. Furthermore, our CVQC protocol also outperforms the magic state based protocol in terms of verification speed since it does not rely on fault-tolerant preparation of a magic state. Finally, our CVQC protocol also offers faster runtime compared to the standard RNI-ZK proof while still maintaining its efficiency advantages. Reinforcement learning has made significant progress in creating policies that adapt to tasks with diverse features. Nevertheless, existing research often assumes a stable environment, where object properties persist throughout training. In contrast, our study indicates that geometric tasks are more likely to succeed when the persistence of features is high. To build upon this discovery, we propose a straightforward approach to modify the persistency of state and action values in off-policy algorithms like SARSA and Expected SARSA. Our empirical evaluations on basic reinforcement learning benchmarks verify the effectiveness of our method, as tasks with persistent features yielded up to a 210% improvement in performance compared to algorithms lacking this modification. Our approach also demonstrated versatility by successfully applying geometric persistence to a 3D navigation task, where a significant performance boost of 53% was achieved. Data augmentation has been effectively used to enhance image classification, but its potential benefits for sound-based classification techniques have yet to be thoroughly explored. A method to create artificially varied sound effects could significantly expand training datasets, potentially leading to improved accuracy in identifying isolated sounds or detecting specific auditory patterns. In the case of overfitting, increasing the model's parameters through data augmentation might be a viable solution. Although data augmentation is often used with continuous sound effects, it is less commonly applied to music tracks. Given the abundance of music available online, there is considerable potential for reducing overfitting by generating musical variations through data augmentation. However, effectively utilizing data augmentation in both sound effect and music classification tasks requires a clear understanding of what constitutes a suitable variation. In order to address this uncertainty, the proposed approach uses generative pre-trained models such as VAEs and ADAs to create sound effect and music variations that align with the labels of the base track. The effectiveness of this method in reducing overfitting and improving accuracy was tested using the DCASE 2019 dataset for sound effect classification and the Million Song Dataset for music classification tasks. Results indicate that data augmentation can improve the average precision in sound effect classification by 8.3% and increase the number of accurately classified genres in the music classification task by 10%. These findings demonstrate the efficacy of the data augmentation method for reducing overfitting and improving model performance. The implementation of this method is available through the open-source repository https://github.com/mdaugskl. Additionally, the project presents an alternative approach to data augmentation that uses generative models trained on unlabelled data to enhance labelled classification tasks. This method is illustrated through its application to audio classification tasks but can be applied more broadly across different domains. In order to quantify the quality of generated samples, the performance of the model when classifying these samples is monitored, allowing for adjustments to the data augmentation process to prioritize high-quality samples. The effectiveness of this method was tested using the Million Song Dataset and found to increase the number of accurately classified genres by 13% and reduce the loss in the validation set by 35%. These findings suggest that data augmentation can be an effective technique for reducing overfitting and improving model performance in sound-based classification tasks. The open-source repository https://github.com/mdaugskl provides the implementation of this method. In addition to its application in audio classification, the data augmentation approach presented can be applied to other visual domains where pre-trained models are available. A novel production channel for heavy black holes, called the collapse of a non-rotating cloud, suggests that its fragmentation pattern could serve as a benchmark to evaluate various heavy black hole formation theories. Based on this analysis, we discover that the fragment mass spectrum of heavy black holes produced through this new pathway significantly varies at lower mass endpoints and displays two distinct distribution patterns, distinct from light seeding scenarios, below $10^{5-6}$ solar masses. Notably, our research indicates that the mass at which the fragment distribution transitions shifts towards heavier masses in the new HS-HBS scenario. Consequently, a parameter fit representing the mass at which the fragment distribution transitions in the standard HS-HBS scenario may not accurately reflect other heavy black hole production mechanisms, necessitating separate analysis. At the same time, our research suggests that the collapse of a non-rotating cloud can facilitate a comprehensive understanding of heavy black hole mass spectra. Ultimately, our findings emphasize the necessity of thorough statistical analysis to ensure accurate inference of heavy black hole formation theories. High-precision line velocity data is essential for studying wide binary star systems and their association with the dark matter halo. Current techniques for measuring velocity dispersion rely on the assumption of uniform velocity distribution across the system, but this is not the case here as sources of error include both proper motion scattering and genuine velocity gradients. By using line velocities and proper motions, we have revised the standard formula for calculating velocity dispersion and tested it on data from 20 systems. The results indicate that using line velocities and proper motions significantly improves the accuracy of velocity dispersion measurements by up to a factor of two, depending on the system's orientation and shape. The new formula also detects velocity gradients in systems that were previously thought to have uniform velocities. Therefore, line velocities and proper motions are essential for a thorough understanding of wide binary star systems and their association with the dark matter halo. Based on these findings, we recommend using line velocities and proper motions to study the dynamics of all stars with sufficient data, including those outside binary systems. Furthermore, we have developed a network of 20 wide binary systems with available data for use as pseudo-observers in dark matter halo simulations, helping to inform future cosmological simulations and analyses. The new revised formula for calculating velocity dispersion is essential for studying the dynamics of wide binary systems and their association with the dark matter halo, and it paves the way for using line velocities and proper motions to study the dynamics of all stars more accurately. Additionally, we have developed a list of 20 wide binary systems that can be used as pseudo-observers in dark matter halo simulations, which will be useful for informing future cosmological simulations and analyses. In multiplicative linear logic, ideal representations preserve the logical meaning of proof networks by linking subproofs with their contextual implications.  Specifically, an ideal representation consists of a collection of subsets in a model that adhere to certain conditions, enabling a direct correlation between the structure of these subsets and the structure of proof nets.  The present research proposes a framework for generating ideal representations automatically in any model that has a proof structure, provided it satisfies a fundamental property called cut-eliminability.  The defined framework relies on a specific relationship between the structure of proof nets and their associated proof trees.  As a result, this framework can be utilized to develop algorithms for identifying ideal structures, which can validate cut-elimination results in specific models, such as in the model of typed $\lambda$-calculus.  Moreover, the research analyzes the relationship between ideal structures and the underlying models they represent, asking questions like what model can be derived from an ideal structure and under what conditions does this ideal structure represent the original model.  The study specifically examines this relationship in the context of multiplicative linear logic and its translation into a programming language called PCF, investigating how ideal structures can be used to derive a model of strongly normalizing terms in the $\lambda$-calculus with a limited set of reduction rules.  The thesis concludes by proposing a modified notion of ideal structure that is consistent with the structure of full cut-free proof nets in multiplicative linear logic.  The research demonstrates that each model corresponding to a full cut-free proof net is strongly normalizing with a limited set of reduction rules, confirming a specific theorem known as the fundamental theorem of proof-net.  Further research examines the general applicability of the concepts developed in this study, particularly in the context of other structured proof systems, and explores the relationship between the structure of proof nets and their associated proof trees, leading to the identification of a new notion of consistency based on the structure of proof nets.  The study specifically applies this new notion of consistency to several systems that have a structured proof structure, including the full cut-free sequent calculus for multiplicative linear logic and an extended version of the $\lambda$-calculus called the λI-calculus, demonstrating its applicability in these systems by showing that it matches the existing definition of strong normalization in these systems.  Finally, the research investigates when the structure of proof nets can be used to derive a model, particularly in the context of a system that has a limited set of reduction rules, by examining two key categories of proof nets

Recent research has demonstrated the capacity of deep learning models to learn patterns
in time series data, ultimately enabling the prediction of synchronization states between
time series. In this study, we examine the performance of a deep learning model designed
to forecast the synchronization state of cryptocurrency pairs, utilizing the time series properties
of these pairs. By leveraging inherent characteristics of cryptocurrency time series, such as
price and trading volume, our model aims to determine whether pairs of cryptocurrencies,
such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, are synchronized. Results indicate that our model can
accurately identify synchronized cryptocurrency pairs while also detecting important
differences between synchronized and synchronized pairs. Moreover, the robustness of
our model is validated by testing its performance on various model parameters, such
as the length of time series segments, which affects the model's predictive capabilities. 
Ultimately, the efficacy of our model suggests the potential for applying deep learning
models in synchronization forecasting and stock market analysis more broadly. 
Keywords: Synchronization forecasting, deep learning models, cryptocurrency pairs, 
time series analysis, cryptocurrency markets.

The primary goal of click-through rate prediction in online advertising is to estimate the likelihood of ad clicks by mapping user behavior to ad characteristics. Recently, incorporating visual IDs, which include ad images and candidate targets, in CTR prediction has become increasingly vital. This is because images convey essential information about ad content and can reflect the similarity or difference between ads and potential targets. However, processing image information in CTR prediction models is complicated due to the high dimensionalality of image data. This difficulty can be addressed by employing Neural Networks. This research investigates the benefits of incorporating visual IDs into CTR prediction models by analyzing the effect of multi-modal input on model performance. The findings show that models incorporating visual IDs outperform those using text-based inputs alone. Moreover, the performance gap between these models diminishes as the number of training samples increases. This study also examines the multi-modal embedding space of the successful models and reveals interesting insights into ad content. Finally, the research applies a parameter tuning strategy to further improve the AUC score of the CTR models. The results show that fine-tuning models with a focus on visual modalities can be an effective approach to obtaining better CTR predictions. This strategy is particularly beneficial when there is an abundance of images but few text descriptions in the training data. Overall, the research suggests that incorporating visual IDs into CTR prediction models is a beneficial approach to achieving improved performance. Additionally, the research provides new understandings of ad image processing in CTR prediction, paving the way for future research in this area to utilize deep learning techniques to process visual information. Mobile app data, specifically location information, is increasingly used for public health research, yielding valuable insights when handled appropriately. Nevertheless, protecting users' privacy remains a pressing concern, as releasing location data without adequate safeguards can lead to unintended exposure. Current approaches rely on synthetic data, created through transformation techniques, to safeguard privacy, but these methods are inefficient for conditional data sets. To address this gap, we propose a novel framework, Privacy-Oriented Synthetic Data Framework (POSDF), designed to produce high-quality synthetic data, safeguarding users' privacy in the process. By integrating the Privacy-Focused Gaussian Mixture Model (PF-GMM) and a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm, POSDF generates realistic data distributions while minimizing privacy losses, even in the presence of interdependent data. We evaluate POSDF's efficacy using real-world location data, demonstrating its capacity to produce superior synthetic data, safeguarded by a robust privacy mechanism, thereby addressing the inherent limitations of synthetic data methods. POSDF's versatility enables it to accommodate various data types, making it an adaptable solution for location-based service providers seeking to integrate data privacy. We conduct an empirical analysis of POSDF, comparing it to existing synthetic data approaches, and showcasing its potential in public health research, as evidenced by our evaluation of geo-location data. We also highlight potential future directions for POSDF, encompassing applications in location-based services, such as traffic forecasting and urban planning. You can access the code for POSDF at https://github.com/alexandrow/POSDF.

This study explores the impact of inter-site variability on functional brain networks and individual or group differences. Using resting-state fMRI data and corresponding functional magnetic resonance imaging data from the Human Connectome Project, we analyzed brain networks interlinked with functional sites. Our findings reveal that inter-site variability significantly influences brain network reliability and individual or group differences are largely caused by variations between sites rather than within sites. By taking site into account, we can improve the accuracy of detecting individual or group differences. Additionally, our results suggest that inter-site effects are mainly concentrated in the default mode network and associated with specific genetic variants. This study highlights the importance of considering inter-site variability in brain imaging studies and provides new insights into the relationship between brain regions. Our method can also be applied to other imaging datasets to better understand inter-site variability. Additionally, our results show that combining site information can improve the classification of individuals or groups. Based on this, we propose a new pipeline for investigating brain networks related to functional sites. Our code is available at https://github.com/ling0533/RSN_reliability. This paper investigates the connection between heat flow and concentration of measure inequalities. It particularly examines the long-term behavior of heat flow and concentration of measure in groups under random walks or group actions. To this end, the paper introduces a generalized heat flow for groups and proves associated concentration of measure inequalities, including specific results for Cayley graphs derived from graphs with optimal doubling properties or Ramanujan graphs. Additionally, the paper contains an application of its theoretical findings to the group of matrices over the field of 2, specifically identifying the critical threshold for the convergence of its random walks to a concentrated set. This critical threshold is found to be the matrix rank threshold. Furthermore, the paper establishes the critical threshold for the convergence of random walks in groups of matrices. These random walks are shown to converge under the condition that the average generator matrix has a higher rank than the dimension of the group. These findings are also extended to the context of tensor product graphs. The study of heat flow and concentration of measure on groups allows for the exploration of various parameters such as group homomorphisms, group actions, and group size, which provides additional insights and generalizes existing concentration of measure inequalities to group settings, thereby discovering new concentration of measure inequalities in groups. One such generalization concerns the concentration of measure in groups with optimal doubling properties, yielding a more refined inequality. Lastly, the study establishes a connection between the heat flow and concentration of measure on groups and the group's diameter, bringing new perspectives to existing group diameter studies. To summarize, the paper presents new generalized concentration of measure inequalities for groups, offers fresh insights into group theory, and provides novel applications of its theoretical findings to group analysis. Previous approaches to code-mixture have concentrated on bilingual data,
overlooking the positional relationships between words. Our proposed model,
SubWord Positional Encoding Model (SPEM), addresses this limitation by
leveraging subword information and positional relationships to enhance neural
machine translation of code-mixed text. The model's subword encoding captures
morphological characteristics, while the positional encoding tabulates word
occurrences in training data. Our experiments demonstrate that SPEM outperforms
the baseline models, including fastText and a state-of-the-art model using
bilinear attention. Furthermore, we validate SPEM's effectiveness across
different code-mixture scenarios. Additionally, we abide by standard best
practices in neural machine translation by releasing our model and data
preprocessing tools. Our model and data resources are available for download
at https://github.com/infocomp/spem. Our database of code-mixed sentences in
Catalan--Spanish is also available at https://cvc.uab.es/sentences-for-speech.

H$_{3}$S is considered a prime material for studying superconductivity under high pressure due to its exceptionally high transition temperatures. In this study, we examine how the nuclear quadrupole interaction influences the emergence of superconductivity in H$_{3}$S using the linearized Microscopic Theory of Superconductivity. Our analysis reveals that the isotopic component of the superconductivity parameter ($\gamma$) can be broken down into nuclear and cellular contributions, both of which align with experimental findings under low-pressure conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the nuclear quadrupole interaction plays a pivotal role in enhancing the transition from tetrahedral to orthorhombic structures, thereby indicating a complex interrelation between the cellular contribution and structural changes in H$_{3}$S. In contrast, the nuclear contribution remains relatively unaffected by changes in cell volume. We also identify that the cellular contribution exhibits a non-trivial correlation with pressure, explaining the initially slower evolution of superconductivity under high pressure in H$__{3}$S and accounting for the discrepancy between experimental and calculated values of the isotope effect coefficient at low pressures. We propose that the cellular contribution be taken into account when interpreting the isotope effect coefficient under high pressure to ensure accuracy and precision. In addition, our theoretical framework can be applied to studying superconductivity in other hydrides under high pressure, with the orthohombic H$_{3}$S being an optimal case study due to its technological significance and the complex interplay of its physical properties. We therefore recommend that the theoretical model presented here be incorporated into future experimental studies of the isotope effect coefficient under high pressure to facilitate a more comprehensive comprehension of superconducting materials. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the nuclear quadrupole interaction has an essentially negligible effect on the transition temperature of the superconducting phase transition. We therefore propose that the nuclear quadrupole interaction be incorporated into the theoretical model, with the ratio of cellular contributions ($\gamma_{orth}$/$\gamma_{tet}$) providing a definitive indicator of the structural transition under high pressure in H$__{3}$S. We also identify potential avenues for future research, including incorporating the effects of phonon-electron coupling and trihydrogen vibrations on superconductivity, and using ab initio calculations to generate the electronic structure of H$_{3}$S, as well as performing experiments to measure the differential thermal conductivity to verify our theoretical predictions. In evolutionary studies of quantitative traits, researchers often analyze how the average effect of gene substitutions changes over time and its implications on evolutionary processes. However,, existing methods lack transparency, making it difficult for biologists to interpret the results in their context. Furthermore, previous analyses only considered small gene substitutions and their impact on population evolution. To address these limitations, a new approach is developed using a Fourier representation. This new framework allows researchers to study the behavior of large gene substitutions and their cumulative impact across multiple generations. By applying this framework to a well-studied model, a classic model, and simulation data, researchers confirmed that large gene substitutions ultimately converge to the small effect predictions. Furthermore, Fourier-based results match the predictions of the classic model, demonstrating the approach's validity. To facilitate the use of this approach by evolutionary biologists, a user-friendly Python package is created, including a Python function to calculate the average effect of large gene substitutions. This package is now freely available for download. Previous research demonstrates that image features derived from local patterns can be effectively learned for camera relocalization tasks. These features, capable of withstanding image transformations, can quickly identify matching patterns across different images, even under moderate distortions. Nonetheless, their efficiency may be compromised in highly complex scenarios, such as severely warped images. To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces a novel technique involving the combination of low-level features and high-level descriptors. By utilizing Learnable Descriptors for Relocalization Assistance (LeDA), even the most challenging image configurations become manageable. LeDA's versatile design facilitates integration with a wide range of image features and localizers, as evidenced by its implementation with two feature types. Experimental results reveal that the incorporation of LeDA boosts performance by at least 5% and often by as much as 20% in difficult scenarios, while also offering improved robustness to severe image distortions. In federated learning, a decentralized machine learning approach, a central server guides multiple clients in developing a distributed model.  The clients, however, have limited labeled data, making the semi-supervised learning process challenging without supplemental data.  We've developed a new personalizable semi-supervised learning approach to enhance model development on clients with limited labeled data.  Our approach assigns a central server the task of providing personalized guidance to each client based on its unique needs.  The server identifies distinct learning rates for each client and adjusts their model accordingly, effectively acting as an expert with comprehensive knowledge.  The clients then learn from the server and update their models based on the received guidance.  The result is that the clients with limited labeled data can develop more accurate models more quickly.  We've tested our approach, referred to as FedSSL, in both federated supervised learning and semi-supervised learning scenarios and found it to be superior to traditional federated learning methods.  Our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in federated learning experiments, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data.  The source code for FedSSL is available at https://github.com/Chen-Hsiao/fed_ssl.  The performance results can be found at https://hksi.github.io/publication/FedSSL. Fahrenheit temperature scale is used in this presentation.  Evaluation was conducted on well-known datasets including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, FashionMNIST, and MNIST with various network architectures and found that FedSSL consistently delivers accurate results.  We've verified the stability and reliability of FedSSL through multiple tests and found it to be a trustworthy solution for personalizable semi-supervised learning.  The key advantages of our approach are its ability to provide personalized guidance, its generalizability across scenarios, and its performance superiority compared to current techniques.  The main challenge in implementing our approach is the potential for communication disruptions during the federated learning process, which affects the stability of the algorithm.  We recommend using the personalized semi-supervised learning approach in decentralized projects due to its strong performance and reliability.  The main limitation of our approach is its susceptibility to communication disruptions, which affects its overall effectiveness.  We plan to investigate new techniques for handling communication disruptions in future research. In the event of a neutron star merger, a significant disparity arises in the
initial mass accretor due to the conservation of angular momentum, causing the
magnetic field to amplify catastrophically. We developed a 2D general
relativistic magnetohydrodynamic model to simulate the evolution of the
accretion disk following the merger, featuring a comprehensive beta force
implementation that accurately balances magnetic and gas pressure. Our results
reveal the generation of fast magnetosonic waves that propagate out of the
disk, leading to a substantial magnetization of the surrounding circumpular
envelope. This process causes a disk relaxation phase of hundreds of seconds,
following an initial turbulent activity phase, and leads to a significantly
stronger magnetic field in the central regions of the disk. The consequences
of this merger are far-reaching, affecting the behavior of the disk in profound
ways and potentially influencing the properties of the post-merger system. 
Our findings also imply the production of intense electromagnetic flares 
in the context of compact binary mergers.

Conditions for a Markov process to reach a unique quasi-stationary equilibrium and achieve exponential convergence are established. These conditions are more relaxed than those required for ergodicity and are applicable even in cases where ergodic behavior is not present. Two examples illustrate the variety of situations where these criteria and outcomes can be observed. Furthermore, it is shown that unique quasi-stationary distributions are inherently isolated from the rest of the support in a Markov process, and the communication closure of its recurrent components is empty. Additionally, it is proven that exponential convergence to a unique quasi-stationary equilibrium can be achieved by contracting processes or those with a contracting core. This research offers an innovative approach to studying ergodic behavior and provides a framework for understanding dynamics of Markov processes undergoing changes. It also has implications for modeling population dynamics and studying processes on graphs. However, the primary focus of this work remains on theoretical contributions to ergodic theory, and its potential applications to practical problems are left unexplored. To accelerate robotic operations, we suggest enhancing assembly tasks with a modular, reinforcement-learning-based robotic arm motion planner. This algorithm repeatedly refines its model to achieve faster execution times. Specifically, the algorithm updates its task representation by replacing any action that doesn't contribute to progress in the task. This approach streamlines the robot's movement, eliminating unnecessary steps and reducing overall steps required. Compared to a comparable task planner, our algorithm successfully reduces the number of steps by an average of 28.1%. Additionally, our method excels in scenarios with unexpected interruptions or periodic maintenance, averaging a 33.3% decrease in steps required. This efficient motion planning algorithm is adaptable to a variety of tasks and can be easily scaled up for more complex scenarios. We investigated the stability of synchronized groups within networks of oscillators, where each oscillator represents a political party within a group of parties. By applying the principles of group theory to model these systems, we created a simplified two-dimensional map of system dynamics. This approach allowed us to analyze the conditions under which synchronized groups maintain stability, even in the presence of uncertainties. Our findings reveal that small fluctuations in system parameters can actually enhance the robustness of synchronized groups, rather than disrupting them. This unexpected effect can be understood through the lens of minority politics, where small deviations can lead to increased resistance against large deviations representing opposing ideologies. Our study also identifies the key mechanisms underlying this robustness, which can be generalized to apply to more complex networks of oscillators representing diverse systems. Ultimately, our work provides a new framework for exploring the dynamics of group interactions and the long-lasting trends that emerge from them. We noticed a peculiar pattern where Google's search results for certain terms would include a link to YouTube, even though the query didn't contain any keywords indicating YouTube content. To better understand this behavior, we decided to investigate this trend in this paper. Our findings show that Google's search results incorporating YouTube links follow a consistent pattern, depending on the number of keywords in the query. This study's analysis sheds light on the general behavior of $\beta$-function in theories with monodromy defects and their implications for defect-based studies of the IR fixed points of conformal field theories. In the spread mode, Ortiz's 1991 protocol maintains consistency across the network, despite delays being less than a certain threshold. In the crush mode, a fixed point is quickly reached, with infinite delays allowed, though actual delay is capped at double the threshold. A specific challenge arises when nodes within the network have varying accuracy in their perceived delay measurements, potentially triggering oscillations in the crush mode. This paper presents a direct method for identifying the fixed point in such a scenario and offers an alternative solution for achieving consensus under uncertain delay conditions by adjusting the threshold. Semi-supervised inductive node classification in graph neural networks is a crucial problem, involving assigning labels to unknown node types based on labeled nodes and their connections. Most existing pseudo-labeling methods have concentrated on assigning labels to unlabeled nodes directly, using the knowledge gained from labeled nodes. However, this can lead to over-reliance on labeled nodes and negatively impact model performance when dealing with complex graphs. To address this issue, we propose a new pseudo-labeling method called Node Uncertainty Reduction (NUR) that focuses on modifying the graph structure to enhance model performance. NUR uses the graph neural network to generate node embeddings and assesses the relationships between nodes, then assigns labels to unlabeled nodes by reducing the model's uncertainty through local changes in the graph structure. This approach can improve model performance and achieve state-of-the-art results on various benchmark datasets, both with and without data augmentation. Our NUR method has been implemented in an open-source repository, accessible at https://github.com/DataToGraph/NUR. Experimental results have shown that NUR surpasses traditional pseudo-labeling methods both with and without data augmentation, and yields superior performance when compared to related self-training and pseudo-labeling techniques. Notably, NUR's performance gains are most pronounced on complex and large graphs. Future research could build upon NUR to develop improved self-training and pseudo-labeling methods, incorporating multiple views and structures into graph neural networks to enhance semi-supervised inductive node classification. Our proposed approach also offers potential applications in graph representation learning and semi-supervised node classification. Our research provides novel insights into the semi-supervised inductive node classification problem and graph representation learning, and opens the door to further research into the self-training and pseudo-labeling strategies. Our work could be extended to investigate the semi-supervised inductive node classification problem from alternative perspectives in the future.
