In the standard treatment of optomechanics, quantum effects are typically described by infinite series, which converge quickly in the optomechanical limit but may not do so otherwise.  Alternative approaches, such as electomechanics, use classical models to accurately simulate quantum behavior, especially when occupation numbers are high.  By applying this method, known as the classical electomechanical model, we can transform the optomechanical system into an entirely classical system, even when it begins as a quantum system.  Our approach effectively eliminates quantum noise.  Additionally, it allows for the elimination of non-Poissonian photonic input, replacing it with classical, Poissonian photonic input, which may facilitate experimental implementation.  Our model has the potential to enhance the detection of quantum behaviors and advance the field of optomechanics.  Our findings are confirmed through experimental application to a membrane-in-the-center setup.  Ultimately, substituting the classical electomechanical model for the standard quantum treatment may yield greater insights into the quantum behavior of optomechanical systems.  Our work also opens the door for the integration of optomechanics within broader quantum simulation projects.  Our model has the potential to facilitate the development of hybrid quantum simulators that incorporate both mechanical and electrical components.  Our study demonstrates that the classical electomechanical model is a feasible, efficient, and accurate approach to simulating quantum behavior in optomechanical systems. Two real Geronimus weights, specifically a generalized sextic Freud weight and a generalized Airy weight, are studied with the aim of identifying a unitary Haar system composed of eigenfunctions associated with these weights. While the generalized Airy weight corresponds to the classical Haar function, the generalized sextic Freud weight requires additional analysis to determine its associated polynomials and a unitary Haar basis. By utilizing a previously proposed method for linear independence of polynomial systems, a unitary Haar system is established on the Fock space $K_{2n}$. Additionally, a unitary Haar basis on the Fock space $K_6$ is found to demonstrate the effectiveness of the method. Furthermore, another unitary Haar basis on the Fock space $K_{2\alpha(\rho+1)}$ for $\alpha > 0$ and $0 < \rho < 2$ is discovered through the application of specialized techniques for $\alpha = 1$ and $\rho = 1$. However, determining unitary Haar bases for other sextic Freud weights remains an open challenge. For the purpose of completeness, an alternative unitary Haar basis on the Fock space $K_6$ is also presented. These findings represent the first known unitary Haar bases associated with generalized sextic Freud weights in the literature. Moreover, a Haar system on the weighted Dirichlet space $L^2_{\rho}(\mathbb{R})$ related to the Jacobi weight $m_{\rho,2}$ is identified for $\rho = -\frac{1}{2}$, along with a Haar system on the weighted Dirichlet space $L^2_{\alpha}(\mathbb{R})$ related to the Jacobi weight $m_{\alpha,2}$ for $\alpha > 0$. By analyzing the impact of the sensor's field of view and distance measurement, we derive mathematical models for the robot's path, identifying the limitations and complications introduced by sensors with narrow or wide perspectives. Our analysis provides insights into the optimal range for sensors' field of view and highlights the challenges at very close or very distant distances. This study aims to stimulate further research into sensor-influenced behavior and encourage the development of better navigation algorithms, as well as more accurate modeling of physical processes. A thorough examination of  B-cation off-centerings in perovskites  has been conducted, with A-site cation and volume factors examined.  Equations predicting off-centering percentages and energy barriers were developed, with both factors influenced by the equilibrium volume and the size of the A cation.  Specifically, off-centering percentages were found to decrease with increasing A cation size and lower equilibrium volume.  In contrast, energy barriers were found to exhibit a more complex behavior, with both factors exhibiting an initial increase before stabilizing at a maximum.  These predictions align well with available data, with some notable exceptions.  Two potential scenarios for the B-cation instability in (Ba$_{1-x}$Ca$_x$)(Ti$_{1-y}$Al$_y$)O$_{3-x}$Cu$_x$ perovskites and the presence of electron holes in BaTiO$_3$ were identified.  Furthermore, it was found that substituting Cu for A cations could activate the B-cation instability, while reducing valences may provide a viable solution.  A theoretical model to quantify the B-cation instability as a function of electron holes was developed, with predictions indicating that even low concentrations of holes can cause significant B-cation off-centerings.  This framework provides a comprehensive understanding of the B-cation instability in ABO$_3$ perovskites and offers a practical approach for managing the B-cation instability through chemical modifications of the A and B sites.  This knowledge can be utilized to investigate the mechanisms of ferroelectric loss and optimize materials properties.  Furthermore, this methodology can be extended to more complex materials such as relaxor ferroelectrics and lead-free materials.  A detailed description of the approach and results is available in a companion paper. enhanced by quantum properties, in a system consisting of two connected optical modes.

amplitude-modulated drive in an optical cavity filled with a Kerr nonlinearity.

of two types of nonlinear media as well as a combination of classical and quantum driving sources 
is explored, showcasing its potential for a wide range of applications in sensing techniques. 
This work has significant implications as it brings us closer to harnessing the power of quantum physics 
to improve our understanding of the physical world. \textbf{Keywords}: two-mode squeezing, quantum sensing, 
optical phase detection, nonlinearity, quantum physics applications.

This study adapts the framework of normalizing flows to create a simulation method for Yang-Mills and $\phi^4$ theories, including both classical and quantum mechanics. To incorporate gauge symmetries, we modify the framework's conditional distributions in a way that guarantees generative flows that are both physically equivalent and minimally violating. This approach ensures that the simulation results for classical and quantum systems align with well-established methods, such as gauge orbit averaging. Furthermore, our method allows for the analysis of magnetic monopole scattering in 2D U(1) gauge theory and the simulation of non-relativistic, complex $\phi$-dynamics with an apparent phase transition as a function of the initial condition. To determine the thermodynamic limit of these simulations, we propose averaging the simulation outcomes based on the maximum entropy principle. This method is applied to the 1D soliton kink solution in the $\phi^4$ theory, resulting in thermodynamic quantities that match theoretical predictions. Our method provides a powerful tool for simulating lattice field theories, offering insights into quantum systems that were previously inaccessible. This research was inspired by the author's undergraduate thesis.  All mathematical code used in this project can be found at https://github.com/UTK-ICST/U1GaugeTheorySimulations. This analysis examines the angular distribution of galaxies in the LoTSS dataset to investigate the likelihood of the ΛCDM cosmological model. By restricting the galaxy sample to 1.5 < z < 2.5 and focusing on specific LoTSS brightness thresholds, we calculate angular two-point clustering statistics for paired galaxies at various separations. Our findings are modeled using the SAM matchmaker tool, incorporating the LoTSS flux uncertainty as a variable. For the brightest galaxies in the sample, our results indicate a possible discrepancy with the ΛCDM model at 2.5σ confidence, with certain higher-order clustering statistics also suggesting deviations. However, the ΛCDM model fits our data well for galaxies near the minimum brightness threshold we considered. Additionally, by accounting for the mass of the central galaxy when analyzing paired galaxies, our analysis suggests that the ΛCDM model provides a good fit to our data with an accuracy of at least 90%. Our analysis indicates that galaxies at 1.5 < z < 2.5 and 1.5 < z < 3.2 are consistent with the predictions of the ΛCDM model, but that galaxies at 3.2 < z < 3.8 may not follow this model as closely. This study's findings could be affected by various biases, with potential sources including how galaxies are selected, the use of flux rather than spectral energy distribution, and inherent limitations of the LoTSS dataset. Possible explanations for the discrepancies observed include that the star-forming galaxies at the focus of this study are not yet fully involved in the formation of cosmic structures, or that there is an issue with the ΛCDM model's prediction of galaxy distribution at high redshifts. Alternatively, our findings could simply indicate issues with the theoretical models used to describe galaxy distribution. Further research is necessary to clarify these findings. The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDR Lasso) has become a fundamental tool for answering broad questions in high-dimensional data analysis. However, its computational intensity becomes exponentially overwhelming, necessitating more efficient algorithms. A recently suggested hierarchical approach reduces the problem but still lacks scalability when dealing with larger data sets. Our research introduces an alternative solution – a versatile and efficient algorithm that uses adaptive sieving to efficiently solve HDR Lasso. By leveraging the hierarchical nature of the problem, our algorithm efficiently explores the candidate space based on relevant features and their predicted importance. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art HDR Lasso solvers in terms of computational speed while achieving comparable accuracy. Our solutions include both a general, adaptable version applicable to various HDR Lasso variants and a optimized variant for the most commonly used HDR Lasso model, which we make publicly available on our website. Our theoretical analysis validates the correctness of our algorithm and we further substantiate its efficacy through experimental studies. Specifically, our algorithm solution accurately matches the hierarchical approach when possible and we found that 99% of the time in our tests it does so, with our method also exhibiting superior performance when operating independently. Experimental studies also demonstrate that our method outperforms other prominent HDR Lasso solvers in terms of both computational speed and efficiency. Specifically, our algorithm solution accurately matches the hierarchical approach when possible and we found that 99% of the time it does so, with our method also exhibiting superior performance when operating independently. Research on graph packing has been an ongoing area of study in graph theory for over five decades, yet multiple variants of this concept remain difficult to solve efficiently. This paper explores tight bounds for two specific graph packing problems, particularly those involving paths and trees. We have established tight upper bounds for both vertex-disjoint paths and trees on a given graph. Due to the inherent hardness in obtaining precise bounds, our approach involves a simplified model where each graph contains a fixed spanning tree. For the problem of finding disjoint paths, we provide a novel algorithm that achieves a tight $n$-factor approximation, where $n$ is the number of vertices in the graph. For the tree packing problem, we propose a dual-based linear programming algorithm that provides optimal performance, and extend this result to obtain a near-tight approximation for the general graph packing problem. We achieve this by combining our findings on tree packing with the concept of tree contaiement, which allows us to transform a given graph into one with a specified spanning tree. Our results show that our algorithm scales linearly with the number of graphs being packed, providing a promising direction for further research. Interestingly, we observe that our bounds are comparable to those obtained through random graph placement, highlighting a promising area for study in probabilistic graph theory. Notably, our results imply the existence of efficient algorithms for finding disjoint paths in planar graphs and graphs of bounded treewidth, building upon the work of numerous contributors to graph theory. Our findings provide novel insights into graph packing, offering potential avenues for further research and extension. When searching for information on the internet, professionals in the public sector often rely on Google's suggested answers, known as "Knowledge Cards," which may contain biased information. Overwhelming search results can make it difficult for these professionals to find accurate information in time, leading them to rely on quick shortcuts like Google's suggested answers. The problem is that these results are sourced from Wikipedia, but Wikipedia's content can contain the very biases these professionals are trying to avoid. Moreover, algorithmic biases in Web search can compound these issues, exacerbating the challenges posed by limited time and information overload. To address these concerns, we conducted a study which analyzed Wikipedia's biases against underrepresented groups, and found that these biases are reflected in Google's algorithmic suggestions. Our research provides practical implications for public sector professionals on effectively using search tools like Google to find reliable information, and offers potential solutions to mitigate the biases that affect decision-making. Based on our findings, we developed three strategies that public sector professionals can utilize to minimize biases when searching online, and we presented them at a workshop where we shared our research with practitioners. The practitioners provided feedback that informed our recommended approaches, which can be applied by any professional who relies on web search for decision-making. The study's outcomes also suggest possible future directions for addressing algorithmic biases, including the utilization of transparency-promoting methods such as counterfactual reasoning, which could supplement existing approaches like surrogate modeling and causal inference. Ultimately, we explored the potential of leveraging machine learning techniques, particularly those involving recursive neural networks and generative adversarial networks, to develop counterfactual explanations that could help mitigate algorithmic biases. The study's conclusions are grounded in the theoretical validity of these approaches, as demonstrated in existing research, and we present practical applications of these models, such as XAI, that could effectively generate counterfactual explanations in real-world scenarios. Consequently, we recommend the use of ablation studies, which can provide insights into the effectiveness of these approaches in facilitating decision-making among public sector professionals. Earth's complex climate system can be better understood through mathematical modeling, although full-scale models are difficult to analyze and understand due to their intricate nature. Two main reduction techniques, averaging and perturbation methods, help simplify models while retaining crucial characteristics. These techniques have a rich history of application in climate research, as evident from previous studies featured in this journal. We are, however, missing a comprehensive guide that explains these methods in the context of climate modeling. This article aims to bridge this gap, providing an in-depth overview of reduction techniques and their utility in climate modeling, as well as their future prospects within the climate research field. We will discuss multiple baroclinic models, starting from the simplest to the most complex, such as the baroclinic model governed by the Quinquin equation, the Benjamin ono equation, and the Primitive Equation Phyiscal Internet Model (BIEM-PE), to illustrate the application of reduction methods in these models. We will also examine current challenges and potential future directions in the reduction of climate models, emphasizing the necessity for a standardized method to evaluate the efficacy of these models, and highlighting the potential of modern reduction techniques such as real event detection and the reduction of dynamical systems with time-dependent coefficients. We hope this review will stimulate the development of new reduction techniques and motivate the in-depth analysis of existing climate models, ultimately contributing to the advancement of climate modeling. We also provide an appendix with practical reduction methods for model variables, illustrating the calculation of model statistics, and summarizing the reduction method for the BIEM-PE model. We further discuss the reduction of the baroclinic model governed by the Quinquin equation, and the Rapidly Exponential Decreasing (RED) method for the partial differential equations (PDE), as well as its application to the climate model of baroclinic wind. Furthermore, we analyze the reduction of the Perfect Mechanical Weather Model (PMWM), documenting the complete reduction procedure, and presenting the statistical representation of the model with a view to its eventual replacement by a stochastic model. Lastly, we discuss the reduction of the Mechanical Weather Model (MWM), governed by the Navier-Stokes equations, with a view to its eventual application in climate modeling. We hope this comprehensive account will contribute to the reduction of climate models, and motivate further research in this domain. Future surveys with the James Webb Space Telescope will detect thousands of kilonovae, allowing us to gather precise data on the narrow wavelength ranges it observes. However, observing the broad spectral distribution of these emissions, which could contain valuable information about the origins of heavy elements, is not possible with current or planned ground-based telescopes. As a result, important spectral features in the kilonova spectrum will remain unknown for the foreseeable future. This study presents a new machine learning technique that uses neural networks to broaden kilonova spectra based on their observed spectra, enabling researchers to estimate the broad spectral distribution of these objects. By testing this method against detailed radiative transfer models, we find that our model accurately predicts the overall energy distribution of kilonovae, including both continuum and line components, from the energy range of 0.13 to 13.4 eV with a median absolute error of 0.03 dex. This method will likely be useful in interpreting future observations of kilonovae with the James Webb Space Telescope and the Athena X-ray observatory. As such space-based telescopes have a higher sensitivity to broader wavelength ranges, our model will allow researchers to estimate the overall spectral distribution of kilonovae based on observed spectra, while a comparison with detailed radiative transfer models shows a high level of accuracy in this process. This method will likely be useful in interpreting future observations of kilonovae, which will significantly increase our understanding of these objects.

By analyzing a range of dark matter and mediator masses from $10^{-3}$ to $10^3$ GeV, we identify three regimes in their interactions. This paper introduces the SIFT-based Color-Particle-Dynamics (CPD) image registration method, which aligns undirected graphs representing medical image characteristics. The SIFT algorithm identifies distinctive image features, translating into stable particles that describe each image, facilitating registration of the tumor segment and surrounding tissue in medical images, unaffected by differences in intensity or local abnormalities. The CPD method determines point correspondence by minimizing a divergence measure, ensuring robust and efficient results. The proposed registration method is independent of image intensity and local variations, effectively using distinctive image features. Evaluations using 182 CT scans of the abdomen, 50 MRIs of the brain, and 30 CT lung scans, demonstrate the robustness and accuracy of the SIFT-CPD algorithm, outperforming current state-of-the-art registration methods. The code is available at https://github.com/Alexandria-Research-Group/SIFT-CPD-Image-Registration. The SIFT-CPD method has been implemented in C++ and MATLAB, providing compatible code at https://github.com/Alexandria-Research-Group/SIFT-CPD-Image-Registration. The computational costs of SIFT-CPD are approximately 0.3 seconds for registering one CT scan of the abdomen, 2.5 seconds for registering one MRI of the brain, and 0.5 seconds for registering one CT lung scan. The SIFT-CPD image registration method effectively aligns images characteristics, robustly handling various imaging modalities, local variations, and different scales. The accuracy of the SIFT-CPD method was validated by experts in medical imaging, assessing 50 registered brain MRIs and 30 registered lung CT scans. The statistical results of the SIFT-CPD method are available at https://github.com/Alexandria-Research-Group/SIFT-CPD-Image-Registration. The SIFT-CPD method provides well-defined probability distributions for tumor growth modeling, using CPD dynamics for accurate and efficient results. The application of the SIFT-CPD method is presented in detail, along with a case study of planning radiation therapy for a patient with lung cancer. This significant event is predicted to occur within the next decade or possibly as early as 2024. To better comprehend these populations, we aim to identify patterns in their distribution within the galaxy's orientation. Focusing on nuclei of Seyfert 1 and 2 galaxies within the 6dF galaxy survey, we analyze their major and minor axis lengths and orientations relative to the surrounding galaxy's major axis. It is discovered that the orientations of these nuclei do not correlate with the galaxy's major axis, but rather exhibit random or weak associations. However, it is observed that the nucleus of type 2 Seyfert galaxies is, on average, more aligned with the galaxy's major axis compared to the nucleus of type 1 Seyfert galaxies, displaying a 10 degrees difference. Additionally, the findings suggest that the nucleus of type 2 Seyfert galaxies is more concentrated near the galaxy's center, whereas the nucleus of type 1 Seyfert galaxies shows a broader distribution. The outcomes of these analyses are consistent with previous studies and may hold the key to understanding the relationships between AGN populations and their host galaxies. It is suggested that type 2 AGNs are more likely to have their accretion discs aligned with the galaxy's major axis due to a proposed toroidal structure, potentially influencing the orientation of the nucleus. Our approach eliminates the reliance on depth estimates and 2D edge representations, making it highly efficient for pre-training on large-scale datasets. Recent advances in Natural Language Processing in the medical domain have centered on addressing health-related questions through the analysis of clinical texts. A key step in this process involves identifying symptoms from clinical documents. Researchers have employed various machine learning techniques to enhance accuracy, typically relying on supervised methods. However, clinical data are often limited by scarcity of instances, leading to low precision and recall in identified symptoms. To overcome this challenge, this paper introduces a domain generalization approach to improve symptom extraction. This method enables models to excel across various hospital settings, extracting more accurate symptoms by reducing reliance on dataset-specific training. Our experiments demonstrate that domain generalization outperforms a supervised model, yielding an F1-score of 0.813 on PASCAL Clinical Substitution and 0.854 on PASCAL Clinical Unseen tasks. Furthermore, our results show that domain generalization enhances the robustness of the model by reducing performance fluctuations between different hospital settings. The source code for this research is publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/AhmedSayed91/Symptom-Extraction-with-Domain-Generalization. The knowledge gained from this study can benefit the development of clinical question answering systems, suggesting that domain generalization is a viable strategy for enhancing performance on symptom extraction and other related tasks. Moreover, this knowledge can inspire future research in the medical NLP community, suggesting the utility of few-shot learning techniques for fine-tuning models to effectively adapt to new clinical settings. Finally, our work indicates that large-scale text corpora may be unnecessary for achieving accurate models, suggesting that targeted text collections with a smaller scale can still yield accurate results. To achieve this, we propose MedDG, a benchmark for evaluating domain generalization in medical NLP, consisting of a set of datasets with varied domain characteristics and a range of applications, including symptom extraction. By utilizing this benchmark, the medical NLP community can engage in comprehensive evaluations of their models to better understand generalization performance and identify effective techniques for enhancing robustness. Ultimately, our work aims to stimulate the development of more effective medical NLP models, encouraging the use of benchmarking to assess the practical implications of their approaches on real-world applications. Moreover, our study reveals that symptom extraction presents a challenging task, particularly when relying on limited clinical data, leading to inaccurate and unreliable models. In the context of strange quark matter, considering both Neumann and Alcubierre potential models for quark interaction in the presence of a highly concentrated magnetic field, we investigate how a strong magnetic field influences the spin-aligned state. Utilizing the Ginzburg-Landau approach, we derive an expanded equation of state that incorporates the effects of the magnetic field. Our findings indicate that the magnetic field has a tendency to harden the equation of state within a specific range of chemical potential and magnetic field strength. Nevertheless, when the magnetic field is extremely intense, it may lead to a softer equation of state, especially under conditions where the strange quark has a higher chemical potential. Furthermore, we identify critical values of the chemical potential and magnetic field strength that could enable the construction of stars composed of spin-aligned strange quark matter. Moreover, our investigation also examines the impact of the magnetic field on quark free energy in the presence of spin alignment. Interestingly, within a particular range of chemical potential and magnetic field strength, the free energy of a spin-aligned state can be lower than that of a normal aligned state. Moreover, the condition $\mu_m \lesssim \mu_m^{cr}$ for this phenomenon to occur is also determined. Additionally, the mass-radius relations for stars composed of spin-aligned strange quark matter are derived under two distinct scenarios for quark interaction and in the presence of extremely intense magnetic fields. These theoretical models suggest the possibility of observing a neutron star composed of spin-aligned strange quark matter with a radius less than 10 km. Lastly, our study explores the energy emission due to the capillary break-up in the presence of a strong magnetic field from stars composed of spin-aligned strange quark matter. Two distinct scenarios for quark interaction are considered, resulting in significantly intense emission compared to the case of neutron stars, potentially reaching $10^{14}$ times higher levels in the form of gamma rays, and of the order of $10^{18}$ times higher levels in the form of X-rays. Moreover, the intensity of capillary emission in the form of soft X-rays from stars composed of spin-aligned strange quark matter may be high enough to explain the observed emission from the capillary system in the neutron star CRX J090712.6-35110. By linking individual devices into a collective computing entity called a Pando, users can harness the power of a vast virtual supercomputer, effectively transforming their devices into a distributed computing network. This innovative approach allows users to expand their computational capabilities beyond what their devices can accomplish alone, achieving speeds of up to 40 times faster performance for data-intensive applications, while also streamlining complex tasks and making them more portable across devices. By integrating science and engineering workflows into Pando, users can effortlessly manage, run, and collaborate on projects across their device network, enjoying improved productivity and flexibility. Moreover, by consolidating workflow management and execution within Pando's virtual supercomputer, users can simplify their workflow administration and enjoy consistent results, regardless of which devices they use or where their data is stored. This paper discusses the concepts and benefits of Pando, outlining its features and functionality in further detail. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive overview of the Pando system architecture and present results from user evaluations and performance analysis. We examine survivor sets derived from beta-transformations with intermediate values of beta for alpha greater than 1. It is known that such sets correspond to numbers with low decimal expansions in base alpha. Our analysis extends previous research by Schmeling and Schweiger, who focused on base-ten transformations. We identify the survivor sets as containing all numbers with specific properties and show that numbers with distinct properties do not overlap. Additionally, we establish a connection between these sets and numbers that resist approximation in non-integral bases. We also determine the sets corresponding to beta-transformations with alpha less than one, which may have applications in fields such as cryptography. Furthermore, we observe a duality between these sets and numbers that satisfy a particular equation in the interval (0,1). Finally, we note that the survival sets do not have a sum that equals one, which resolves a previously open question. Our work builds on research by Darboux and allows us to apply Schmidt's theorem on relatively prime numbers. We also utilize Katok-Burckel's compactification of the rational line, as well as Minkowski's boundedness theorem. Utilizing the properties of beta- expansions, we develop new inequalities that enable us to explore the geometry of survivor sets, which allows us to apply and extend classical results from various fields, including the theory of numbers, ergodic theory, and holomorphic dynamics. Our analysis also leads to the discovery of new properties, such as the sets' Hausdorff dimension, which is beta minus two for alpha greater than one, and its connection to the lyapunov exponents of certain polynomial maps. We establish that the lyapunov exponents are zero, and this, in turn, enables us to apply Cusumano-Deschamps and Lices' recent research on non-integer beta-values. We extend their results, which are based on Gouezel-Ledrappier-Scheffer's work, to obtain new bounds for the lyapunov exponents, which are negative for alpha less than one and non-negative for alpha greater than one. Our key insight is a connection between the exponents and the survivor sets, which allows us to apply dimension-related properties to establish these bounds. We also utilize Hill's compactification of the julia set of a polynomial, along with Minkowski's boundedness theorem, to achieve these results. Interpreting machine learning models, especially in high-stakes domains, is crucial to ensuring fairness and preventing biases. Many existing methods are designed for binary classification, but identifying the partial effects of categorical variables on predicted outcomes is essential. To tackle this issue, a novel diagnostic tool called Disentangled Attribution Curves (DACs) has been developed, allowing for the partial effect analysis of categorical variables. DACs have been successfully applied to analyzing the impact of weather and day of the week on bike-sharing usage. The findings reveal significant, statistically-supported influences that align with empirical expectations, thus validating the method's effectiveness in uncovering relevant trends. Furthermore, the approach demonstrates flexibility and can be adapted for use in models with binary classification outcomes. However, traditional FEDME approaches either sacrifice efficiency for security or vice versa. To address this challenge, this research proposes novel, efficient, and reliable approaches to support secure model encryption in FL frameworks.  Specifically, it assumes the role of a semi-honest client and introduces new techniques for securely contributing local models to the server. To overcome existing flaws in the literature, this research develops new approaches for maintaining data privacy and guaranteeing accuracy in the aggregate function.  In particular, it focuses on a linear learning problem and develops two new mechanisms for facilitating secure distributed linear learning under the presence of malicious servers. This research presents a testing approach that allows drivers for microcontrollers to be thoroughly tested, leveraging the capabilities of full-node computers and microcontrollers through a reliable and efficient driver testing framework. By establishing a connection between a microcontroller and a computer using a serial interface, a testing environment is created, where the computer serves as a test driver, sending input requests to the microcontroller, which then responds with output data. These interactions are interpreted by the testing framework to formulate expectations, enabling the detection of driver errors. To optimize testing efficiency and minimize congestion, the framework employs a class-based asynchronous testing method, where all tests are conducted concurrently in separate threads. By adopting this solution, bugs in driver code can be identified early in the development process, reducing the complexibility of microcontroller programming. Our testing framework has been applied to the Arduino MKR IoT Dev Kit, which we utilized to evaluate its effectiveness in testing driver code. Our evaluation revealed that, depending on the driver and test suite used, the framework can either approximately match or significantly exceed the performance of native compilers generated code, including when the driver code involves complex algorithms like the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). Furthermore, the proposed testing framework was found to be more efficient than alternative approaches, such as partial-code testing, in validating driver functionality. Our study demonstrates that the presented testing approach and associated framework can reliably and efficiently evaluate driver code for microcontrollers in conjunction with a computer-based testing environment. These findings are meaningful because they address the common challenges of testing driver code on standalone microcontrollers and inefficiently revising driver code to work on full-node computers, as experienced by the developers of the Arduino project. By offering a comprehensive driver testing solution for microcontrollers, our approach effectively mitigates the drawbacks of current methods, thereby accelerating the development of reliable driver code and accurately reflecting the performance of driver code on microcontrollers when used in conjunction with a computer-based testing environment. Our experience with this process is valuable, encouraging other researchers to apply similar testing frameworks to other embedded systems, such as the Raspberry Pi. Protecting applications with sensitive system interfaces from malicious libraries is a challenging task.  The main issue arises because mechanisms such as sandboxing and API wrapping incur significant performance overheads, making them unsuitable for applications like web servers, databases, and scientific simulations, which often harbor compromised libraries.  The authors of Timeloops propose a novel technique for system call filtering that leverages hardware-supported page walking trees (PWTs) to enable efficient detection and prevention of attacks on untrusted applications, including those written in interpreted languages like PHP and Python.  By utilizing Timeloops, developers can create secure versions of applications with minimal performance overheads, amounting to just 5% in this study.  The authors' research demonstrates the effectiveness of Timeloops in protecting various applications, including a PHP web server, an image processing program, and a database, against malicious libraries, yielding a 100% success rate.  The authors acknowledge that Timeloops has certain limitations, primarily its inability to support microkernel architectures and full virtualization, which prevent its use in certain environments, particularly Linux microkernels and full virtualization environments and Intel ME.  The authors also acknowledge the potential security risks associated with hardware-assisted mechanisms like PWTs, which could be exploited by malicious actors, and the need for improved hardware protection mechanisms.  The authors outline future directions for enhancing Timeloops, including the development of techniques for identifying malicious libraries at hardware level, and leveraging hardware features for protecting applications more effectively.  The Timeloops project is currently hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/UCSD-CSE242B/Timeloops.  The authors invite feedback and contributions from the security community to help further develop Timeloops into a robust system for protecting applications against malicious libraries. Our investigation into the application of PCA for scRNA-seq data led to the surprising discovery that using PCA on the compressed expression matrices does not consistently yield meaningful results. Upon closer examination, it was observed that PCA identifies patterns rooted in data collection, such as sampling bias, rather than intrinsic biological mechanisms. This realization prompted an exploration into alternative methods for unsupervised classification and clustering of scRNA-seq data. By reducing the dimensionality of the Jaccard distance between binary matrices derived from the top expressed genes, our approach proved effective in accurately classifying 9 datasets across various species with a success rate of 125 out of 129 (96.9%), achieving up to 18.6% improved performance compared to the widely used Euclidean space. Additionally, our method proved adaptable to data with varying sizes and scales, classifying 9 datasets with different sample and gene counts with a success rate of 114 out of 129 (88.3%). Furthermore, our method demonstrated improved interpretability, associating clusters with low-dimensional subspaces composed of relevant biological features. Using human scRNA-seq data, for instance, our approach identified a low-dimensional space of 4 dimensions that effectively distinguishes lung from brain tissue with high accuracy, outperforming the 50-dimensional PCA space. Our novel method offers improved performance, adaptability, and interpretability over traditional approaches, making it a more suitable choice for scRNA-seq data analysis and machine learning applications. We establish a complete characterization of von Neumann algebras that arise from the local observables of ground states exhibiting frustration-free behavior. Our classification aligns with the conformal classification of one-dimensional invariant von Neumann algebras. This result is further used to demonstrate that the von Neumann algebras generated by the local observables of critical models defined on the entire real line, specifically the Ising, free Fermion, and Boson models, cannot be maximally extended with periodic boundary conditions. This conclusion stems from the properties of strictly periodic subalgebras, which we show to be equivalent to algebras generated by compact operators in this context. We also explore the properties of strictly periodic subalgebras in general, deriving both necessary and sufficient conditions for their existence. We introduce a novel Bayesian approach that maintains the accuracy of the original model's posterior uncertainties while performing variable selection in high-dimensional data. Our method iteratively refines the posterior distribution by eliminating irrelevant variables and incorporates an additional layer of uncertainty resulting from the initial variable selection process. We derive the updating formula for the posterior distribution and prove its equivalence to a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm, allowing for efficient computation. Our approach is validated through comprehensive simulations and real-world data analysis, which demonstrate its superior performance in retaining original model accuracy and achieving optimal variable selection results. Our R code is available for reproduction of the results. Furthermore, we illustrate the methodology's applicability in several practical scenarios, including the analysis of RNA-seq data and currency exchange rates. A crucial distinction exists between Man-in-the-Middle (MIM) attacks, which involve intercepting data en route to a DNN, and traditional adversarial attacks that aim to exploit DNNs on the source device. Our analysis shows that robust inputs offer significantly greater protection against MIM attacks than defenses designed for adversarial examples, both in terms of classification accuracy and the amount of data manipulation required. Furthermore, our study reveals that robust inputs can also perform well against adversarial examples, which has important implications for the development of classification systems in safety-critical applications. Climate change is often referred to as one of the most critical issues of our time, yet many people still deny its existence or downplay its significance, often spreading conspiracy theories about it on social media platforms. Despite its severity, there has been surprisingly little research on the topic, particularly concerning the characteristics of online environments that facilitate the dissemination of conspiracy theories. To fill this gap, we examined conspiracy theory-related content about climate change on Twitter, aiming to identify the source of this content and the strategies employed to disseminate it. Our in-depth analysis of climate change conspiracy theory content revealed that far-right extremist groups predominantly circulate this type of content, using tactics like "echo chambers" to amplify their messages and "seed planting" to gradually influence public opinion. Our findings have significant implications for counter-narrative initiatives, highlighting the need to target the source of conspiracy theory dissemination and compete with extremist groups' social media presence. Counter-narrative efforts should also address the semantic nuances of conspiracy theory content to effectively challenge them. Finally, our research underscores the importance of ongoing analysis of online environments to prevent the spread of conspiracy theories. As the landscape of online conspiracy theory discourse continues to evolve, future research should explore the role of "mainstreaming" in the emergence of conspiracy theories. Furthermore, we suggest that future research can benefit from incorporating quantitative methods to map the complex and dynamic landscape of online conspiracy theory narratives. Additionally, it is essential to investigate the impact of social media platforms' policies on the spread of conspiracy theories and the experiences of users who encounter these narratives. Lastly, the relationship between the spread of conspiracy theories and cognitive dissonance remains an intriguing area for further research. Systematically exploring conspiracy theory-related content is essential to understanding their role in facilitating their spread, as seen in the case of climate change conspiracy theories. To achieve this, we recommend developing the "Conspiracy Theory Life Cycle Model," which involves identifying the core characteristics of conspiracy theory-related content, the role of "mainstreaming" in their development, and the impact of social media platforms' policies on the spread of these narratives. This model can serve as a foundation for future research on the topic, as well as for applications in counter-narrative initiatives. Building on our previous findings, we now propose the "Conspiracy Theory Life Cycle Model," and we plan to apply it to three distinct areas: (1) investigating the role of "mainstreaming" in the development of conspiracy theory-related content, (2) exploring the connection between conspiracy theory narratives and their impact on public opinion

We carried out a comprehensive set of two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations for the long-term accretion behavior of binaries within a surrounding gas disk. Notably, our research indicates that a smaller binary within a hierarchical systems generally experiences less effective accretion compared to a standalone star of equivalent mass, and this trend is more pronounced for more massive outer binaries. The lower accretion rate in binaries is attributed to several key factors. Firstly, the binary's orbital motion leads to a lower accretion velocity of gas onto the binary, and this effect is more pronounced for closer binaries. Secondly, the binary's orbital plane becomes aligned with the disk's axis, reducing its surface area available to interact with the surrounding gas. Lastly, the binary's mass is distributed more evenly, leading to a lower mass accretion rate per unit mass. Our simulations also reveal that a larger binary within a hierarchical systems generally experiences a higher accretion rate, but one that is still generally lower than that of a standalone star, and this result is more pronounced for farther outer binaries. The lower accretion rate in larger binaries is primarily driven by their lower eccentricity, which leads to a higher accretion velocity of gas onto the binary, and this effect is more pronounced for closer binaries. Additionally, the binary's orbital velocity and mass distribution contribute to a higher accretion rate, and our findings provide a useful approach to model the long-term evolution of binaries within a gas disk. We also provide a simple model to quantify the long-term accretion behavior of binaries in such environments. Based on our long-term simulations, we find that a smaller binary within a hierarchical systems generally fails to experience sufficient accretion to transform into an equal-mass binary, and this result holds true for a wider range of model parameters, including initial disk masses and binary masses. However, a larger binary within a hierarchical systems may experience a higher accretion rate, and our findings suggest that this could lead to the formation of equal-mass binaries, and potentially even result in the creation of multiple hierarchies through the process of binary mergers. Our research also provides a theoretical framework to extend the observations of the binary-mergers to the longer timescales of stellar activity, and could potentially shed light on the processes that govern the formation and evolution of multiple hierarchies in planetary systems. Our simulations are available for further analysis on the Research Institute for Advanced Technology's website, and the associated python code can be accessed on github through the Research Institute for Advanced Technology. Inspired by the flatness and horizon problems, we'll be investigating how the universe behaves dynamically in a given spatial framework, assuming it has a consistent structure throughout time. This assumption is based on a theoretical model where matter is evenly distributed across the universe without any fluctuations, except for one unique feature – a tiny inhomogeneity at the edge of our observable universe. As the universe begins to expand, we'll examine the impact of this initial inequality on its overall geometry, finding that the smaller the inhomogeneity, the more precise our approximation of the flatness problem becomes. Conversely, when we consider fluctuations on a larger scale, the dynamics of the universe tend to compensate for the initial inequality, resulting in a solution that is accurate within a 10% margin – a level of error that improves with larger scales. To understand the underlying physics, we'll be comparing our findings with theories such as the Multi-Faced Universe theory and the "you are a coordinate" model, ultimately discussing the implications for life's probability within the universe. Lastly, we'll look at the potential observational evidence for these theories, including the distribution of galaxy distributions and the behavior of dark energy, which may serve as a test to differentiate between these theories and our fundamental dynamic model of the universe. In doing so, we'll derive a general equation for the dark energy's EoS based on the universe's spatial average, rather than its average curvature. In conclusion, by analyzing the dynamic model of the universe, we can gain valuable insights into the nature of the universe's inequality, its structure, and the behavior of dark energy, paving the way for possible empirical verification. This research is the final outcome of our 2022 Summer Research Program in Astrophysics.

We explore the piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model, adapting it to the piecewise planar model for the purpose of segmentation. However, this approach is vulnerable to noise, which distorts the result. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new algorithm that utilizes both the curve evolution principle and the influence function. The curve is forced to be piecewise constant through the imposition of an obstacle field that incorporates both the gradient and the normal direction of the curve. The evolution of the curve is then subject to resistance from the obstacle field, resulting in which the curve assumes piecewise constant values. The incorporation of the influence function allows for the accurate calculation of the curve's normal direction, thereby enhancing the algorithm's precision and preventing aberrant behavior. The effectiveness of the algorithm has been confirmed through both two-dimensional and three-dimensional simulations. Additionally, when compared to the curve influence model, our approach outperforms it in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. The proposed method also possesses applicability in three-dimensional segmentation of medical images, as demonstrated by the example of calculating the dura mater from MRI images of a human brain. The calculated dura mater is found to be free from the inherent noise present in the images. Furthermore, the approach has the potential to be applied in a range of other image processing domains. In neuromorphic computing, computers are designed to operate at the speed of neurons, enabling the processing of large amounts of data quickly. To achieve this, they employ learning techniques that adapt rapidly, often using data available during operation to refine their performance. This on-chip learning approach differs from traditional machine learning, which relies on extensive offline data processing. Unlike other neuromorphic learning methods, the novel Spiking Neural Network learning framework incorporates temporal relationships within individual data samples. This allows the adaptation of models without the need for extensive training, making them suitable for a wide range of tasks, including classification, clustering, and data visualization. Our study demonstrates that SNN learning can be efficiently implemented in hardware, offering a promising solution for applications where data must be processed rapidly and accurately, such as real-time video analysis, robotics, and autonomous systems. Our results show that SNN models can achieve comparable performance to more complex deep neural networks, but with significantly faster adaptation times and lower computational costs. This makes neuromorphic computing an exciting and promising field, with numerous potential applications in areas like bio-inspired robotics, feature extraction, and more. We performed a detailed analysis of the stellar cluster Westerlund 2 to study its mass distribution and the stability of its upper mass range. Our goal was to assess the cluster's efficiency in forming massive stars, as predicted by the stellar initial mass function. We aimed to determine whether the cluster's instability is a prerequisite for the supershot event that occurred approximately 2 million years ago, as suggested by the presence of a runaway star. To achieve this goal, we created a mass distribution array, comparable to that obtained from the Massive Star Forming Region Catalog by the McLean Telescope. We then calculated the mass of each star in the cluster by using a standard bolometric magnitude table and a bolometric correction table. Accurate text extraction from IDs is a complex task hindered by varying extraction methods and unclear formats. This complexity is compounded by the presence of crucial information such as expiration dates, which are often encoded as numbers with special implications. To overcome this, a multi-layered approach is proposed, beginning with Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) to enhance text extraction and its meaning. The initial OCR stage produces text with special implications denoted by specific characters, which is then processed by NLP to identify relevant keywords and their expected forms. Subsequent analysis of part-of-speech tags and semantic categories enables the replacement of special characters with standard alphabet characters, producing a standardized output. As evidence suggests that keywords extracted through this multi-layered approach are more informative than raw OCR output, this nlp-aided approach offers improved extraction and is more amenable to automated system development and maintenance. Furthermore, this nlp-aided approach is more resistant to errors introduced by OCR, as exemplified in the case of a driver's license featuring a distorted expiration date (e.g., '26/04/50' instead of '2050'). While this error would prevent a system using raw OCR output from indicating that the license has not expired, the nlp-aided approach can correct these errors and accurately determine expiration dates even from poorly scanned IDs. Overall, the proposed nlp-aided approach offers enhanced text extraction with corrected errors and improved implications. Additionally, this technology is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of ID card types. Experimental results validating the efficacy of this approach are presented, including a comparative analysis with raw OCR output. Unlike traditional approaches, this algorithm does not rely on data augmentation or regularization but instead relies on the diversity of encoded samples to mitigate overfitting. We introduce a new estimator that significantly reduces bias while maintaining the existing variance properties in nonparametric regression models. To achieve this, we developed a fast-converging estimator, which efficiently estimates the smoothing parameter with minimal computational complexity. Unlike previous approaches that relied on arbitrary cutoff values, our method seamlessly integrates bias reduction and smoothness, allowing the bias to smoothly decrease as the cutoff changes. We also provide asymptotic normality results for the estimator and demonstrate its superiority over existing approaches through simulations and real-data analyses. Notably, our proposal is versatile and can be applied to various contexts, including enhanced sparse nonparametric regression and point process models. These applications are illustrated through case studies. Furthermore, our work offers a valuable theoretical foundation for tackling related challenges in the future. This paper focuses on knowledge graph link prediction, a crucial task that utilizes data from both relation extraction and knowledge graph construction to generate predicted links. While current methods heavily rely on relation extraction data, we argue that this data is insufficient for accurately identifying all missing links. Consequently, we introduce a novel framework that incorporates additional information from knowledge graph construction to enhance link prediction performance. This framework utilizes a graph convolutional network to process the entire knowledge graph and leverage the global structure, particularly the properties of connected entities, to improve link prediction. Additionally, we introduce a new evaluation metric that rewards models for correctly identifying multiple types of links, including but not limited to, those extracted through relation extraction. This metric helps optimize models that can generate a diverse set of links beyond just extraction data. We test our framework with a newly created knowledge graph construction dataset, called FGATKGE, and demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods that solely utilize relation extraction data. Notably, our results show that integrating knowledge graph construction data improves link prediction accuracy by 21.1% compared to solely using relation extraction data. A new semi-supervised statistical model known as the semi-generative model (SGM) has been developed with the goal of effectively capturing high-dimensional complex relationships between variables by separating a target variable into its underlying causes and effects. In contrast to existing approaches that either identify factors or analyze associations, SGM is a generative model which generates samples in an inverse Bayesian network structure, where variables are arranged in a specific hierarchy. By reversing this hierarchy, two probability distributions are defined: the causes-to-effects distribution, which models the effects of variables given their underlying causes, and the effects-to-causes distribution, which models the causes of variables based on their surrounding effects. These distributions are estimated using a joint analysis of both supervised and unsupervised data, resulting in a Bayesian approach that incorporates prior knowledge and is robust to high-dimensional variables. In experiments involving synthetic and real data, SGM outperformed existing methods in identifying the underlying factors and effects of variables. Furthermore, the identified causes and effects showed a high degree of agreement with existing knowledge on the variables, as assessed by experts. The proposed model is particularly effective in high-dimensional analysis and is robust to common issues such as noise, missing data, and confounding variables. Overall, SGM provides a valuable tool for exploring and understanding the structure of complex variables. The approach is useful for discovering the underlying biological and environmental mechanisms in omics studies, the relationships between financial variables in an market, and the structure of molecular networks. The proposed model is also applicable in a wide range of fields where there is a need to understand high-dimensional complex variables. The approach is versatile and can be applied to various scenarios, such as discovering the underlying causes of a disease from its symptoms, understanding how genes are regulated, and learning about the properties of materials by analyzing their properties. The model is also used to identify the underlying causes of a target variable in high-dimensional data. The approach is based on a semi-supervised statistical model that is used to analyze data in scenarios with both supervised and unsupervised components. The model is robust and can estimate the probability distributions in both the causes-to-effects and effects-to-causes directions. Deep learning achieves impressive results across various applications, yet its foundational principles remain somewhat mysterious. By examining the geometric structure underlying deep learning systems, researchers aim to gain insights that can inform algorithm and infrastructure design. In this paper, we outline GeomL, a framework for analyzing the geometric properties of deep learning models. By utilizing GeomL, we discover linking relationships among distinct neural network architectures and their inputs/outputs, which suggest new training methods. Furthermore, we apply GeomL to investigate the effects of data augmentation on neural networks, revealing that common practices may introduce unnecessary complexity and illustrating how the framework can guide design decisions. Additionally, we use GeomL to analyze the connectivity patterns within deep learning models, suggesting that existing models may be topologically simple and therefore potentially improved by introducing artificial gaps within their neural layers. Overall, the proposed framework supports further research into the geometric structure of deep learning systems, enabling the development of more efficient and scalable models. Additionally, we establish the upper limit for the number of lattice minima in cubic fields and calculate their counts for deg-2 cubic fields. Our proposed method, referred to as attention relevance propagation, has been tested on well-known benchmark datasets and compared to established models within the field of feature importance. The performance of this model has been validated through experiments on various datasets, where it consistently surpasses the accuracy of comparable state-of-the-art deep neural networks. Notably, the framework's layerwise feature importance values were found to be consistently stable and accurate. The potential of this method for use in explaining the behavior of deep neural networks, particularly in medical image analysis applications, has also been explored and demonstrated. Our study showcases a novel, interpretable deep learning model, known as RProp-Net, which combines the strengths of layerwise attention propagation and deep neural networks to achieve superior predictive performance and transparency. This research focuses on increasing the efficiency of Monte Carlo simulations by combining certain transformations. Existing methods have found some optimal combinations, but the overall efficiency is still limited. We introduce a novel approach by combining multiple complex-valued affine coupling layers. These layers are effective in expanding the Monte Carlo sample space, but suffer from inefficient use of latent variables. We analyzed the layers under a specific scenario and derived a mathematical expression for determining the optimal layer parameters. The analysis indicates that complex-valued affine layers are more efficient than their real-valued counterparts when certain conditions apply. Additionally, we derive closed-form expressions for common distribution parameters, such as entropy and KL divergence, which enables efficient latent variable disposal. We compared the proposed method with other established techniques and found that it results in more efficient simulations, while also matching the performance of current state-of-the-art methods in terms of training efficiency. The benefits of the new approach are particularly pronounced in scenarios involving multi-dimensional sample space transformations. The source code for the proposed method is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/alexhathaway/cc_layer. The repository includes a TensorFlow implementation with accompanying numerical examples. The code is compatible with Python 3.6 and above. The numerical experiments were conducted using the Google Colab platform and are documented in the GitHub repository. Specifically, the 'efficient_mc_sampling' notebook demonstrates the application of the new method for efficiently sampling from complex, multi-dimensional distributions. The notebook can be found at https://github.com/alexhathaway/cc_layer/tree/master/efficient_mc_sampling. The research was inspired by the EfficientMC paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.08975, which focused on developing a new approach for efficient Monte Carlo simulations. The idea of combining multiple complex-valued affine layers originated from the discussion with Alex Archavi on 2021-02-09. The analysis of complex affine layers was influenced by the MC2 paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.05646, which explored the expansion of Monte Carlo sample space through transformations. The combination of standard affine layers with MC2 is inspired by the Model Mean paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.08975, which focused on the efficient simulation of complex distributions. The analysis of affine layers in the latent variable disposal scenario was influenced by the Latent Variable paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.08975. The proliferation of social media has led to widespread use, with users employing platforms to voice opinions on various topics. Social media content is often informal, consisting of narrative structures that mirror real-life conversations. Effective comprehension of social media posts relies on grasping their narrative frameworks, which is crucial for grasping the intended meaning. In this study, we focus on extracting the narrative structures from social media posts to facilitate informed decision-making. We recognize that human annotators are irreplaceable due to the subjective nature of narrative structures and the diversity of social media content. Thus, we undertake an in-depth examination of existing narrative detection methods. Our analysis reveals a lack of thorough investigations into this topic and identifies gaps in current research. As a result, we initiate a new suite of tasks centered on detecting narratives in social media posts. We have released a freely accessible corpus of annotated data, known as NarrMD, comprising 1,968 posts from Twitter and Facebook. We have also developed a baseline benchmark consisting of machine learning and deep learning approaches. We conduct thorough experiments and introduce an innovative strategy, Compose-CNN, which yields exceptional performance. In task 1, related entities are accurately identified with an F1 score of 0.6344, while in task 2, we achieve an F1 score of 0.6944 in categorizing entities. Task 3 demonstrates that stories can be accurately reconstructed from limited information with an F1 score of 0.5444. We have made our implementation available for reproduction of results. In addition, we believe the released corpus and benchmark will serve as valuable resources for future research on detecting narratives in social media posts. We intend to continue exploring this topic and welcome the participation of researchers in developing more sophisticated models. Deep neural networks are susceptible to minor alterations in input data, 
undermining their reliability. Although recent studies have explored ways to 
boost robustness through constraints on model weights and inputs, these methods 
fail to provide a comprehensive framework that addresses both aspects simultaneously.
 Moreover, they often lead to suboptimal performance due to the imposition of 
excessive constraints. In this research, we develop a framework for training deep 
models robustly against arbitrary input perturbations. By introducing an adaptive 
upper limit on the predicted output, we enable the model to withstand extreme 
perturbations. This approach is combined with an information-theoretic loss function 
and iterative calibration, resulting in a framework that optimizes robustness and 
accuracy simultaneously. The efficacy of our method is demonstrated through 
experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, yielding exceptional robustness-accuracy 
tradeoffs compared to the current state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our model 
demonstrates remarkable resilience against unseen input transformations, such as 
removal of key features. The code for our framework is publicly available at https://github.com/srushicd/adaptive_deep_robustness.

We introduce a new diffusion model for evaluating rumor propagation, where the spread and decline of rumors are analyzed through nonlinear equations mimicking diffusion processes. By applying this model to real-world data, we can gain insights into how different factors influence a rumor's peak and decline. Our analyses reveal that a rumor's impact is affected by its initial promotion, surrounding information, and the presence of counter-information. We can predict a rumor's peak intensity with high accuracy when we consider both precursor features and spatial information. Additionally, using this framework, we can forecast a rumor's lifespan and assess the efficacy of counter-measures in a timely manner. This framework has broad applications, such as evaluating crisis management strategies and predicting a rumor's magnitude before it reaches its peak. We can also modify the model to study the propagation of multiple co-existing rumors. Our approach can serve as a powerful tool for understanding social network phenomena. We can apply this framework to any given diffusion process, such as the propagation of flu outbreaks, by replacing social network data with transmittal records and adjusting the model accordingly. For instance, we use this framework to investigate two notable rumors from WeChat and Sina Weibo, as well as a major flu outbreak in Guangdong, China in Spring 2020. Our results show that there is a close resemblance between the predicted and actual patterns of rumor propagation and flu diffusion. This framework and its resulting findings can guide policymakers in understanding rumor propagation and developing effective counter-measures. Our analysis offers a novel and practical approach to studying social network phenomena and provides a useful tool for comprehending and predicting various types of social network-driven processes. Our method is also versatile and can be applied to different types of diffusion processes by modifying the data and model parameters accordingly. Furthermore, we have made our analysis code and data available on GitHub for reproduction and further investigation. In addition, we have developed a user-friendly GUI tool using Python's PyQt5 library to facilitate the selection of input data, running the code, and plotting the results in accordance with our methodology. This tool enables users to execute our analysis on their own social network data by choosing the relevant files and clicking a button. We have included a detailed explanation of the code and data in the repository for easy reference. We hope that our study will inspire researchers to utilize our model to investigate various social network phenomena and provide valuable insights to policymakers. We also hope that our code and data will promote reproducibility in social network research and encourage further study on social network phenomena. Deep neural networks have created remarkable achievements in various fields but face challenges due to their large size, which poses significant compression challenges. Various methods, such as quantization, pruning, and compact architecture design, have been applied to reduce the network's dimensions. Nevertheless, the existing research often focuses on a single compression technique and lacks a comprehensive framework for combining different methods. This study introduces a novel framework known as Neo-NPP, which utilizes the neural process theory to capture the inherent characteristics of data and accurately preserve the original information even when the network is compressed. By embedding a memory module and utilizing the neural process theory, Neo-NPP is capable of compressing deep neural networks under various constraints while maintaining superior performance. Comprehensive experiments were conducted on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, ImageNet, and Mini-ImageNet datasets, and the results show that Neo-NPP achieves superior accuracy compared to the current state-of-the-art compression techniques, which were either accuracy-limited or hard to generalize, and demonstrates excellent generalization capabilities. Furthermore, the proposed theorem-related theories provide valuable insights into the underlying characteristics of deep neural networks, which may contribute to improved understanding of generalization in the future. The proposed framework and related theories are made available on a public GitHub platform for the benefit of the research community. The proposed framework has potential to accelerate the development of compressed deep neural networks. Based on the authors' knowledge, this is the first study to apply the neural process theory for compressing deep neural networks. The authors are not aware of any previous studies applying the neural process theory to deep neural networks. This research is original and contributes to the field of compressed deep neural networks. The potential applications of this research include accelerated deployment of deep neural networks on edge devices such as smartphones, drones, and autonomous vehicles. The main challenges addressed by this research include the existing gaps in compression methods that can lead to reduced model accuracy, the difficulty in combining different compression techniques, and the lack of generalizable compression frameworks for deep neural networks. The proposed framework, Neo-NPP, addresses these challenges by proposing a new framework for compressing deep neural networks that can easily combine different compression techniques and is generalizable across different scenarios. The experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed framework in compressing deep neural networks without losing their accuracy. In deep learning, choosing the suitable loss function is of utmost importance. Although Cross-Entropy is widely adopted for classification tasks, other loss functions like KL Divergence may be preferred in certain situations. This paper challenges the conventional wisdom that using Cross-Entropy is the best approach and demonstrates, through both theoretical and practical analyses, that under-represented loss functions like KL Divergence can achieve superior performance when compared to the commonly used loss functions. To achieve this, the paper introduces a dynamic scaling factor applied to the loss functions, allowing the model to learn from its predictions with varying levels of confidence. The results are validated on the datasets of CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, where the KL Cross--Entropy loss functions are successfully used in the training of deep neural networks. This research highlights the significance of loss function design and shows that KL Divergence can be an effective choice for deep learning applications. Notably, the novel amplitude meets the requirements of conservation and crossing symmetry more strictly than the traditional parquet amplitude. The strict satisfaction of these constraints enables the novel amplitude to accurately describe both tree-level and loop-level scattering processes at lower energy levels than the traditional parquet amplitude. At the level of two-loop contributions, the novel amplitude accurately describes the correlation of wavefunctions at energy levels as high as $1/N^2$, while the traditional parquet amplitude only achieves this at $1/N$. As an added benefit, the strict conservation and crossing symmetry constraints of the novel amplitude allow it to be applied in the study of non-relativistic scattering processes as well. As such, the novel amplitude provides a more robust model for Hamiltonian-derived amplitudes generally. We investigated the emergence of charge-density-wave (CDW) states in monolayer TiSe$_2$ through comprehensive many-body calculations, focusing on electronic and phononic aspects. Our findings reveal that CDW arises from the self-organization of electrons at the Fermi surface's topological features, driven by electron-phonon interaction and resulting in exciton condensation. Moreover, our model accurately reproduces the observed low-frequency phonon softening phenomenon associated with CDW formation. Our in-depth analysis provides a comprehensive understanding of CDW formation in monolayer TiSe$_2$, encompassing both electronic and phononic aspects. The results show that CDW formation shares similarities with excitonic insulators, and our discovery may pave the way for the development of new excitonic states in 2D transition metal dichalcogenides. Additionally, our calculations are in agreement with experimental observations, highlighting the importance of comprehensive theoretical investigations in advancing our understanding of transition metal dichalcogenides. Moreover, our study introduces a theoretical framework that can be applied to other 2D materials to identify potential excitonic states. This framework analyzes the stability of possible symmetry-allowed CDW patterns in our calculations, demonstrating that the resulting lattice distortions are accompanied by significant changes in the electronic structure, and that the formation of any of these patterns is accompanied by the formation of a van Hove singularity at the Fermi level. However, our discovery in TiSe$_2$ demonstrates that under certain conditions, the excitonic nature of CDW can manifest even in the absence of such singularities, and that the excitonic state may thus represent a new category of quantum many-body effects unique to two-dimensional systems. Finally, the existence of multiple possible CDW patterns in our calculations suggests that their formation may be influenced by an applied strain, allowing for a level of control over their creation and orientation. This capability could be leveraged to modulate their electronic properties, enabling the exploration of new states and phenomena that arise at the interface of strain and electron physics. By adjusting the orientation of the CDW patterns, the excitonic nature of the resulting insulating states can be manipulated, potentially allowing for the development of new methods for controlling quantum many-body effects and their associated electronic properties.
