Emergency dispatch centers gather and process text-based reports of incidents, which dispatchers use to assess risks and dispatch emergency services. Dismissal of these reports, or "risk reports," is a critical task in automating this process. However, reducing manual labor does not necessarily imply lower costs, as accurately categorizing risk reports is a necessary step. Current methods rely on trained machines, but the most effective way to train these models is unknown. Researchers have classified risk reports into "location" and "emergency type" categories to inform development, but these categories underrepresent the complexity of language in these texts. Furthermore, existing work fails to account for the specific characteristics of language used in risk reports, such as the information collected by dispatchers from users in different situations. This paper addresses these shortcomings by providing more detailed categories of risk reports, introducing a data set with thorough annotations, and experimenting with the most effective training techniques. Findings show that models trained on small, high-quality datasets with adjusted training methods can achieve superior performance over prior work on the task. The proposed data set and experiments are designed to support further research in risk report categorization. Additionally, the methodology can be applied in related areas where text categorization is essential. Research on superconductors' properties relies heavily on understanding their electronic structures, particularly how their Fermi surfaces respond to external magnetic fields. Although computational methods can provide detailed band structures, experimental data are often required to validate theoretical predictions. In this study, we utilize ab initio calculations to examine how superconducting materials' topological Fermi surfaces contribute to their magnetic susceptibilities. By analyzing both closed and open Fermi surfaces, we show that certain topological features can lead to non-zero magnetic susceptibilities, with both temperature and field dependencies influenced by electron interactions. Our findings also reveal that both pairing mechanisms and Fermi surfaces play crucial roles in determining superconducting properties. As a case study, we apply our approach to HfGa$_2$ and find that its particular Fermi surface topology results in a distinctive shape, giving it a notable magnetic susceptibility at low temperatures when exposed to a magnetic field. Most surprisingly, however, is that HfGa$_2$ displays no magnetic susceptibility in the absence of a field, yet still exhibits a possible high-temperature superconducting state when doped with impurities. By exploring the electronic structures of superconductors in more detail, we can gain a deeper understanding of their properties and how they respond to external stimuli, paving the way for advancements in theoretical and experimental research in the field. Moreover, our study demonstrates that Fermi surfaces can be effectively modified through mechanical stress, offering a promising new direction for research in materials science. Finally, our work also indicates the potential of using magnetic field alignment to control the orientation of superconducting thin films, an area that warrants further investigation. In addition, our results have significant implications for the design of new superconducting materials by tuning electronic structures through chemical doping, a process that can result in novel quantum states emerging at the Fermi surfaces. In particular, we examine the case of Sgraffiti, a previously unknown quantum state that arises when the Fermi surface topology undergoes a sharp topological transition, and we show that it can be realized in the superconductor HfGa$_2$ through a gradual chemical doping process. In this new regime, Sgraffiti exhibits unique features such as fragmented Fermi surfaces, a rich phase diagram, and distinctive responses to external stimuli, including a magnetic field. In conclusion, our theoretical framework offers a valuable tool for exploring the electronic structures of superconductors in the Sgraffiti regime, and it can be applied to a wide range of materials in the near future. This paper addresses the issue of biased model sampling by introducing a new
approach to active learning that strikes a balance between semi-supervised and
deep learning techniques. The proposed algorithm, semi-supervised minimax
entropy-based active learning (SSEAL), aims to mitigate the limitations of
uncertainty and diversity in traditional methods. By incorporating both class
probabilities and pairwise sample similarities, SSEAL optimizes the acquisition
of new labeled data points by minimizing discrepancies between predicted and
true distributions, while also encouraging similarity among classes and maximizing
entropy among non-selected data points. The effectiveness of SSEAL is evaluated
through comprehensive experiments on multiple datasets, which demonstrate its
superior performance compared to established active learning algorithms. The code
is publicly available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/sravijeet/SSEAL.

In the realm of audio, the unique character of voice or instrument sounds is referred to as timbre. Although the impact of audio processing technology has increased the variety of timbre available, the average musical instrument sound used in popular songs remains remarkably similar decade after decade. This study examines the similarity of timbre in popular songs across various decades from the 1950s to the 2010s. Interestingly, the data reveal a distinct pattern of groups, each with distinct timbre characteristics, spanning five decades each. Notably, the timbre profiles of songs released in the 1960s, 1970s, and 2000s are notably different from one another, while those from the 1950s and 1990s also have distinct features. This research also involved identifying genres based on timbre, which showed that specific genres like hip-hop and electronic music have consistent timbre characteristics across different decades. Additionally, the analysis explores how the use of digital audio workstations has influenced the development of timbre over the past three decades. Overall, the findings suggest that the evolution of timbre in popular songs is a gradual process, spreading from the entry of electronic music in the 1960s to the widespread adoption of digital music production by the 2000s. Unfortunately, the data do not fully capture the diversity of African music, which is known for its distinctive sound characteristics. Therefore, the inclusion of additional data from non-Western sources is recommended for a more comprehensive understanding of the evolution of timbre. This research is significant in that it sheds light on the dynamics of sound characteristics in the popular songs of the 20th and 21st centuries. Furthermore, the findings highlight the significant impact of technological advancements on the development of sound profiles over time. Additionally, the data show that the variety of sound characteristics in popular songs is relatively stable, while the classification of genres based on sound characteristics is more dynamic. In the framework of proof-theoretic semantics, different types of sequent calculi are associated with distinct roles: some serve as base systems providing a direct interpretation of semantic properties through cut elimination, whereas others are derived and can be regrounded in terms of the base systems. The original intentions behind this approach are reflected in the way containment relationships between systems are defined, where the existence of a base system is a necessary condition for the existence of a derived system. Conversely, the existence of a derived system is seen as indicating derivability, effectively making the base system redundant. However, the purpose of this article is to challenge this stance by arguing that base and derived systems should be equally valued. Therefore, a revised definition of containment is proposed that is independent of cut elimination, and the article continues by exploring the implications of this definition on the classification of sequent calculi. Specifically, it is discovered that for a particular type of sequent calculus, positive and negative, base and derived systems are interchangeable, and as a result, the article offers an alternative classification that is independent of cut elimination. Ultimately, the article concludes by examining the implications of the proposed definition on the classification of predicate calculus. In particular, it is observed that the widely recognized distinctions between different types of predicate calculus - such as intuitionistic, classical, and minimal - are not necessarily reflected in the classification of their base systems. Consequently, the article proposes the introduction of a new type of minimal predicate calculus that is distinct from both intuitionistic and classical predicate calculus. Finally, the article concludes by exploring the prospects and challenges of applying proof-theoretic semantics to other areas of mathematics, and in particular to set theory and category theory. In this context, the article notes the presence of two distinct types of semantic objects - namely categories and cut elimination theorems - and offers an interpretation of their relationship through the lens of containment. The configuration space of vortex loops in a 2D ideal fluid, where extra information about the direction of each point on the loop is available, is studied.  The reason for introducing this extra information is to fix and study the configuration space of 'pointed' vortex loops.  A pointed vortex loop is a loop in the 2-dimensional plane with a fixed point at its center, representing the location of its 'point'.  Including this extra information results in a changed topology compared to the standard vortex loop configuration space, specifically a pointed vortex loop cannot be deformed into a different pointed vortex loop if their enclosed areas are different.  Calculations of the paired action for the standard vortex loop configuration space, modified to account for the included point, show that it mirrors the configuration space of loop coordinates with a fixed area, effectively reducing to the standard vortex loop scenario.  These calculations also reveal an infinite set of paired actions for the configuration space of pointed vortex loops, each corresponding to fixing an enclosed area and including additional information about the loop's configuration.  These findings demonstrate that the paired action can be effectively utilized in studying the properties and dynamics of a wide array of loop-based configuration spaces, with varying parameters.  Furthermore, an analogy with the statistical mechanics of 1-dimensional gas was utilized to derive paired actions for the standard vortex loop configuration space at different temperatures.  These findings show that the paired action shows temperature dependence, contradicting initial conjectures.  Finally, an approach to studying the duality between the paired actions of the configuration space of pointed vortex loops and the loop's hyperbolic version, known as the Vortex ring, is introduced and explored.  These findings suggest that the paired actions for the Vortex ring's configuration space can be derived from those of the pointed vortex loops, by fixing an enclosed area and including the point at its center. The tau Collaboration's experiment, conducted at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory from 1979 to1999, gathered a substantial amount of tau data but did not measure certain decay modes that use the tau's full momentum. To evaluate the risk of airborne transmission, we examined particle transport on a per-person basis in various models, including a simple well-mixed model, an airflow-based model, and a more intricate airflow-resolved model. We calculated aerosol concentration using the average distance particles travel, and applied Gaussian distributions to represent the particle plumes. Subsequently, we used Monte Carlo simulations to calculate the probability of exposure to particles exceeding a certain threshold, either by integrating the concentration over time or utilizing the peak concentration and duration of particle transport. We found the well-mixed model to be a reasonable, yet conservative approximation for estimating aerosol concentration, with an average error of 17%. Notably, the ratio of aerosol size was a crucial factor in distinguishing between well-mixed and airflow-based models, highlighting their respective domains of applicability. Ultimately, while the complex model yielded the most accurate predictions, the well-mixed model proved adequate for rapid assessments of infection risk. Our study provides a framework for evaluating the risk of airborne transmission in various environments. For a fully isolated room with a particle size of 5 $\mu$m, we found the probability of transmission to be less than $10^{-4}$, even at a particle concentration of 100 $\mu$g/m$^3$. In contrast, in a community where the new coronavirus has spread, the probability of transmission could be as high as 0.4% when wearing no mask and distanced at least 1.5 meters, or 0.3% when wearing a mask and distanced at least 2 meters. We have made our model and code available to facilitate further analysis of airborne pathogens. In the realm of autonomous navigation, both local and global mapping techniques are crucial for efficient operation.  Local mapping involves correcting current pose estimates through sensor data and is essential for maintaining low-dimensional maps.  Global mapping, on the other hand, involves reconstructing a detailed 3D environment from sensor data, often using optimization techniques.  While these approaches are effective individually, integrating them can lead to complex and inefficient computation.  This paper presents a model-agnostic method called MemoNav that streamlines the navigation process by selectively utilizing sensor data and map information, ultimately resulting in a significant improvement in computation efficiency.  Compared to traditional navigation methods, memoization-based navigation using MemoNav shows a remarkable 10 times faster response time and 6 times faster convergence time when using a simulated dataset of outdoor scenes.  This improvement in computation efficiency enables real-time navigation on mobile devices, even when using global mapping.  A video demonstrating MemoNav's capabilities is available at https://youtu.be/6K1q1kF7C9E.  A detailed description of the work is included in the paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.00677.  All related code is publicly accessible at the GitHub repository https://github.com/stratigosimo/MemoNav.  A related paper titled "Real-time Outdoor Localization on Mobile Devices" has been published at the International Conference on Robotics and Mechatronics (RaM'20) and is included in the conference proceedings as paper number RAME20-01.  This work was previously presented in an invited speech at the International Symposium on Robotics (ISR'19) and is included in the conference proceedings and opening address as paper number 1. This article examines the hypothesis that complex numbers are the underlying foundation of Quantum Mechanics. We conduct an in-depth analysis of which aspects of Quantum Mechanics rely on complex numbers and which do not. It is evident that expressing wave functions as complex functions, employing Hermitian operators for observables, and using unitary transformations for state transformations are core, essential principles of the theory. These concepts cannot be eliminated in favor of alternative approaches based on real functions, such as the proposed real-based Riemann-Hilbert problem. We further demonstrate that not only are complex numbers beneficial in understanding Quantum Mechanics, but they also facilitate elegant mathematical treatments, allowing for straightforward derivations of nontrivial consequences like the Compton scattering formula and the calculation of absorption and reflection coefficients in Quantum Electrodynamics. In conclusion, complex numbers make significant contributions to the formulation and mathematical coherence of Quantum Mechanics. Additionally, our study reveals that the standard approach to perturbative calculation, rooted in perturbation theory, is incompatible with the principle of superposition and that the total absorption amplitude invariably emerges through interference. This understanding is crucial for interpreting cross-talk in multiple Quantum Electrodynamics cavities. In response to this finding, we propose an inductive approach to perturbative calculation, which we believe may serve as a more effective template for analogous problems in various contexts of Quantum Mechanics, such as Quantum Field Theory. In contrast to the traditional approach, which often delays the introduction of complex numbers until the start of a Riemann-Hilbert problem using real functions, we recommend integrating the principles of complex numbers and complex calculus into the very beginning of the course, as this promotes more efficient learning. In the spirit of this recommendation, we present an innovative, computationally efficient method for calculating higher-order perturbations in Quantum Electrodynamics, which involves using the Cauchy integral formula to bypass the need for ad-hoc division of the complex plane into intervals. This simple, general approach for perturbation calculations can serve as a valuable teaching tool and inspires the development of novel algorithms for calculating real physical quantities, as exemplified by the example of calculating absorption and reflection coefficients. In addition, we show that our method facilitates the straightforward derivation of the Landau-Lifschitz gyromagnetic effect equation, found to be equivalent to an integral equation involving only real functions, which has potential applications in the study of ferromagnetic quantum mechanics. This study examines the effectiveness of oxygen-containing aerosols in enhancing sulfur dioxide removal through photofalloff reactions in an ozone-ultraviolet reactor. Optimal reactor size and reaction time were determined by computational models, considering various initial sulfur dioxide and ozone concentrations. Experimental trials using a 30-mL reactor verified the predicted conditions, revealing that a 10-minute reaction time and 5.0 μm aerosol diameter yielded the highest removal rate of sulfur dioxide. Furthermore, the study investigates how aerosol density and initial sulfur dioxide concentrations affect the removal efficiency of sulfur dioxide. It was discovered that increasing sulfur dioxide concentrations do not significantly alter the required aerosol density, indicating that a minimum aerosol density is necessary to achieve a certain level of sulfur dioxide removal. This research provides a fundamental understanding of using ozone and ultraviolet radiation for fossil fuel combustion flue gas desulfurization applications. Based on the results, it is recommended to utilize a 30-mL reactor for both low and intermediate sulfur dioxide concentrations, whereas a larger 60-mL reactor is advised for high sulfur dioxide concentrations and/or extended reaction times. Additionally, the study explores potential alternatives to silica for producing the desired aerosol properties, identifying that a 50% glycerol solution demonstrates similar effectiveness. This research is expected to contribute to the development of innovative, ozone-based technologies for the removal of air pollutants in the future. As artificial neural networks continue to advance, complex models are being implemented on neuromorphic accelerators, but accurate software-based simulations on conventional CPUs are becoming increasingly time-consuming. To speed up simulations, hardware-based prototyping involves building and mapping digital versions of the hardware on Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), but accurate software-based hardware models are lacking. To address this, a proposed model extracts the structural characteristics of neuromorphic accelerators from hardware description languages and uses these to create a software model that can mimic the hardware's behavior. By converting the FPGA-based models into software models, the models can run directly on the GPU, allowing for faster comparison of simulated and actual outcomes. Furthermore, this abstract model can also generate input data, enabling the simulation of different hardware models, evaluation of their performance, and identification of correlations between their structural characteristics and functional capabilities. Preliminary results indicate that changes in hardware architecture have a significant impact on simulation speed, while software model architecture affects accuracy and throughput. Consequently, optimizing hardware architecture affects both accuracy and throughput. Additionally, varying hardware models' accuracy and energy efficiency, software models can be fine-tuned based on desired results. Future work involves incorporating more complex neural network patterns and evaluating how hardware architecture affects software models' input data. This research has the potential to accelerate simulations of neuromorphic accelerators in computational neuroscience and hardware-based prototyping in the electronics industry. A new concept called Indecision Trees is introduced, which are graphical models that formalize computational uncertainty and non-determinism in machine learning algorithms. By combining uncertainty and action dimensions, Indecision Trees encompass a broad range of methods, including Thompson sampling, exploratory learning, and counterfactual reasoning. Indecision Trees offer a general approach for designing sampling policies that balance exploration and exploitation, and this methodology is applied to solving the most difficult bandit problems. It is shown that Indecision Trees yield accurate general-purpose machines capable of performing well on a variety of tasks without the need for task-specific training. Furthermore, Indecision Trees provide a useful framework for analyzing and generalizing known solutions to bandit problems as well as developing new methods for handling complex observational dependencies. The concept of Indecision Trees offers a novel perspective on machine learning algorithms and provides a useful tool for designing sampling policies and empirical generalization. The utility of Indecision Trees is demonstrated through its application to a complex real-world problem, and the approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on various benchmark tasks by continuously adapting a general-purpose machine capable of providing accurate predictions for bandit problems. The results reveal that Indecision Trees produce predictions on par with specialized machines in a range of scenarios, and the approach outperforms comparable methods on several benchmark tasks. The accuracy of the model is assessed through a novel metric called the confidence-calculated squared error. Given its utility and the ease of its implementation, Indecision Trees offer a useful framework for addressing complex machine learning challenges. The code for reproducing the findings is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/alexh73/indecision-trees. Similarity search over time series is a crucial operation with numerous applications, including signal detection and classification. The existing indexes such as EAHT, AEAHT, and TEEAHT, have achieved significant success in improving search efficiency, but their efficiency is restricted by the fixed tree structure and do not adapt to the characteristics of the given database. This study proposes enhanced techniques including early abandoning (EA) and approximate editing distance (AED) to optimize search process, and proposes adapted versions of these indices with efficient tree reconfiguration capabilities. Experimental results show that the proposed techniques can reduce the average time complexity from O(log^2 N) to O(log N), and the average distance from O(log^2 N) to O(log N), respectively. Furthermore, the integrated proposed index can reduce the overall processing time by up to 27 times compared to the original index without adaptation. The proposed index also demonstrates superior performance, up to 2.85 times faster and 1.88 times faster than other competing indexes, including TEEAHT and AEHT, respectively, across various databases and distance measures. Online judge platforms and testing systems for code allow instructors to assess student submissions against predefined cases, measuring performance in terms of code efficiency and quality. However, giving individual feedback to multiple students can be a daunting task due to the large number of submissions a system handles. This problem is addressed by introducing a rapid feedback generator, an AI-powered tool that provides instant feedback to students. The tool has been trained on a comprehensive dataset of code samples, defects, and associated feedback from experienced programmers. When a new submission is made, the AI model uses this dataset to identify patterns and potential issues, providing feedback in the form of diagnostic messages. An experiment was conducted to compare the effectiveness of human-provided feedback against feedback generated by the AI model. The results showed that code efficiency, as measured by the AI model, closely mirrors human assessments, indicating that the tool is a reliable alternative for providing feedback, especially in scenarios where resources are limited. The implementation of the rapid feedback generator is also discussed, highlighting its potential to enhance the efficiency and scalability of online judge systems and testing systems for code. Complex machine learning models are often referred to as "black boxes" due to their non-transparency. This makes it difficult to understand the basis of their decisions, which is critical in fields like medicine and law. We propose using simplified symbolic models to interpret complex classifiers. By extracting general rules from selected data examples, these models shed light on the decision-making process of their black-box counterparts. To test the effectiveness of symbolic models, we assess their ability to replicate the decisions of a complex classifier and compare the results of two different symbolic model construction methods. The analysis demonstrates that symbolic models can accurately predict new data points and reveal how the black-box classifier uses specific input features to make decisions. Furthermore, symbolic models can identify and eliminate redundant features, potentially reducing the number of necessary inputs. We outline potential future applications of symbolic models, including using them to create more efficient classification systems and to explain the decisions of existing systems. Additionally, we suggest the symbolic model as a robust classifier in its own right, which can provide stable predictions even on datasets with inconsistencies. We outline a future research agenda, which could involve assessing the performance of symbolic models against other types of machine learning models, as well as using symbolic models to create more accurate regression models. Our analysis utilizes high-resolution weak-lensing maps of 139 galaxy clusters from the KiDS survey, creating detailed mass maps that correspond to the distribution of subhalos within the clusters. These mass maps show significant small-scale features that align with theories predicting subhalos at comparable magnitudes. To test this further, we examine the impact of mass perturbers as small as 10% of the central galaxy's mass that are embedded in the core of the galaxy cluster. We discovered that subtletial mass perturbers as small as 10% of the central galaxy's mass can produce noticeable lensing distortions, which implies that many of the galaxy cluster mass maps are likely affected by internal subhalos. Additionally, we found that the mass maps tend to overestimate the abundance of subhalos by approximately 30%, with the largest discrepancies observed in the mass ranges between approximately 10-400 M⊙. This overestimation may contribute to the previously observed discrepancies between the predicted and observed number of subhalos in galaxy clusters. Our study sets the stage for future surveys such as LUKE to have higher precision and resolution to study the internal dynamics of galaxy clusters in depth. A comprehensive analysis within the $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model assesses the performance of two types of cosmological models in explaining observational evidence - a polynomial and an exponential model, each featuring the $\alpha$-attractor mechanism, thereby incorporating a dynamical scalar field with a specific potential form. By examining the likelihood of these models using the WAFT++ simulator and combining Planck, Supernovae, Hubble, and Alcock-Cock cosmological observations, results indicate that the polynomial model displays a marginally better fit than the exponential model and a slightly better fit than the $\Lambda$CDM model, with the latter being the most suitable for explaining the observed data. Furthermore, a combined examination of cosmological observations reveals that the marginally better fit of the polynomial model translates into a slight preference for this model over the exponential and $\Lambda$CDM models, with the highest likelihood. Consequently, the study's findings suggest that the $\alpha$-attractor mechanism in the polynomial model offers a more suitable description of the observed evidence compared to both the exponential model and the $\Lambda$CDM model. This paper explores these challenges and offers solutions to ensure the efficient design and implementation of quanity of annotated data biobanks, which will in turn facilitate the integration of artificial intelligence in medical image analysis. Specifically, we examine the current state of biobanks from the perspective of technical feasibility and discuss the practical implications of existing design models. Ultimately, we suggest an innovative model for quanity of annotated data biobanks that harmonizes current trends and sets the stage for the successful deployment of artificial intelligence in medical image analysis. This model emphasizes the importance of having a unified view of the biobank's data and functions, which can be achieved through the application of modern information technology concepts to support the storage, organization, and governance of medical images and associated data. This model also serves as a guide to help users evaluate the technical aspects of biobanks and identify the characteristics that make a biobank suitable for the deployment of artificial intelligence technologies. This assessment is instrumental in identifying potential and providing a strategy for optimizing the technical infrastructure of existing biobanks to meet the requirements of efficient deep learning workflows. This study was conducted as part of the HADES project, which received funding from the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation program. Our findings are based on the analysis of 14 biobanks that participate in the project and are presented in relation to the deployment of a specific deep learning pipeline for the diagnosis of quantiative lung diseases. These recommendations are grounded in the principles of modern information technology and are founded on the successful experience gained through the implementation of the HADES platform. Excessive reliance on hospital data has hindered the development of accurate predictions for less represented conditions. We aim to determine the effectiveness of data augmentation in enhancing diagnosis for skin conditions, with and without clinical features. Augmenting skin cancer images using data augmentation methods is tested alongside utilizing an autoencoder to generate virtual skin cancer images. The techniques are evaluated on two datasets, including the PH2 dataset with clinical features and a custom dataset without clinical features. The results show that while data augmentation methods have a limited impact when used with clinical features, they significantly improve accuracy when clinical features are absent. Conversely, the autoencoder method fails to yield notable improvements in both scenarios. These findings suggest that supplementing limited datasets with augmented images can be an effective strategy. The generated images may also share characteristics with real images, enhancing model performance. However, the benefits come with increased risk of misclassifying images, highlighting the need to assess model performance on real and augmented data separately. The generated images are observable to humans but also detectable by algorithms, raising questions about their potential use in training medical models. We examined stable patterns of oscillations within populations of coupled oscillators, where each oscillator has multiple stable states. Unlike systems that only switch between states when triggered by external events, these oscillators change states based on their neighbors' current state. We discovered that a type of non-linear interaction, typically prevalent in systems biology, can create long-term stable periods of oscillation. These periods are characterized by repeated cycles of a specific state, lasting for an even number of steps. We found that a wide range of stable periods can coexist, even when the system is driven by identical oscillators. Additionally, we identified conditions under which a wide range of stable periods will emerge, by analyzing the system's behavior during small changes over time. Notably, we observed that periods of 2, 4, 8, etc., are inherently stable, and other periods can also be stable under specific circumstances. We found that a type of weak dispersion, affecting how oscillators interact with each other, can create long-term stable periods, even in systems where a type of strong dispersion is present. The goal of tuning algorithm hyperparameters is to optimize model performance, yet the usual optimization methods often struggle to achieve consistent results. This paper reveals how interacting hyperparameters can significantly impact the stability of learned models, as well as the accuracy of predictions made using these models. Through statistical analysis, we identify a clear indication of interaction effects on algorithm performance and confirm these findings experimentally, shedding light on the stability of hyperparameter configurations. Interestingly, our results also demonstrate that the presence of noise can both enhance model generalization and undermine algorithm performance, often in a dependent manner. These findings are substantiated across multiple benchmark datasets and algorithms, offering a framework for future research on algorithm stability. Additionally, our study highlights the importance of considering both prediction accuracy and model stability when evaluating hyperparameter configurations, suggesting a more comprehensive assessment of algorithm performance. Overall, our investigation promotes a deeper understanding of algorithm stability, paving the way for more effective hyperparameter optimization strategies. Based on these insights, we introduce a straightforward approach to optimizing algorithm robustness, which can be incorporated into existing optimization frameworks as a means of enhancing model performance. The potential of using low-quality video for representation learning is also examined, showing promising outcomes. Ultimately, the results suggest that utilizing visual information can contribute substantially to representation learning in speech processing, even when the video quality is poor. Additionally, we examine the subgroup numbers of the direct products $C_{2^{2k-1}} \times C_{2^{2k-1)}}$ and $C_{p^{2k-1}} \times C_{p^{2k-1}} \times C_{p^{2k-1}}$ for $k \geq 2$ and odd prime $p$. Further research involves the analysis of the subgroup numbers of the Camina groups $2^{2k-1}$$\cdot$$C_2$ and $p^{2k-1}$$\cdot$$C_2$ for $k \geq 2$ and odd prime $p$. In machine learning, graph neural networks are widely used to analyze nodes connected in complex networks, but social relationships within these networks are often not considered. To address this gap, we present Relationship Graph Neural Networks (R-GNNs) that effectively learn from node relationships, incorporating social aspects into the machine learning framework. By leveraging a learned graph, R-GNNs' key component is a social relationship updater module based on Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), which iteratively refines relationship states through recurrent neural network interactions, ultimately producing node relationship vectors that are combined with node features for node classification. Experimental evaluations on four datasets demonstrate that R-GNNs outperform baseline graph neural network models, including Deep Graph Neural Networks and Graph Convolutional Networks. Our approach also autoconstructs meaningful graph topologies, showcasing its capability to automatically generate effective social networks for classification tasks. Our implementation is available on GitHub at https://github.com/y0y0y0/R-GNN. Our code has been successfully tested on Ubuntu 18.04 and PyTorch 1.5.0. Our visualized results are available at https://y0y0y0.github.io/2020/07/09/R-GNN.html. Our research was conducted at Purdue University, supported by the generosity of University.

Implementing neural networks on smaller-scale systems such as RISC-V is becoming a requirement. However, existing neural network architectures are designed for larger-scale CPUs like Intel Core i7, which leads to inefficient execution and inefficient use of on-chip resources on RISC-V-based systems. To overcome this challenge, we are developing a first fully integrated neural network accelerator for modern, general-purpose RISC-V processors. To achieve efficient execution, we propose a new adaptive sampling technique that prunes fewer nodes from the graph. Additionally, we introduce a resource-aware algorithm that optimizes the microcontroller's resources for image classification. Moreover, our solution excels in poor-quality datasets, matching the performance of state-of-the-art transformers like ResNet 50 for semantic segmentation. The proposed adapter and algorithm combination successfully reduce the number of operations, resulting in up to 25 times fewer computations than existing accelerators, without affecting precision. The proposed solution also successfully reduces the energy consumption by 20 times. In the field of Digital Signal Processing, the design of Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) circuits plays a crucial role, particularly in the context of Fixed Point Hardware Implementation. The conventional rule for approximating the MCM area under Weighted Error (WRE) has been widely utilized. However, this approach involves computational complexities that scale with the number of bits in the representation of inputs. In an effort to streamline this process, we have developed a set of rules for propagating errors, which can be utilized in a graph-based approach for efficiently estimating the area associated with MCM circuits and their approximate variants. The proposed error propagation rules enable the determination of the least significant bit position without requiring the representation of inputs. Additionally, we have developed a graph-based algorithm for determining the most significant bit position in a weighted vector, thereby eliminating the need for input representation in such cases. The proposed error propagation rules can be employed simultaneously to determine both the least and most significant bit positions. The proposed approach was validated through comparative studies with existing methodologies, revealing that it results in a reduction of computational complexity by a factor of $O(N)$, where $N$ denotes the number of bits in the representation of inputs. Comparative evaluations with other approximate logic synthesis methodologies revealed that the proposed approach results in an $O(N)$-factor improvement in performance. The proposed methodology was further validated through the design of approximate MCM circuits, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in yielding both accurate and efficient results. For instance, an $8$-bit MCM circuit was estimated to be approximately $1.3$ times more area-efficient when employing the proposed approach for a $9$-bit representation of inputs, compared to an $8$-bit representation. In the field of parsing, achieving accurate results with minimal training data is a key goal, especially with the increasing availability of large-scale treebanks. Our proposed model, FPIO, which incorporates a module to encode tree structure information called the Parse Tree Structure Encoder (PTSE), outperforms existing few-shot parsing models when trained with as few 10 annotated tree branches. By enhancing the model's ability to exploit branch structure information, FPIO improves its overall performance, with our experiments demonstrating improved results both in terms of accuracy and speed compared to the existing state-of-the-art models. Our source code and model weights will be made available for public use.

Semi-supervised semantic segmentation in hyperspectral images remains an underexplored topic in current research. Due to the coarseness of standard labels, semi-supervised methods have been hindered in extracting precise image information. To address this issue, we introduce a new hyperspectral image segmentation framework, Leveraging Precise Labels for Efficient Segmentation (LAPLES). This approach incorporates refined labels from hyperspectral images through transfer learning, allowing existing models to adapt to the new images. By utilizing the derived features, a base classifier can accurately segment the images. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by adapting a widely used model, DeepLabv3+, and comparing its performance with other self-supervised and supervised methods on three diverse hyperspectral image datasets. The results reveal that our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of segmentation accuracy, particularly on datasets with limited labeled data. This research showcases the potential of semi-supervised segmentation in diverse real-world applications with refined labels. The associated code is accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/Indigo-Technologies/LAPLES. A prevalent class of recurrent neural networks called RNNs has been widely employed in object categorization using image descriptors. Nonetheless, there hasn't been a thorough examination into how auxiliary variables influence the performance of these models. To address this gap, we introduce auxiliary variables as additional inputs to RNNs, acting as contextual cues during testing. Our findings indicate that tailored design of these variables, available only during testing, can yield a noticeable enhancement in the models' accuracy by approximately 1%. We also discovered that these variables can simulate diverse environmental conditions such as lighting, view points, and image quality, effectively acting as contextual cues. To facilitate the application of these cues in real-world scenarios, we design a system that can generate them on the fly, ensuring their relevance and effectiveness. Our proposed approach comprises a comprehensive search strategy that involves searching both the structure and the parameters of the RNN jointly. Notably, the resulting model surpassed the state-of-the-art performance on the ImageNet dataset for 10-way multi-digit classification tasks. Our auxiliary variables also demonstrate their efficacy on other visual recognition tasks by boosting the models' accuracy and achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Places205 and Caltech256 datasets. Moreover, we found that the RNN's performance is highly sensitive to an approximate 10% change in the variables' values. Based on these findings, we developed a testing-time optimization approach, dubbed RNN stripping, which removes the auxiliary variables from the RNN while minimizing its performance impact. Our experiments confirm the efficacy of this approach, with minimal accuracy loss of only 1% when removing the variables. Interestingly, we observed that the RNN's accuracy declines by at least 5% when its parameters are randomly perturbed, highlighting the importance of the variables in achieving the models' performance. Our proposed approach and the generated contextual cues are available online for reproduction of our results. Moreover, our RNN stripping method can be applied to other deep neural networks to improve their robustness against various adversarial attacks. Our findings suggest that the choice of testing data is a valuable resource that can be leveraged to improve the models' performance, robustness, and efficiency. The field of optimization has seen a surge in interest due to its vast applications in various domains. Researchers and practitioners need a comprehensive and reliable library to test their proposed optimization algorithms against established methods, a requirement that did not have a suitable solution until now. To bridge this gap, we introduce the LibOPT library, an open-source collection of benchmarking functions that supports multiple programming languages. Currently, the library offers 12 basic optimization tasks in real-parameter and integer spaces, along with 12 discrete optimization problems. Each problem has been formulated as a minimization task, allowing users to modify and expand the implementation to suit their needs. LibOPT is designed for ease of use and can be utilized through a variety of example problems, enabling users to reproduce results from recent papers. Our benchmarking functions are consistently formatted to facilitate the comparison of different algorithms, a crucial aspect for producing reproducible results. To verify the correctness of the implemented problems, we conducted a series of validation tests. An in-depth tutorial is provided to guide users through the various features and available problems in the LibOPT library. In the future, we intend to incorporate more optimization tasks and problems to further enhance the library's capabilities. Ultimately, the LibOPT library aims to promote benchmarking as a essential step in the optimization process, allowing researchers to systematically evaluate and compare different algorithms. To our knowledge, LibOPT is the first open-source library dedicated to benchmarking optimization functions, a significant contribution that we hope will benefit the optimization community for many years to come. A Python version of the paper is available online. The source code of the LibOPT library can be freely downloaded from the GitHub repository. Additionally, the GitHub repository includes a comprehensive benchmarking test, benchmarking, and validation code. This research formalizes the Scott model for a programming language that includes exceptional search features, building on earlier work by Russell and Rycroft. We demonstrate that every well-typed program in this language has a corresponding Scott model value, while maintaining the ability to model partial computation through search. This is achieved without resorting to non-constructive reasoning, thanks to the incorporation of introduced axioms for handling exceptions and search results. These introduced axioms enable the derivation of key properties for Scott models, such as extensionality, without relying on non-constructive principles. This study introduces degenerate Eisenstein series derived from the $p$-adic loops on Shimura congruence pairs, specifically focusing on analyzing their linear combinations as they relate to the infinite-dimensional Weyl group cosets. It's essential to understand that boundary contributions from the loops can be challenging. To overcome this, the concept of 'generalized diagonal' is established within the $p$-adic loop domain. This simplified approach enables the calculation of contributions from cosets, ultimately allowing for the creation of characteristic polynomials with degree corresponding to the size of the coset. Notably, one of the series exhibits factorization in terms of the $p$-adic L-functions of weight 1/2, as defined by Gekko and Hida. This finding implies that one of the degenerate Eisenstein series can be represented as a $p$-adic L-function of weight 1/2, as previously proposed by Gekko and Hida. This text presents preliminary results obtained by Fukuda, Gekko, Hida, and Rallis. Also included are additional findings and outcomes. In particular, the concept of degenerate Eisenstein series proves applicable to general linear groups, as demonstrated through the analysis of a specific example involving $SL_2(\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q}))$. Furthermore, the approach presented may find application in the study of general linear groups and their representations. Lastly, the collected data suggests that one of the degenerate Eisenstein series may possess a $p$-adic extension of the Ginzburg-Rallis tensor product of L-functions, as defined in reference [6], a relationship that warrants further investigation. In addition, the concept of degenerate Eisenstein series may also find application in the study of representations of general linear groups, as seen in the included example of $SL_2(\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q})$.

This paper presents a new approach to collision avoidance for mobile robotic arms based on their spatial structure. By transforming the arm into a set of connected frames and converting it into a weighted graph, we develop an efficient collision avoidance algorithm that leverages minimum weight bipartite matching. Compared to a traditional method that treats the arm as a unified entity, our approach results in significantly lower computation times, ranging from 5.8 to 67 times faster, and remains effective even with large numbers of obstacles and internal nodes. Furthermore, we introduce a variable sampling method to optimize arm point selection and propose two strategies to establish a uniform cost function, ensuring the method's applicability across various arm configurations. Numerous experiments validate the efficacy and speed of our proposed collision avoidance algorithm. The code is publicly available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/Chen-Hang/Mobile-robotic-armCollision-Avoidance.

Language processing seeks to analyze and generate diverse forms of communication, including spoken and written dialects. Achieving high-performance models capable of capturing the underlying structure of language, while also facilitating efficient model training and evaluation, remains an ongoing challenge. In particular, models trained on large datasets containing much information irrelevant to the task at hand tend to reproduce noise in their outputs, while evaluation methods often measure task-relevant performance to a limited extent. Furthermore, the reliance of model evaluation on human assessors introduces subjectivity and expense. This research proposes to address these issues through the following contributions: (1) introducing a new measure to correct biases in task outputs; (2) developing an unsupervised approach to eliminate unnecessary information from text data; (3) leveraging expert programming to create customized evaluation tools, including one that requires minimal reliance on human input. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these solutions on a critical task in natural language understanding, where our results indicate that the model with the lowest number of parameters across architectures achieved the highest accuracy in our objective evaluation, while evaluations by both experts and non-experts indicated significant improvements in task performance using our developed tools, underscoring the value of these solutions in related applications. Pulsar halos are large, extended structures composed of energy generated by pulsar winds. Their location near the galactic plane makes them ideal for studying the cosmic positron excess and the diffuse TeV gamma-ray excess. Pulsar wind energy is accelerated and forms a halo through interactions with the surrounding magnetic fields, heat up due to synchrotron cooling, and emit X-ray and gamma-ray radiation. This research examines the characteristics of pulsar halos, identifying their potential to form through magnetic reconnection, and predicts the properties of the emitted radiation. The study also analyzes a pulsar halo's ability to explain the 130 GeV gamma-ray excess and the TeV excess at the FERMI and HESS locations. The results show that a pulsar halo around PSR J1834-0739 could account for the 130 GeV excess, but its contribution to the TeV excess is limited due to its smaller size. The study suggests that a pulsar halo's size and age play a crucial role in its ability to explain the 130 GeV and TeV gamma-ray excesses. The gamma-ray spectra from pulsar halos show that a broken power-law is a better fit than a single power-law, and that a diffusion-limited shock model may be able to reproduce these spectra. The X-ray spectra from pulsar halos can be explained by a thermal plasma model, but additional radiation from a relativistic electron population may be needed to account for the hard X-ray tail. The study also finds that a pulsar halo's energy emission could significantly reduce its Pulsar-driven energy injection into the galactic magnetic fields over a long period of time. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through experiments on standard image classification benchmarks, where Vectorized NGD exhibits improved performance and greater ease of use compared to the existing Natural Gradient Descent algorithm. Furthermore, an in-depth analysis of the underlying mathematical theory of NGD is provided, offering a deeper understanding of this optimization technique and its potential for use in future deep learning applications. Finally, our method can determine the irreducibility of modules for a more general class of algebras, including any algebra that would correspond to $U(𝕙)$ if it were generated by a single element. In text editing, suggestions play a crucial role in assisting users and boosting productivity. A well-trained suggestion system can save significant time when users encounter writing difficulties. The primary goal of this study is to develop an advanced editor with intelligent suggestions, capable of suggesting words that are not only present in the text but also semantically relevant. Building on previous research, we've created hybrid models that combine syntactic and semantic analysis, leveraging both context-free grammar and WordNet. These models, trained on extensive datasets, can suggest words for any given text with remarkable accuracy. Specifically, our "Hybrid 1" model, integrating both analysis methods, achieved an 88% cross-validation score and demonstrated superior performance compared to models utilizing sole syntactic or semantic approaches. Furthermore, by incorporating semantic disambiguation, our model minimized unnecessary and context-inappropriate word suggestions, demonstrating great potential for applications in text editing and related fields. A comprehensive comparison of our hybrid model's performance in comparison to prominent baselines is presented, along with inspiring use cases and future prospects for this research. A personalization framework called attention-based graph embedding learns node representations by focusing on key edges and nodes in graph data, such as social networks, knowledge graphs, and item recommendation graphs. The approach incorporates numerous advances in deep learning, including recurrent neural networks and optimization algorithms, to enable node representation learning. Unlike existing methods, it uses attention mechanisms to enable adaptive edge weighting and node focusing, leading to more efficient graph representation learning. The experiments conducted demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in social network-based learning for tasks such as node classification and link prediction, as well as its application in recommender systems, which yields improved accuracy and transparent decision-making. The source code is available at https://github.com/Sun-Weiguou/AGEN. The framework has potential applications in recommender systems, social media platforms, and graph mining. In addition, it visualizes the learned node representations as clusters in a low-dimensional space, providing insights into node groups and applications in recommender systems, social media platforms, and graph mining. The results show that attention-based graph embedding achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets while performing efficiently. A novel mesh adaptation technique for simulating cracked porous media involves a complex variable partial differential equation that accurately predicts the behavior of fractures by modeling their intersection as conic surfaces. To achieve this, a mesh that accurately reflects the geometry of fractures is essential. The conforming Delaunay tetrahedralization technique can generate such a mesh; however, the growing literature on mesh morphing and transport may offer more efficient alternatives. The potential of these methods for adapting meshes in simulations of porous media is yet to be fully explored. A critical evaluation of current research on mesh adaptation techniques aims to identify the most effective approach, focusing on both the efficiency of mesh generation and the accuracy of the resulting solution. The analysis also examines the scalability and flexibility of these methods in solving problems involving complex geometries and porous media simulations specifically. The objectives of this work are three-fold: to examine the effectiveness of mesh adaptation techniques for simulating porous media, to identify areas for improvement in the existing literature, and to suggest potential avenues for future research. For regions far from the fracture, a mesh with a coarse resolution is desired, while a finely resolved mesh is necessary for the fracture itself to ensure an accurate numerical solution. The study of eigenvalue problems for the Dirac operator, a crucial tool in nonrelativistic quantum mechanics, leads to Heun's equation and connections with tridiagonal operators. This paper explores these connections and, going beyond Dirac's case, examines the general eigenvalue problem for $n \times n$ matrix operators with specific constraints, including a lack of off-diagonal elements. It's notable that some of these operator eigenvalue problems are linked to polynomial properties of exact degree $2n-1$ or $2n$. This understanding enables the derivation of recurrent relations for eigenvalues, including surface criticality examples. Additionally, the study extends to discrete Dirac operators, drawing parallels with Heun's equation and establishing relationships between eigenvalue problems for $2n \times 2n$ matrix operators. Crucially, the study identifies which eigenvalue problems can be considered discrete analogues of Heun's equation. This comprehensive study provides a framework for solving eigenvalue problems, offering insights into the spectral theory of these operators. It's especially significant that many of its findings are applicable to the Standard Model and its extensions in high-energy physics. This research was initially presented in a joint presentation at COST185-P10 at the University of Alcalá de Henares in 2018. Given the audience's diverse backgrounds, the presentation incorporated educational material, making this study an excellent resource on the subject. In this article, we examine vehicle-to-ground communications in heterogeneous vehicular networks, which incorporate vehicles, ground users, and relays operating within the 5 GHz frequency range. By employing stochastic geometry tools, we develop a comprehensive model that enables us to analyze how the deployment of relays influences the average effective communication rate of users on the ground. Our findings reveal that relay placement has a significant impact on ground users, and optimizing vehicular frequencies can lead to a substantial gain in overall network throughput. Moreover, we identify the conditions under which these benefits emerge and provide actionable advice for implementing such communication systems. Additionally, our model allows us to derive bounds on the system's performance across diverse scenarios, including both high and low densities of vehicular deployment. Our results show that in high-density scenarios, the bound on the average effective rate of ground users is influenced by the square root of the ratio of ground to vehicular deployment densities, while in low-density scenarios, the bound is directly proportional to the ratio of ground to vehicular deployment densities. Furthermore, we observe that in high-density scenarios, the bound on the average effective rate of ground users as they communicate with the base station is directly proportional to the square root of the ratio of ground to vehicular deployment densities, while in low-density scenarios, the bound on this rate is directly proportional to the ratio of ground to vehicular deployment densities, and is also directly proportional to the logarithm of the ground deployment density. A new approach, known as decision-based black-box knowledge distillation (DB3), enables a trained student model to learn from its performance on real-world tasks and not just data. DB3 involves pushing the student model to make specific decisions, with the guidance of a trained teacher model. This process aims to enhance the student's performance on a target task. In contrast to conventional knowledge distillation methods that focus on mimicking a teacher model's characteristics, DB3 seeks to boost the student's capabilities by defining better data distribution. This definition, known as the posterior, serves as the ground truth for future data samples and guides the distillation process. In this study, an efficient optimization method was created for DB3 to find the optimal posterior, yielding superior results in comparison to conventional knowledge distillation methods. The findings show that, in many scenarios, the optimal posterior does not match the original data distribution, and DB3 offers a flexible framework for data augmentation, query augmentation, and target shifting. Additionally, it was observed that DB3 enhances the robustness and performance of student models against adversarial attacks. To automate the DB3 process, a simple and efficient algorithm was developed. In experiments involving multiple networks and datasets, including ResNet, MobileNet, and CIFAR-10, among others, it was found that DB3 outperforms conventional knowledge distillation methods by 0.7% to 3.2% in top-1 accuracy. Moreover, the study investigates the relationship between the optimal posterior and data samples, revealing an intriguing connection. To facilitate the use of DB3, a public tool was created and made available on the GitHub platform. In conclusion, this research presents an innovative approach, DB3, as an effective means of black-box knowledge distillation, offering superior performance and adaptable posterior definition. In addition, it was found that the optimal posterior does not necessarily match the original data distribution, offering potential avenues for further exploration. Our approach has the potential to revolutionize learning behaviors by incorporating elements of social interaction and imitated behavior. This paper examines the maximum likelihood (ML) performance of a sequential decoder that operates on binary, independent, memoryless channels with unknown transition probabilities. A key aspect of the decoder's operation is how the decoder initiates on unknown channel state. We investigate how the probability of the decoder erring is influenced by the method of determining the initial channel state uncertainty, specifically the impact of the tradeoff between accurate and uncertain channel state information provided to the decoder. We find that increasing the level of confidence in the channel state information supplied to the decoder leads to more conservative decoding strategies and subsequently, reduced error probabilities. Notably, we identify a critical cutoff rate in channel capacity, below which the decoder benefits from complete information about the channel state, whereas above this threshold, the decoder can tolerate some level of uncertainty. We also determine sequential decoding performance upper bounds for scenarios with uncertain channel state information and establish a decoding method that approaches this maximum, validating the optimality of a specific decoding approach in the case of known channels. We further extend our research to scenarios with evolving channel state information, where we find that utilizing the best available information at each decoding step yields the lowest error probability and demonstrate the benefits of adaptive decoding over fixed channel state information approaches. We also investigate the error asymptotics for scenarios with uncertain and evolving channel state information. We evaluate the performance of these decoding methods in popular channel models - the binary symmetric and binary erasure channels - and explore their application in practical scenarios, including the case of communicating over a binary erasure channel when the other user has significantly higher transmission power. Occlusion poses a significant challenge to model-based hand tracking methods when hands and objects intersect. To overcome this issue, we have developed a novel approach, providing a clear understanding of object geometry, which enables accurate hand and object segmentation as well as interaction prediction even within complex occluded scenarios. Notably, our method demonstrates improved results in handling complex interactions such as crossing hands or using utensils. We obtain the object model's geometric details through an analysis of motion patterns rather than relying on a pre-trained shape prior. This allows our method to effectively predict interactions involving utencils, cutting tasks and other similar actions. Our approach is designed to work in tandem with existing hand tracking methods, providing segmented hand and object representations. A relatively equitable distribution of opportunities is a foundation of a just and fair society, where current decisions do not unfairly impact future generations' chances. In this research, we develop a decision-making framework to create opportunity allocation policies that consider the long-term effects on individuals' socioeconomic status. This is cast as an open-ended multi-objective problem, where each objective represents a socioeconomic factor, such as income or health. To address this complexity, we apply two approaches: one using a simplified model to approximate the long-term effects and another leveraging deep reinforcement learning, which enables us to learn the long-term effects directly from data. Both methods allow us to explore the trade-offs between different opportunity allocation strategies and their impacts on individuals' socioeconomic outcomes. We demonstrate our approach by analyzing a simplified decision-making scenario based on Dynkin's model of genealogy, which helps us to identify opportunities' long-term effects and inform policies that consider the long-term effects on a population's socioeconomic status. This research is presented at the ICML 2021 conference. Therefore, we recommend training language models on larger, more comprehensive datasets such as the one we developed, which incorporates the questions from the LongFormQuestions dataset. This paper explores the trade-offs between cost reduction and performance gain in edge computing, focusing on optimizing a metric that isn't directly measurable. To address this issue, we utilize two approaches: transferring data to the nearest edge server and distributing computations to the nearest edge server. For the first strategy, a data center optimization method with adjustable parameters is proposed, allowing the transfer of multiple blocks at once. This approach is further enhanced by introducing a variable number of parameters that adapt to changing network conditions. For the second strategy, a distributed computation method with adjustable parameters is developed, capable of executing multiple functions simultaneously. Both of these strategies involve changing parameters that must be adjusted in real-time to accommodate network changes. To resolve this problem, we formulate a multi-objective optimization model and utilize an anti-decay particle swarm optimization algorithm to adjust the parameters. Exhaustive simulations reveal that the proposed strategies yield substantial improvements in energy efficiency, achieving a 30% average reduction in energy consumption. Moreover, the simulations demonstrate that the parameters of the first strategy remain relatively stable in various scenarios and can be accurately estimated through two simplified formulas. This allows the parameters to be easily calculated without solving the complex optimization problem, making the strategy suitable for practical implementation. Notably, the results show that the second strategy exhibits a contrary behavior, where increasing the transfer rate often reduces energy efficiency. This means that the benefits of the second strategy may not extend to scenarios with higher transfer rates. To gain insight into the trajectory of these models as they learn, we applied a technique to identify repeating patterns in the output of a pretraining process. Using this information, we developed an alternative that utilizes steady-state speech segments to preserve linguistic integrity, and as a result, achieved a notable enhancement in performance when applied to the task of speech synthesis. This improvement was verified across multiple evaluation metrics and comparison points. We also observed a steady increase in speech segment similarity over time, indicating that the models we tested require a minimum amount of data to establish a base level of accuracy. Our analysis suggests that speech pretraining models enter a period of rapid improvement where they consistently produce high-quality speech, but may still improve their performance in response to additional data. As such, models based on steady-state speech segments present an efficient method for achieving optimal results with a reduced amount of data. Optimizing motion planning for multi-limbed robots is an intricate problem, particularly in searching for collision-free joint configurations that satisfy kinematic constraints. A conventional flatness-based optimization approach can effectively address this issue, but it tends to have a high computational cost associated with the repeated resolution of algebraic equations and differential constraints. To tackle this challenge, we suggest a multi-stage optimization framework that decouples equation resolution from motion planning and utilizes the results in subsequent stages. This approach enables the reuse of equation solutions, offering improved efficiency through batch processing. The proposed framework is evaluated using the SWIM robot and produces meaningful results that outperform traditional optimization methods in terms of performance and accuracy. Furthermore, we investigate the design of multi-limbed robot controllers using this approach and successfully apply it to the control of a 4DOF planar quadruped robot. The developed controller is tested and validated through simulations and real-world experiments. As an added value, we create a open-source simulator built with Madmax to facilitate multi-limbed robot motion planning and control simulations. This tool is accessible at the following repository: https://github.com/laas-cnrs/madmax_swim_simulator. This study proposes an object classification system that employs geometric information from point cloud data. An existing point cloud registration network is initially trained to convert 3D point clouds into a uniform coordinate system, and its learned representations are extracted and utilized as features for object classification. Two approaches are investigated to harness the extracted information: feeding the extracted features directly into a classification model, and combining these features with the transformed point clouds. Moreover, the proposed techniques have been shown to add value in scenarios involving partial occlusions. The proposed system achieved a 2.44% improvement in accuracy on the ModelNet dataset. We introduce the concept of $R_\infty$-nilpotency for groups and study its relationship with other nilpotency variants. Additionally, we establish a nilpotency criterion for groups based on the occurrence of $R_\infty$-elements, and explore the nilpotency levels of certain subgroups of $R_\infty$-groups in relation to their core and radical. Furthermore, we establish that every abelian group with a finite set of generators can be expressed as an $R_\infty$-group, and identify the nilpotency levels for certain class of groups that are not necessarily abelian. This research also includes an examination of nilpotent products of groups with very restricted commutativity. In addition, we derive nilpotency results for certain upper central lengths and other group properties. These findings are validated with numerous examples. This presentation will outline the specific requirements and feasibility of achieving this goal using the International Linear Collider (ILC), emphasizing the potential of the vertex detector in addressing three key challenges associated with precision top quark mass measurement. Firstly, the vertex detector's high vertical resolution can effectively counteract the effects of beam polarization, which decreases the statistical value in Yukawa coupling measurements. Additionally, the vertex detector can help mitigate the impact of radiation effects on the detector's internal sensitivity. Finally, the vertex detector's vertical resolution can improve the precision of rare process data, enabling the achievement of a precise top quark mass as low as approximately 67 MeV/c^2. This presentation will provide an in-depth examination of the ILC's potential to determine the top quark mass, underscoring the significance of a highly performing vertex detector in precision top quark mass measurement and in addressing the associated systematic uncertainties. The study specifically utilizes the 250 GeV center-of-mass energy configuration of the ILC, which is targeted for the initial operational phase. As such, the presentation is well-suited for designers, engineers, and future users of the vertex detector. Furthermore, the presentation highlights the cutting-edge ambitions of the future lepton colliders in terms of precision top quark mass measurement, as well as the innovative contributions that a highly advanced vertex detector can make to the success of these endeavors. Action anticipation, which involves predicting future actions in videos without explicit temporal ground truth, is a crucial aspect of human behavior understanding. Recent work on anticipating actions has mainly focused on utilizing neural networks to model both appearance and dynamics features. However, these models often require extensive annotation for training. In contrast, this study explores the use of kernel-based methods to take advantage of any temporal ground truths available, as well as to model long-term spatiotemporal dependencies in videos. To this end, we propose ActionAnticipator, a novel action anticipation model that combines radial basis function kernels with neural networks. By utilizing radial basis function kernels to model long-term temporal dependencies and taking the gradient with respect to the predicted action labels, ActionAnticipator is able to leverage both appearance and temporal features. Experimental results show that ActionAnticipator achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets, including UCF101-24 and JHMDB-21. Additionally, our ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of using radial basis function kernels. While ActionAnticipator was designed primarily for anticipating actions, its proposed methodological contributions have broader applications in human behavior understanding and related computer vision tasks. The code for ActionAnticipator can be found at https://github.com/hykim96/ActionAnticipator. The pre-trained models and experimental data can be found at https://www.hykim96.com/action-anticipator/. This project was funded by NSF grants 1734833 and 1939136. Hyunsoo Kim is also supported by a Google Research Award. Please contact hyunsoo96@umd.edu for further inquiries. In particular, our proposed radial basis function kernel method can be adapted for use in more established two-stage action recognition models, as well as deep neural network-based models, to anticipate actions. In addition, our work on ActionAnticipator highlights the significance of radial basis function kernels in modeling long-term spatiotemporal dependencies in videos, as well as their integration with neural networks for anticipation. To our knowledge, this is the first time radial basis function kernels have been used in computer vision for anticipating actions. As a result, our proposed method of using radial basis function kernels can be considered an innovative contribution to the field of computer vision.
