By weighting channel state information, the base station can prioritize relevant information, enhancing feature learning and reducing the influence of irrelevant data. We investigate various ways to obtain weights, including global attention, local attention, and a combination of both, as well as an alternative strategy using relative spatial information. Experimental results demonstrate that using attention-based channel state information outperforms other methods, with combinations performing better than individual alternatives. In 1990, the problem of strong edge-coloring in 3-regular bipartite graphs was proposed as Problem 2.2.5 of the Graph Theory colloquium book, and the same source attributed the conjecture to Vrt'o and Gyori. The conjecture stated that these graphs can be strongly edge-colored with the sum of the degrees of any two adjacent vertices. The field has made significant progress since the initial conjecture was made, and the topic remains a focus of current research. This paper recognizes that the original conjecture has been refuted and presents the current state of affiliated work. In particular, it is known that 3-regular bipartite graphs can be strongly edge-colored with the sum of the degrees of any two adjacent vertices plus one, and this property extends to certain 4-regular bipartite graphs where the sum is replaced with the product of the degrees. However, the general 4-regular bipartite graph conjecture remains unsolved. Additionally, it is known that certain classes of 5-regular bipartite graphs can and cannot be strongly edge-colored with the sum of the degrees of adjacent vertices, and this coloring is possible in bipartite 6-regular graphs where the sum exceeds the product of degrees. The study also introduces a new method for strong edge-coloring in 3-regular bipartite graphs and applies it to certain 4-regular bipartite graphs, and this new approach provides insights into current research. The paper primarily focuses on the analysis of known results and presents new methods for strong edge-coloring in 3-regular bipartite graphs and certain 4-regular bipartite graphs. The study aims to contribute to the resolution of the general 4-regular bipartite graph conjecture. The paper is dedicated to the memory of Miklos Vrt'o. The authors would like to hear from readers about their thoughts on strong edge-coloring in 3- and 4-regular bipartite graphs. The study is part of the authors' PhD theses. The lower bound is 2^((i^2 4j) / (4n - i^2)) when i and j are both less than the square root of n, with an implicit constant of 2, although this constant can be quite large. When i or j exceeds the square root of n, the lower bound is 2 to the power of ((\sqrtqn - (qn^(-2i^2)))}, with the implication that the minimum number of coordinates in a function's representation in the j-th eigenspace of the Hamming graph's n vertex edition on q colors is limited only by a quadratic function of the square root of n, subject to the condition that n is sufficiently large, with the bound ranging from \Omega(\sqrtqn) when j equals i, to \Omega(n) when j equals zero. The ability of neural networks to learn complex mappings between input data and output spaces makes them suitable for a wide range of applications, including data analysis, where they can often outperform more traditional methods. This review aims to provide an overview of neural network applications in solving inverse problems, focusing on areas such as spectral data analysis, magnetic resonance imaging, and gamma-ray tomography, as well as underdetermined problems, with an emphasis on compressive sensing. In this research, we've established a set of necessary and sufficient conditions for achieving robust learning from uniformly distributed data without assumptions about the distribution. These conditions enable us to compare the ease of robust learning across different concept classes. A notable outcome from our study is that the radius of the query impacts the feasibility of robust learning from distribution-free data. Moreover, we've derived a reduced version of our conditions applied to specific hypothesis classes, allowing for more precise generalization than the existing bounded complexity principle. Our research further explores the relationship between robust and efficient learning, highlighting that efficient learning does not necessarily encompass robust learning, but efficient learning with loss bounds can imply robust learning under specific data distributions. To support these claims, we provide theoretical examples and demonstrations. Our study is the first to examine robust learning from general datasets and its relationship to existing literature on learning from uniformly distributed datasets. These findings are partially derived from our previous work on robust learning [Arachi et al., 2020]. Additionally, we include an overview of the main contributions from [Arachi et al., 2020], specifically the establishment of robust learning as a special case of learning with properties and the derivation of a data-efficient version of the bounded complexity principle.

We examine the effects of noise models and data sets on the Prospector analysis pipeline, particularly focusing on how well it can determine star formation histories and initial mass functions by analyzing mock galaxy samples at various wavelengths. This approach targets supernovae with unclear host galaxy measurements, a common issue in photometry data. Initially, the model treats each supernova independently, then incorporates a correlation penalty to minimize differences within each group. Notably, our model outperforms existing methods, with results including:
A penalty-only model that significantly improves variability modeling by identifying structure in the data,
A mixture-model that discovers two distinct groups within the data and accurately models their diversity,
A mixture penalty model that simultaneously analyzes diversity and variability, resulting in more detailed understanding of each group.
Mixture penalty models yield superior results compared to existing methods in classification and variability modeling, especially for pre-maximum data. Notably, these models also highlight the need for future observations to focus on the u and J bands. Our code and data are publicly available for verification and replication.

The rapid spread of misinformation through social media platforms has significant real-world consequences, as seen in the instance of false health rumors that led to violent mob attacks in India. In response, WhatsApp has taken steps such as limiting the ability to forward messages and introducing educational alerts about the potential risks of spreading misinformation. However, these efforts have not been sufficient to eradicate the problem, particularly in regions with limited internet access and mobile device usage. WhatsApp's large user base in India poses a significant public health risk, as false information about health and coronavirus can cause harm to the public. In an attempt to mitigate this issue, we propose an automatic misinformation detection system that analyzes the content of suspicious messages in real-time, leveraging contextual clues and machine learning algorithms. Our system has shown promising results, with accuracy and F1 scores above 90% on publicly available datasets, outperforming other machine learning models. We acknowledge some limitations, such as the need for additional training data, particularly in Indian languages, and propose a neural architecture that can enhance the system's performance. We investigate the impact of discrete mutations on a population's genetic landscape over extended periods in the limits of small and large population sizes. In the case of small populations, the distribution of genetic differences falls into three distinct regimes, characterized by long-tail behavior similar to the effects observed in the standard model. Conversely, for large populations, the distribution converges towards a normal pattern. Our analysis, incorporating the effects of multiple mutations within a fixed time frame, indicates that the genetic difference distribution either converges towards a normal, exhibits long-tail behavior, or remains constant. The outcomes are further accompanied by substantial changes in the population's genetic structure. The presentation of our results transitions from the gradual changes in small/ large populations to the relatively rapid modifications in medium-sized populations. This paper presents a zero-shot framework that enables collaborative, adaptive learning across different datasets. By utilizing meta-knowledge to connect model parameters and task inputs, our framework allows for generalization to tasks and inputs outside of the training scope. To address the issue of data distribution discrepancies, our framework incorporates a federated learning component. The quantum Fourier transform has significant potential in quantum computing and quantum communication, particularly in high-dimensional multi-photon systems. However, implementing the classical Fourier transform in high dimensions is challenging due to the vast number of possible states. Our study demonstrates the feasibility of constructing a quantum Fourier transform in high-dimensional systems using a probabilistic approach. By applying random unitary operators, we show that the probability distribution of the outcomes can be concentrated into a low-dimensional space, allowing for the design of efficient quantum Fourier transforms in high-dimensional systems. Our results are further illustrated by numerically analyzing the probability distribution of errors in the quantum Fourier transform for two specific cases. Firstly, the case of 2 photons in a 2-dimensional space is considered, with the calculation supported by partial findings from a 3-photon system in a 2-dimensional space. Secondly, the case of 2 photons in a 2-dimensional space with multiple outcomes is examined, with the outcome amplified from random instances. Our research provides a new insight into the quantum Fourier transform, offering a probabilistic approach that might be useful for near-term quantum devices and future quantum simulations. The ability to systemically extrapolate beyond initial training data limits is crucial for achieving efficient counting, a fundamental limit of modern deep learning models. However, traditional extrapolation methods often rely on functional approximations, making it challenging to count accurately. To address this limitation, we introduce a framework that enables systematic extrapolation through a regularization-based generalization framework, allowing for efficient counting without imposing data constraints. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets, including Cifar-10, Cifar-100, and ImageNet, with a fixed memory footprint of 1.25 GB, 1 GB, and 625 MB, respectively. We establish that the Alexandrov embedding can be derived from the Zariski decomposition by applying a non-linear transformation to the embedding induced by the canonical class. This understanding allows us to reinterpret the geometry of numerical divisors through the lens of Zariski decomposition, thereby revealing the Alexandrov embedding as a consequence of the decomposition's intrinsic properties. Moreover, our findings generalize to varieties with canonical singularities, allowing us to generalize the Alexandrov embedding and its properties to this context. This research examines how various types of market data contribute to capturing market trends and sets a time frame for this effect in seconds. Analysis using Principal Component Analysis indicates that the longest-time impact of market influence on price movements is within milliseconds, primarily driven by market order imbalances. By comparing the performance of different models, including Bayesian learning and information theory-based approaches, on historical Emir exchange transaction data, the study reveals that the best models are those that account for both hidden market factors and explicit market behavior. Furthermore, assessing the quality of these models and their ability to identify market trends and price reversals shows that the most effective models are those that use high-frequency data while also considering the relative contributions of market transactions and non-market transactions to capturing market trends and price movements within seconds. The results indicate that the average time frame for market influence is around 250 milliseconds. Developing and disseminating machine learning models that prioritize data privacy is a growing concern. In this context, a technique called federated learning has gained traction. A novel approach, referred to as semi-honest, enables the construction of a clustering model without compromising personal data, by leveraging multiple data contributors. Each contributor only shares the function of their data, regarding the class labels, towards a central aggregator. Aggregator \textit{FLVoogd} guarantees that only benign data is used in the learning process, without compromising sensitive personal information, by employing a data contributor verification process. This process includes contributor verification and a trusted third-party facilitator. Additionally, \textit{FLVoogd} ensures the integrity of its protocol by employing both cryptographic concepts and efficient code design, resulting in a more robust and efficient clustering process. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of \textit{FLVoogd} in several datasets. As an extension, this work also presents \textit{FLVoogd} with support for multiple data contributors, unknown data properties, and unbalanced data distributions in a univariate Gaussian setting. This research further explores the application of programming languages \textit{Python} and \textit{R}, along with publicly accessible tools, in developing and implementing \textit{FLVoogd}. As a result, this research provides a foundation for developing robust, efficient, and fair machine learning models in a semi-honest federated learning environment. mission objectives, and scenario configurations. Our results suggest that
autonomous vehicle systems requiring extensive sensor data may require substantial
adapations to transfer skills from simulated to real-world settings, while systems
with focused objectives like navigation may exhibit better sim2real transfer.

The growing sophistication of deepfakes poses significant concerns for society, largely due to the spreading of misleading information through media. To combat this issue, it is crucial to develop effective techniques for identifying deepfake videos that rely on minimal computational resources and can be applied in real-world, low-latency scenarios. Although deepfake detection methods utilizing machine learning and computer vision techniques have shown promising results, they often require substantial computational power and may not be sufficient to tackle the complex challenges of future deepfake scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose employing neural network-based video classification methods that utilize audiovisual features and can be applied in real-time. Our approach leverages lightweight neural networks and relies on short, 1 to 6 second video segments for classification. Our experimental findings demonstrate that our proposed method can classify deepfake videos with high accuracy while maintaining low latency. Specifically, our results show that our model achieves false positive rates of 9% and 20% on the ChaLearn Deepfake and YouTube Poisoned datasets when trained on the former, and when trained on the latter, respectively. Notably, our classification technique exhibits low latency, requiring only 15 milliseconds to process each segment. To facilitate the development of better deepfake detection methods, we provide open-source code for our proposed classification technique. A recent surge in neural networks research has highlighted the importance of studying classic models such as the McCulloch-Pitts network and the Hopfield network. These models form the foundation of today's sophisticated neural networks and understanding their theoretical limitations helps in comprehending the capabilities and constraints of modern neural networks. Unlike the Hopfield network, which is known for its stability, the McCulloch-Pitts network is recognized for its ability to learn through backpropagation, a process later adopted in various other neural network models. Building upon this, we introduce the supervisory McCulloch-Pitts network, an extension of the original model that incorporates supervisory capabilities. We demonstrate that even with an external supervisor, the network's cycle-free property cannot be guaranteed. Furthermore, we analyze the cycle patterns in the network and their relationship with the error gradient, showing that training cycles are an inherent aspect of the learning process. To validate our findings, we employed numerical methods and examined the dynamics of several two- and three-neuron configurations. Our research reveals that the McCulloch-Pitts network, when paired with a suitable activation function and gradient descent, is capable of learning tasks even in the absence of backpropagation. These findings are corroborated through numerical experiments. Additionally, we successfully employed the supervisory McCulloch-Pitts network to solve a straightforward but critical regression task, a result that serves as evidence of the network's learning capabilities. Notably, the process of learning this task led to the emergence of cycle patterns that persisted even after training, as anticipated by our theoretical analysis. To a limited extent, we also explored the applicability of the supervisory McCulloch-Pitts network in tackling more complex classification tasks, such as the MNIST dataset. Our attempts to adapt the supervisory McCulloch-Pitts network for use with the MNIST dataset were unsuccessful, which we attribute to the network's overfitting issues. As a result, we suggest the integration of regularization techniques to mitigate overfitting and potentially enable the successful application of the supervisory McCulloch-Pitts network to more complex datasets. Building upon the successes of the supervisory McCulloch-Pitts network, we extended our methodology to the supervisory Hopfield network, an extension of the classic Hopfield network that incorporates supervisory capabilities. We examined the star formation history of two ultra-faint galaxies, searching for patterns that could help explain their origins. These satellites, namely Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) and Wukong/LMS-1 (LMS-1), share similarities with other disrupted structures like Salaris and Nemesis. Our analysis revealed the onset and duration of star formation within GSE to be approximately 1 billion years, while LMS-1's star formation history is still shrouded in uncertainty. Interestingly, both potential satellite galaxies exhibit different star formation profiles, with GSE's being more turbulent and unpredictable and LSE-1's being more stable and regular. These results suggest that both galaxies had dynamic histories, influenced by various internal and external forces, potentially shedding light on their disrupted states in the Milky Way's disk. Moreover, our study discovered an unusual correlation in GSE's metallicity, which may indicate an internal structure or an external interaction that affected the galaxy's development. Our findings also imply that both galaxies likely formed early in the universe, with estimated ages between 13 and 15 billion years. This is consistent with simulations predicting that disrupted galaxies would be found throughout the Milky Way's disk, potentially explaining the observed number of ultra-faint galaxies discovered in recent years. Our analysis primarily relied on Gaia Data Release 2 and EDR3, combining this data with star counts from the LEGUS survey, which provided spatial and color information for stars in both galaxies, helping to confirm their membership in the Milky Way's disk. Acquiring labeled data for machine learning model training can be a costly and resource-intensive process. A technique called selective labeling aims to mitigate these costs by limiting the labeling required in training by only collecting data from specific, high-yielding examples. This approach involves using data prediction from untrained models to guide example selection and labeling. While effective, the method has its drawbacks: it necessitates training separate models for each new data set, and relies on assuming data distribution stability. This paper presents a method called iterative selective labeling, which uses a single model trained end-to-end to guide example selection and labeling across multiple data sets by learning their common features and transformations. Experimental results show that iterative selective labeling surpasses traditional model-based data prediction in terms of data set diversity and labeling efficiency, measured by the number of labels acquired. Furthermore, the method shows benefits in scenarios involving concept drift, where data distribution stability ceases to exist. This technique's capabilities extend beyond data set example selection to informing labeling tasks. We demonstrate the method's value in boosting the performance of training data by actively pursuing diversity in labeling examples. This process allows the model to leverage data set features and dynamics to improve its accuracy and adaptability. Overall, the method outperforms traditional model-based data prediction in terms of labeling efficiency while actively promoting diversity in labeled data, which can positively affect model training and adaptability. This technique effectively mitigates cost-associated challenges in acquiring labeled data and shows promise in boosting model accuracy and adaptability. We present the method's benefits through various numerical evaluations of its applications. A theoretical study of the interface electronic structure of EuS/InAs using density functional theory with spin-orbit coupling has been conducted. The results show that the interface forms covalent bonds with dispersive states originating from the InAs surface states, effectively screening the Eu ions. A 2D density of states analysis reveals that the interface electronic structure is primarily governed by interactions at the InAs surface with the upper valence band states. Furthermore, the results indicate that hydrostatic stress has a negligible effect on the interface electronic structure. An alternative interface configuration, EuS(111)/InAs(111), is also examined, confirming that the (111) orientation is unlikely to alter the overall findings. The study's outcomes are consistent with experimental observations of our previous research on the EuS/InAs interface, where no evidence of EuO bonds was found. The results also demonstrate that the interface electronic structure is largely determined by the InAs surface properties. Consequently, modifying the InAs substrate is suggested as a means to manipulate the interface electronic structure. Based on these findings, the (In,Ga)As substrates with optimized surface properties are proposed as an alternative to InAs for reducing carrier freeze-out in EuS/InAs nanolasers. Finally, examining multiple interfaces formed by sparsely coated EuS layers, the results indicate that the interface electronic structure remains largely unchanged. The study's outcomes provide valuable insights to understand the nanoconfined system of EuS and InAs. We examine Borel Wadge determinacy within second-order arithmetic and show that its provability is equivalent to a modified version of arithmetic transfinite induction. This finding is then used to establish the consistency of certain theories by demonstrating that their models adhere to a certain determinacy standard. For example, we prove that a model of open determinacy, believed to be the strongest theory of its kind, is consistent in arithmetic. This determination aligns with a long-held conjecture. Furthermore, we find that Borel Wadge determinacy is also implied by certain notions of set existence in second-order arithmetic. The proof involves an analysis of Turing-compatible sets with certain properties and its relationship to determinacy in sets of limited complexity. This analysis leads to the discovery of an interesting property: every Turing-complete set contains a subset, which has a complexity bound of $\boldsymbol{\Delta}^0_2$ and yet is not necessarily bounded in size. Lastly, we establish that Borel Wadge determinacy is consistent with several theories of time bounded computation, including linear bounded calculation, but is incompatible with a weaker notion of computation, defined by restricted Turing machines with a 1/2 slowdown factor. This finding highlights an interesting distinction between two concepts of computation, their respective determinacy conditions, and their relationships to second-order arithmetic. To boost the efficiency of computer vision models via neural network pruning, we introduce ClickTrain. This innovative approach transforms the pruning process into an self-supervised learning task, turning each step into a meaningful training phase. By doing so, it maximizes the effectiveness of each model component, resulting in substantial improvements in model accuracy without sacrificing its core capabilities. In experiments, ClickTrain consistently outperforms other comparable methods, yielding an average 0.42% to 1.49% boost in top-1 accuracy for various models and datasets, including the resilient ResNet, while also achieving a notable speed-up in inference time. Our full code and models are openly accessible on GitHub. In addition, we include a detailed guide on adapting ClickTrain for other neural network architectures for the use of others. This work develops a rigorous framework for semantic analysis in substructural modal logic through the introduction of a novel sound and complete relational semantics. This framework accommodates a wide range of additional axioms beyond those covered by traditional Kripke semantics, enabling a systematic exploration of the derived theorems within this extended family of substructural modal logics. Furthermore, our relational semantics provides a natural translation into cut-free sequent calculus, thereby establishing a clear connection between sound and complete inference systems for these logics. By focusing on these events, we can gain a more in-depth understanding of the behavior of neutron stars under extreme conditions. Initially, we generate networks with a single transition parameter (σ) that range from ordered (bridged) to disordered (unbridged) networks. By tracking the critical transmission rate and average epidemic size, we identify the impact of network architecture on epidemic spreading. Our results reveal a clear distinction in epidemic spreading between bridged and unbridged networks. The former exhibits more predictable patterns, with the average epidemic size decreasing as the critical transmission rate decreases, whereas unbridged networks display less predictable behavior. Furthermore, we investigated the long-tailed distributions of epidemic sizes and found that clustered networks tend to produce longer tails, indicating a greater likelihood of larger epidemics in these networks. To validate our findings, we conducted supplementary analyses on two real-world contact networks. Our research provides novel insights into the relationships between network architecture, epidemic spreading, and predictability, suggesting the importance of network clustering in modulating epidemic size and its long-tailed distribution. These findings can inform and guide public health interventions by targeting critical bridge nodes to mitigate epidemic transmission. Additionally, under the assumption that all primes are generated by the sequence, we outline a method for identifying twin primes by analyzing the sequence for gaps. Furthermore, we modify the approach to accommodate gaps in a triad, thereby identifying triplets of prime numbers. Under the same assumption, we also identify a group of prime numbers, known as Cullen prime numbers, by mapping Faure's sequence to a Cullen prime. Furthermore, we identify another group of prime numbers, known as Woodin prime numbers, by establishing their connection to the Cullen prime numbers. Lastly, we outline a method for generating proof codes for the primality of Faure's sequence elements. These proof codes hold potential for recurring patterns in the sequence and can aid in analyzing its distribution. This paper presents a control architecture called Layered Control System (LCS) that navigates mobile platforms with sensors such as sonar, infrared, and radar. Inspired by the mammalian brain's hierarchical organization, LCS consists of multiple layers, each addressing a specific task, and utilizes sensory data through neural networks for decision-making. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our system by implementing three layers: Motion Control, Sensor Fusion, and Avoidance Control, and evaluate its performance in challenging environments using simulation. Our results reveal that LCS successfully tackles obstacles, fuses sensory information, and avoids hazards, proof of its capability to manage complex tasks. We applied an analysis similar to that used for Arche, using the data with the 2-layer thermal model developed by the Arche team, and our results indicate Nereid may have ice that is 10% blue-tinted, and our model also suggests Nereid has a subsurface layer approximately 30 km deep. Our analysis suggests Nereid may have ice that is 10% more blue than other objects in the outer solar system, such as Arche, and our findings are consistent with Nereid being composed primarily of water ice. We also used our model to estimate Nereid's thermal conductivity and found it may be as low as 0.020 W/m/K. Our analysis of Nereid's characteristics offers insights into its composition and thermal properties. We further discuss how our analysis can help map Nereid's interior. We establish a formal connection between the theories of quantum interference, entanglement, and contextuality. Our framework introduces a general approach to describe correlations exhibited by multiple systems, enabling a direct comparison of state configurations. This enables a unified exploration of the nonlocal properties of quantum mechanics through a systematic analysis of the transformations between different correlation configurations. Furthermore, our framework allows us to identify common features among different correlation configurations that exhibit similar behaviors when subjected to various transformations, which we refer to as "family relationships" among these configurations. This conceptual framework provides a systematic method for identifying and categorizing correlation configurations that reflect equivalent relationships among nonlocal properties, which have significant implications in the study and classification of nonlocality and contextuality in quantum mechanics. To illustrate the efficacy of our framework, we apply it to study the nonlocal properties of Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states in 3-qubit systems and discover new insights into the contextuality of these states, which reveal deeper connections among the system's properties. Our framework also enables a direct comparison of state configurations to reveal nonlocal properties that are inherent to the quantum mechanics framework, which is demonstrated through a study of quadripartite states shared by four parties. Additionally, our framework provides a general approach to identify necessary and sufficient conditions for eliminating nonlocal properties through marginalization, which is explored in detail through a study of contextuality in quantum mechanics. Cluster analysis of species presence/absence data across different sites is commonly employed in biogeography, ecology, and evolution to identify groups of locations with similar species compositions.  However, the diversity of data sets and analytical methods makes it challenging to draw reliable conclusions.  While some cluster methods produce meaningful results, others fail or yield misleading outcomes.  In an effort to improve the reliability of cluster analysis, we propose eight principles of good practice for clustering site data based on species presence/absence.  These guidelines are designed to assist researchers in selecting suitable methods and interpreting their results effectively.  We also review a range of candidate cluster methods and propose a flexible, open-source software tool for performing good-practice clustering, which includes an example application to a dataset of Antarctic island insect data.  The proposed approach allows researchers to verify the robustness of the resulting clusters and their associated statistical measures across different site data combinations using a variety of methods, thereby increasing the reliability of the analysis.  In addition, we provide guidance on how to present the results of the cluster analysis in a clear and understandable manner.  In conclusion, by adhering to these good-practice guidelines, researchers can enhance the reliability of the cluster analysis, gain insights into the species composition of the study sites, and achieve more accurate and robust results.  In our case study, we were able to apply these principles to gain new insights into the species composition of the study sites in Antarctica, and to make a significant discovery regarding the evolutionary history of the insects of the region.  In particular, we found that the species present on the sub-Antarctic islands of South Georgia and Tristan da Cunha share a common species composition, and that the species present on the island of South Georgia share a common species composition with the nearby South Georgia Island seamount.  The analysis also showed that the species present on the island of Kerguelen share a common species composition with the nearby Kerguelen seamount, and that the species present on the island of Heard share a common species composition with the nearby island of MacDonald and the nearby seamount of Phoenix.  The discovery of these results was made possible by the open-source software tool, and the results are presented in a clear and understandable manner in the abstract, and in the figures and tables presented in the study.  In addition, the study shows that the species present on the island of Heard share a common species composition with the nearby island of MacDonald, and the nearby seamount of Phoenix. This paper presents our approach to detecting abusive content in Arabic social media posts. We developed a multi-layered system for identifying offensive posts, which consists of two primary components: a classification layer and a ranking layer. The classification layer utilizes a pre-trained universal sentence encoder to generate semantic features, which are then fed into a pre-trained support vector machine classified under relevant categories. Additionally, we leveraged a pre-trained word2vec model to extract features from words with high abuse likelihood. We employed a combination of deep neural networks and traditional machine learning algorithms to identify top-ranked posts. Our system demonstrated outstanding performance on the Arabic Twitter Abuse Dataset, achieving a macro F1 score of 0.64 and an accuracy of 0.79. We further analyzed the effectiveness of different machine learning algorithms on the same dataset, highlighting their strengths and limitations. We also explored the application of our system in other domains, such as detecting hate speech in Facebook posts. Moreover, we worked on automatic hate speech detection on WhatsApp using a dataset provided by King's College of London. Our main contribution is the development of a system that identifies abusive content in Arabic social media posts effectively. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work on Arabic abusive content detection. Also, as far as we know, this is the first attempt to detect abusive content using the King's College of London's WhatsApp dataset. \par

Yet, learning program generators for tasks that require sequential, top-down planning, like handwriting, has been a challenge. We've developed a new approach, Bayesian Program Learning, that incorporates prior knowledge of the program distribution to leverage minimal data and common stylistic patterns. This method demonstrates its effectiveness in creating handwriting samples similar to those of human professionals with only a few examples in each of three styles, producing output of high aesthetic value and accuracy. Our approach has the potential to expand the scope of program learning to domains with complex, well-structured sequences, like image generation and design. 

Our system's performance is comparable to that of state-of-the-art generative models, but with the notable advantage of efficient and dynamic model adjustment based on limited new data. We've found that program learning can effectively produce multiple, coherent sequences of strokes, even when the starting points vary. The generated patterns are as varied and 'human-like' in style when the model is trained on drawings by a single artist as they are when the model is trained on drawings by three artists with distinct styles. We've produced over one hundred high-quality, professionally applicable drawings in three styles, including humor comics, medical illustrations, and scientific diagrams, making a significant contribution to the program learning field.

We've used the tool to investigate the program generators, analyzing the structure of the generated drawings, the diversity of possible drawings, and the effect of artistic style on the generated illustrations. Gpu memory allocation can significantly impact application performance, with poorly optimized allocators causing slow downs and exposure of unnecessary latencies. Despite the prevalence of dynamic memory allocation in scientific and data-driven applications, most modern gpu allocators are inherently sequential, neglecting parallelization opportunities and limiting application scalability. The DynaSOAr allocator addresses these limitations through the utilization of a parallel, tree-shaped memory management structure that facilitates concurrent allocation and deallocation of gpu memory. By optimizing memory fragmentation and minimizing unnecessary communication between different memory segments, DynaSOAr has demonstrated a substantial improvement in performance, specifically a 2x to 20x factor, when compared to other state-of-the-art allocators. The DynaSOAr allocator is now publicly available under the Apache 2 license, with supporting information and benchmark data included in the supplementary materials. Additionally, a series of performance benchmarks can be found on the DynaSOAr github page. Moreover, a future-looking perspective for gpu allocators is presented in the accompanying paper, with the performance benchmarks and related content being made accessible through osdi.org. The formation of supersolid phenomena is commonly linked to the stabilization of a highly ordered state, yet its dynamics in response to perturbations remains largely an open question. Our research provides a solution to this inquiry by examining how an oscillating impurity influences the phonon spectrum within a supersolid $\mathrm{^{4}He}$ droplet. Through the utilization of a dual-funnel potential model, we develop a precise mathematical framework, grounded in non-perturbative methods, to analyze the coupled impurity-phonon system. Our findings reveal that as the impurity moves back and forth, it gives rise to the creation of new phonon modes, which exhibit increased softness and a more pronounced minimum. Our model's predictions are in agreement with the experimental observations of Nelson et al., and we have also identified the emergence of a new, excited phonon state. Our research further suggests that as the height of the potential funnels varies, the phonon modes undergo a series of transformations, ultimately resulting in the disappearance of the roton minimum and the ordered state at around 0.32 PHF. Our analysis also uncovers two critical thresholds at 0.55 PHF and 0.88 PHF, beneath which the impurity's movement has a significant impact on the phonon spectrum. Our non-perturbative approach enables us to precisely determine these critical thresholds, whereas perturbation theory fails to do so. Moreover, our findings also shed light on the long-wavelength behavior of the impurity, showing that as the impurity's frequency decreases, its movement can be effectively described by a modified version of the Jansen-Van der Zant model. Our research provides a significant advancement in the understanding of how a system responds to perturbations in a highly ordered state, and our non-perturbative approach may be effectively applied to the study of other low-entropy helium droplets that feature stabilized electronic clusters. Our study has also led to the creation of the "phonon-trap" hypothesis, suggesting the existence of self-organized dark matter with low entropy at the heart of ultra-low-entropy helium droplets. If validated, this hypothesis has the potential to revolutionize our understanding of dark matter, leading to the creation of a new, controlled environment at the NEOS facility that is specifically designed to optimize the utilization of dark matter. Our analysis assesses the two-dimensional density of the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) in the Milky Way using radio continuum data from a 20 cm wavelength observation. By assuming the CMZ's center to be at longitude 0.0, latitude -0.89, we calculated the density pattern at 20 different spatial intervals and analyzed its properties at different scales. At large scales (greater than 1.5 pc), the CMZ's density varies significantly along the Galactic center axis, but its variation in other directions is relatively minor. At smaller scales (less than 1.5 pc), the density anisotropy in the CMZ decreases, but its variation along the Galactic center axis remains more substantial than that in other directions. Our findings indicate that the CMZ's density structure is not solely determined by the rotation of gas disks and suggest the presence of other mechanisms, such as magnetic fields. Additionally, the data reveal that the CMZ's density is more anisotropic near the Galactic center than in more distant areas, which might be related to the influence of star-forming activity. Our analysis further confirms that the CMZ is denser along the Galactic center axis in the central 30 pc region and that its overall density is more concentrated near the center compared to more distant areas. Our results are consistent with previous studies using different methods and suggest that the CMZ is structured in a hierarchical, multi-scale pattern. Based on our findings, we offer two possible explanations for this pattern: first, that the CMZ is influenced by a spiral arm or ring-like structure; or, second, that the CMZ is a bar-like structure that is not well-represented in gas density maps due to its elliptical shape and the presence of anisotropic gas dispersion. Our analysis also discusses the potential role of gas feedback in shaping the CMZ's structure. Our study paves the way for future research examining the CMZ's two-dimensional density using higher-resolution data and other observational approaches. Additionally, we present a novel and efficient algorithm for calculating the density gradient, which may be applied in various areas of astrophysics. Starting with multi-photon entangled states of a specific type and known by a single basis set, we utilize a network of quantum circuits to generate more complex multi-photon entangled states. This process involves mapping the multi-photon states onto a single quantum channel, allowing us to extend the concept of quantum teleportation to multi-photon entangled states. This method not only prepares complex multi-photon entangled states but also enables the transformation of multi-photon entangled states into the desired forms when they match a specific pattern. This method further allows the creation of multi-photon entangled states from single-photon entangled states through a process involving probabilistic measurements. We demonstrate the efficacy of the scissor technique by preparing a two-photon cluster state from a two-photon Bell state and a four-photon Bell state from the product of two Bell states. Additionally, we outline a strategy for generating long chains of polarized photons starting from single polarized photons, thereby expanding the scope of quantum computation and information processing to include multiple qubits. To efficiently manage the growing number of IoT devices, it is crucial to accurately identify their types, which can be a challenging task due to similar devices. To resolve this issue, we propose an innovative approach, risk-aware cost classification, to improve the efficiency and adaptability of IoT device classification. This approach optimizes the selection of features and classification rules by considering both the accuracy and the risk level of devices. By reducing unnecessary investigations, we can lower the risk of security breaches and increase the robustness of the system. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach outperforms traditional methods in terms of both accuracy and risk minimization. Additionally, we identify the key factors that influence risk awareness and assess the feasibility of this approach using the Cyberspace Traceability Testbench. Based on the analysis, we provide practical recommendations for integrating risk-awareness into IoT device management. This research fills gaps in the fields of risk assessment and decision-making by considering both random and intentional factors. We examine the relationships between feature variables and thoroughly discuss the ethical implications of classification in the context of IoT devices. Finally, we explore potential avenues for future research, including the integration of deep learning and the quantification of risk awareness. These ideas have the potential to significantly improve the efficiency and adaptability of IoT device classification. This work has been submitted to Journal of Network Security, vol. 22, num. 5. Consecutive data across time intervals often exhibit correlations that are localized in time, yet these associations can also be observed over extended periods. Failing to account for the sequential order of such data can lead to inaccurate predictions and a lack of understanding in various fields. This research develops an asynchronous learning algorithm for building longitudinal models by utilizing the Lagrange interpolation method to create proxy variables that correspond to target variables at specific time points. By leveraging the properties of Lagrange interpolation, the asynchronous block-iterative decomposition algorithm is derived from a convex relaxation of a nonconvex optimization model in convex cone complementarity problems. This theoretical foundation enables the development of an algorithm, whose convergence is verified through mathematical analysis. Experimental results also demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in handling sequential data by utilizing a dataset from the text classification field. Additionally, the application of the asynchronous learning algorithm in both Lagrange and nonlinear cases is illustrated through a numerical example that demonstrates its ability to generate asynchronous models on proxy variables. These generated variables are then evaluated for their performance in both asynchronous and synchronous settings to emphasize the importance of considering the sequential order of data. All the code used in this research has been open-sourced on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/rajaykutti/Asynchronous-Block-Iterative-Decomposition. As a liquid foam undergoes dryness, its surface becomes covered in polymer-rich clusters that determine the level of surface roughness. A novel method has been developed to measure surface roughness factor by simulating real-time flow through the dry foam and analyzing the resulting rheological properties. The surface roughness was found to significantly affect the foam's rheological behavior; as roughness increases, so do the linear elasticity and nonlinear stress-swinning characteristics of the foam. An advanced numerical technique was utilized to obtain accurate solutions to the Snell, Green, and Curie equations, thereby validating existing analytical approximations and providing further analysis of their validity. The integration of the polymeric and dry foam approaches enabled the development of a comprehensive coarsening theory, providing unified explanations for dry foam and bubbly behavior. Using advanced computational methods, we studied how electron and hole interactions influence excitation energies within hole-doped sodium within the limit of strong coupling. We identified that by incorporating mass corrections, the energies of dipolar electron-hole pairs matched the predicted values from a model called Langreth-Nozieres-Altshuler, while the energies of monopole pairs matched those from a model called Feshbach. We found the mass enhancement of dipolar pairs to be about 0.8 times their predicted value, and the mass enhancement of monopole pairs to be about 0.9 times their predicted value. We also discovered that the ratio of the dipolar to monopole excitation energies was roughly 1.3, closely aligning with theoretical expectations in the strong coupling regime. These findings provide evidence that the excitation spectrum of sodium conforms to the strong coupling theory of electron-phonon interaction. We further found that by incorporating the effects of electronic QFL, the Feshbach values are significantly (by about 50%) underpredicted for monopole pairs, suggesting that the influence of the electronic QFL on dipolar pairs is likely to be minimal. We also found that the positive charge of sodium results in a significant reduction (by about 3 orders of magnitude) of the effects of Coulomb interactions on dipolar pairs when compared to the effects on monopole pairs, thereby allowing the study of the effects of electron-phonon interactions in sodium with high accuracy. Our results indicate that the feature exchange in the potential can be detected through the variation in the equilateral-type non-Gaussianity signature in the $f_{\rm Nl}$-$\sigma_8$ plane. We investigate two models of interacting walkers in one dimension: (1) a conservative model with paired walker interactions mimicking the collisions of hard spheres, and (2) a conservative model with collinear interactions simulating the attraction and repulsion of dipoles. Both models exhibit distinct phases: a low-density phase where walks diffuse independently and a high-density phase where walks are linked together in a high-traffic regime. To study the transition between these phases, we introduce a simplified model, referred to as the conservative model, which avoids the complexity of pair interactions. This conservative model is similar to model (2) but without the dipole's rotation effect, leading to a more complex time-dependent behavior. We focus on two relevant parameters: the participation ratio and the pair correlation function. For the participation ratio, our results show that, near the "detrapping angle," the ratio remains steady and exhibits a predictable, fluctuating trend in the high-traffic regime. In contrast, the pair correlation function displays a more intricate behavior within the high-traffic regime. To deepen our understanding, we analyze the associated Langevin equations and hydrodynamic equations for models (1) and (2), which involve non-markovian dynamics with memory effects that we elminate to derive a stochastic model with memory effects. Ultimately, we validate our findings through numerical simulations, matching our theoretical predictions for the participation ratio and pair correlation functions. Furthermore, we explore the average propagation velocity in the high-traffic regime, a topic that has yet to be theoretically analyzed. To this end, we used numerical methods to study model (2), which exhibits a non-linear relationship between the average velocity and density. Notably, our results show that the observed velocity is significantly influenced by the dipole's initial orientation. To gain insight into the dynamics, we analyzed the persistence of velocity, defining it as the probability that a walk maintains its initial direction. Our analysis shows that, in the high-traffic regime, the persistence of velocity is approximately proportional to the density, a phenomenon that has not been previously reported. We demonstrate that the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critically ill-posed behavior in three-dimensional space when the initial data is incorporated using Littlewood-Paley frames. Specifically, we find that perturbing the initial data with higher frequency components results in significantly longer durations of non-solution regimes as the frequency increases. Notably, this critical ill-posedness does not occur in one- and two-dimensional spaces for the Cauchy problem. Building on the research of Bourgain and Li, we employ a technique of adaptive perturbation that utilizes high-frequency data to create non-linear interactions at lower frequencies, which are then propagated to significantly longer time periods than the frequency of the perturbation. This method can also be applied to other partial differential equations that include the incompressible Euler equations, such as the 3D constrained Euler equations and the 2D constrained compressible Euler equations. Furthermore, we prove that the adaptive perturbation method preserves the non-local characteristics of the frequency products and their interactions, which are crucial for understanding the behavior of the solutions. As a result, we are able to derive ill-posed behaviors of the frequency products and their interactions, which are critical for understanding the adaptive perturbation method. To expand on the research of Bourgain and Li, we also find a frequency-dependent threshold below which the adaptive perturbation method loses its effectiveness, while also generalizing their results to the constrained Euler equations. We introduce Stable Artist, an innovative tool allowing users to direct artistic creations with guidance. Unlike existing image editing tools, Stable Artist operates without relying on open-ended text prompts, instead utilizing discrete instructions and achieving impressive results in record time. Building on CLIP, a powerful image and text comparison model, Artist leverages the power of latent codes to perform image editing tasks with ease. Our system enables users to craft instructional sequences comprised of multiple steps and actions, resulting in the generation of custom visuals. In testing Artist on a variety of tasks, including editing sketches and photographs, the algorithm consistently outperformed DALL-E 2 and produced more accurate results. Furthermore, Artist's design is remarkably efficient, requiring minimal computational resources compared to other models. This study marks a significant advancement towards creating more user-friendly and efficient artistic creation tools. The research and code are available online. https://tinyurl.com/StableArtist. An analysis for dark matter particles interacting with nucleons via a Higgs-like mediator in light dark matter scenarios has been carried out. This analysis utilizes data collected by LHC experiments ATLAS and CMS in 2015-2016, seeking signs of dark matter production accompanied by invisible decays of $J/\psi$ and $\Upsilon$ mesons. Finding no evidence, constraints are imposed on dark matter-nucleon cross section interactions, yielding stringent limits for dark matter masses up to 10,000 GeV, especially in regions where the dark matter interacts effecively with nucleons through an isospin-invariant manner or via a heavy quark mediator. The presented results represent the most stringent limits on dark matter interactions with nucleons to date, matching or surpassing existing limits in certain mass ranges while outperforming previous studies in other areas. This analysis's sensitivity to dark matter interactions with nucleons is further enhanced by considering the decay of dark matter particles into neutrinos, effectively limiting their mass interactions. This study provides significant constraints for various dark matter models, including Scattering-Mediated Freeze-Out and Higgs Portal Dark Matter, where it limits the parameter space to the unexplored regime, and also provides a comprehensive review of current limits on dark matter interactions with nucleons, illustrating the potential of future experiments in this area to outperform even the high-energy variant of the next-generation experiment in limiting the dark matter interactions with nucleons. \end{abstract}

We conducted an in-depth analysis of magnetic bright points and their properties observed at the solar surface using the SDO/HMI dataset, covering a time period of 12 years from 2010 to 2021. The dataset comprised over 350,000 magnetic bright points detected through the 1800 GHz Fe XXIV line observation. This comprehensive study included statistical assessments of the magnetic bright points' velocity, latitude, longitude, and evolution times. Notably, our results indicate that magnetic bright points' velocity vectors follow a bi-modal distribution, with the respective components (x, y) exhibiting different statistical characteristics. The x component was found to be predominantly positive, whereas the y component was predominantly negative. This asymmetry may be an indication of the influence of the solar rotation, which could be responsible for observed biases. Furthermore, our findings also revealed that magnetic bright points are predominantly concentrated in the northern hemisphere, with their distribution skewed towards the western longitude. The observed magnetic bright points were found to be mobile, with a majority exhibiting changes in location within a time frame of less than 30 minutes. Interestingly, their disappearance was consistently longer than their appearance by a margin of approximately 0.5 hours. The duration of magnetic bright points' evolution ranged from 30 minutes to 9 hours, with an average of approximately 3.5 hours. To evaluate the effectiveness of weather forecasting models in terms of spatial coherence, we created a novel metric that rewards precise weather predictions at specific locations. Initially, we put our proposed evaluation method to the test using a normalized version of the Weather4Cast dataset, which we found significantly improved the accuracy of our evaluations by removing biases resulting from common location naming conventions. We compared the performance of four advanced weather forecasting models, employing either traditional or transfer learning techniques, on the normalized dataset. Our results indicate that utilizing transfer learning yields better outcomes compared to employing traditional learning methods. Moreover, we analyzed the potential for further improvement in weather forecasting accuracy by investigating the impact of increasing resolution in location coordinates. Our analysis suggests that enhancing the resolution from a coarse 50x50 km block size to a finer 10x10 km block size corresponds to a 14% decrease in MSE value. With a 2.5 km resolution, the MSE value exhibits minimal further improvement. To facilitate the testing of our proposed evaluation method, we made our codebase publicly available. Our study's findings are significant, as they open the door to employing spatially aware weather forecasting models and demonstrate the value of rigorous evaluation methodologies in guiding the development of such models. Additionally, our normalized dataset contributes to the field, serving as a resource for unbiased comparative studies of weather forecasting models. We believe that our proposed evaluation method, combined with the Weather4Cast-d normalized dataset, will inspire more accurate and effective weather forecasting models. Graph representation learning has emerged as a prominent graph machine learning method, with numerous applications including image recognition, molecule identification, and fraud detection in banking. In banking fraud detection, designers create synthetic graphs that mirror real-world banking transactions to train their models. A typical issue arises when the generated graphs do not align with the format used in the training dataset, leading to poor performance and low accuracy. Current methods either ignore this challenge or simplify the problem by assuming all graphs have a similar structure. Real-world banking transactions often feature diverse patterns such as repeated payments and one-time expenses. To tackle this limitation, an innovative method called BankGraphGen is introduced, which produces valid banking graphs with desired formats and suitable architecture. An important advantage of this approach is its ability to generate graphs with varying structures while improving the model's accuracy. To assess the effectiveness of this method, an experiment is conducted on three different graph models, which demonstrates BankGraphGen's ability to outperform existing methods by creating conform graphs for benchmark datasets. Furthermore, a comprehensive investigation is performed on three benchmark datasets to confirm the consistency of this method in producing conform graphs with repeated payments and one-time expenses, enhancing the model's performance. A widely recognized issue in optical systems, deblurring, impairs image quality and hinders subsequent analysis.
The most effective approach involves employing a data-driven model that utilizes a neural network to derive a reverse process of the blurring operation, thus obtaining sharp images from blurry ones.
However, incorporating a blur estimate module within such an inverse framework proves inefficient because it only contributes to image improvement after subsequent iterations.
Therefore, a more efficient method is proposed by moving the blur estimate module before the forward process, allowing the blurring factor to be accounted for in each iteration.
The proposed reblurring module is then incorporated into a state-of-the-art deblurring model to enhance its performance with quantitative results showing significant improvements over the standard model and a popular benchmark method.
Furthermore, the proposed method outperforms a commercial deblurring software in real-world image deblurring. Moreover, under specific conditions, it's possible to obtain O(1/K) convergence rates, even in the presence of errors, which are typically associated with non-convex objectives. A crucial insight revealed in this research allows determining the optimal convexity parameter of the cost function, thereby enabling its adjustment and enhancing the performance of adaptive algorithms. The proposed algorithm and results are applicable to a range of problems, including anisotropic least-squares regression and quadratic inference functions. Even in scenarios where the cost function is not strictly convex, its non-convexity components can be effectively handled. Moreover, empirical studies have consistently validated the theoretical findings and demonstrated the efficacy of the adaptive algorithm. It's also comparable to state-of-the-art algorithms, such as Finsiel, in terms of its performance, while offering the advantage of lower computational requirements. As a result, the proposed algorithm has potential uses in online monitoring tasks. Moreover, its adaptability makes it suitable for various data-driven problems, such as PDEs, optimal control, and multi-agent networks, particularly when the point of equilibrium is subject to variations or uncertainties. Consequently, the development of adaptive algorithms can provide valuable insights into the nature of these problems. Moreover, the relationships observed between the algorithm's step size, cost function, and Jacobian matrix hold significance beyond the context of algorithms. Therefore, the proposed algorithm and theoretical findings can be utilized to investigate the stability of dynamics that are naturally present in these problems. This research provides evidence of this stability through the continuous quadratic constraint, which is a key aspect. Furthermore, the results obtained from the algorithm's analysis can be employed to derive stability theorems for the dynamics of interaction systems, such as multi-agent networks, through the continuous quadratic constraint. This research offers new insights and understands the relationships between adaptive algorithms, dynamics, and problem characteristics, ultimately facilitating the derivation of stability conditions and convergence results. The proposed algorithm and theoretical analysis are versatile and can be applied to a range of problems, including online monitoring, data-driven problems, and optimal control, as evidenced by the provided numerical case studies. The method involves constructing the set of non-invertible symmetries using local operators that generate equivalences among regional symmetry transformations, which is distinct from previously suggested definitions. We investigate the complexity of counting solutions to linear equations in finite fields, especially when equations involve multiple variables. This problem can be addressed using tools from finite projective geometry and algebra. In contrast to the situation over finite fields of characteristic zero, the number of solutions for a given set of linear equations in a finite field can vary greatly based on the size of the field. This variation makes it challenging to establish general results regarding the complexity of counting solutions using geometric techniques. However, we can provide precise statements of complexity for specific scenarios. This paper answers an open question from Cai, Chen, and Lee by showing that the counting solutions issue is complete for PPA (probabilistic polynomial-time arithmetic) and co-PPA, and even CTC (counting Turing complete) and co-CTC. We can also rephrase PPA and CTC as Turing complete problems using a simple logic formula. Additionally, we can provide a comprehensive classification of complexity for various counting solutions problems based on the number of variables. For these problems, the complexity can be categorized into four distinct cases: PPA, co-PPA, P #P, and co-P #P, and these classifications are the best possible under a widely accepted hypothesis. We can also extend our results to linear equations involving modules of finite fields, including the case when equations involve multiple variables. This more general issue is complete for PPA and co-PPA, and even CTC and co-CTC. Our proofs use a combination of algebra, geometry, and arithmetic techniques, including a novel application of the Zariski density property over finite fields. This geometric approach allows us to establish a relationship between the complexity of counting solutions and the dimension of projective varieties over finite fields. A proposed method for teleporting quantum states between polariton condensates has been challenged by demonstrating that using entangled anti-polariton states can also perform quantum teleportation with high accuracy, similar to traditional approaches. Through a realistic simulation, we find that using entangled polariton states results in a significant decrease in fidelity compared to the standard method. However, by leveraging the multi-particle entanglement properties of polariton clusters, we show that the teleportation process can be accomplished with high fidelity even when using thermally generated entanglement. Furthermore, this method's effectiveness is likely due to the presence of embedded dark states within the system, which protect the entangled state from thermal degradation. We believe that utilizing entangled states of polariton clusters could serve as a promising resource for quantum information processing at room temperature. \textit{Copyright 2021 Author(s). As computers become more powerful, creating realistic three-dimensional models of humans has become a crucial task for various industries, including filmmaking and gaming. However, generating detailed and photorealistic 3D human models, particularly in terms of skin textures and facial expressions, remains a significant challenge. Previous studies have explored automatic 3D face creation from images, but the resulting models often lack the level of detail found in high-quality photographs. To address this limitation, we propose HUMBI, a novel and comprehensive dataset consisting of 80,000 high-resolution images of human heads with varied skin types, lighting conditions, and expressions. By leveraging HUMBI, we develop an approach for creating highly detailed and realistic 3D human models. While our method demonstrates improvement in photorealism, it is essential to note that it also facilitates the creation of models with specified characteristics. Therefore, HUMBI has the potential to enable the mass production of realistic 3D human models for use in animation, gaming, and related applications. This paper introduces a new framework for multi-language entity annotation that eliminates the need for individually labeled datasets in each language. The framework assumes that all language datasets share the same entities, allowing it to transfer annotations from one language to another through a multi-lingual model. The approach relies on two key components: entity linking and zero-shot annotation. Entity linking involves linking text passages to entity vocabulary, while zero-shot annotation involves using text to predict entity labels. The framework's entity embedding is then used to train models on pairs of entity mentions from different languages. The results show that the proposed framework outperforms baseline models that use only data from a single language. The study examines the performance of the proposed framework on three datasets: Wikipedia, PubMed, and Twitter. The data show that the entity linking model achieves 80.3% accuracy on entity linking, while the zero-shot annotation model achieves 57.4% and 52.1% accuracy on entity label prediction for single and multi-word entities, respectively. The study also demonstrates that the proposed framework can be used for entity annotation in over 100 languages. Further analysis reveals that the performance of the entity linking model correlates with word embedding similarity, while the performance of the zero-shot annotation model correlates with the number of training samples. The study notes that the proposed framework relies heavily on language models that may not always accurately represent entity vocabulary. As such, the study suggests the need for more research on the topic. In recent years, video super-resolution has gained significant attention, and top-notch methods often employ advanced processing techniques, including motion prediction, frame confinement, and convex optimization, which can be extremely computationally demanding.
The high costs associated with these methods make them impractical for practical applications, either on desktops or mobile devices.
The proposed framework, BasicVSR++, addresses this challenge by incorporating a simplified motion prediction approach, leveraging frame downscaling and upsampling, to significantly reduce computational requirements.
As a result, BasicVSR++ offers superior performance, surpassing the original BasicVSR and competing models by substantial margins on various benchmarks in terms of accuracy and efficiency.
The source code will be publicly available.

In multi-objective reinforcement learning, agents must adapt to resolve conflicts between different rewards by selecting optimal actions. However, using a single dynamics model in multi-task reinforcement learning can lead to a phenomenon called'moral hazard,' where the agent takes risks that compromise performance in favor of stable outcomes. This paper proposes modifying the reward in RL to discourage excessive risk-taking by introducing a new element - a predictive model of the agent's actions. This punitive model adjusts the RL reward with an opposing sign, effectively penalizing actions that deviate from predicted paths. Experimental results confirm the approach's effectiveness in limiting excessive risk-taking and striking a balance between risk aversion and performance efficiency. This method is particularly well-suited for control problems with predictable dynamics, and its process-noise-based variation offers an alternative that doesn't require such assumptions to be met. This penalization method is highly versatile and can be applied in a variety of RL problems involving trade-offs between risk and reward. Specifically, the process-noise-based variation was tested on a pole-balancing task and found to be an effective means of adapting to unexpected changes in dynamics while balancing risk and stability. Overall, the approach offers an attractive middle ground between risk-averse behavior and efficient performance. Additionally, the method's properties make it an attractive option for multi-objective reinforcement learning; this was confirmed through an evaluation of its performance in a mission planning task. This analysis provides valuable insights into the effectiveness of the method in limiting risk while balancing multiple objectives. In conclusion, the proposed approach represents a useful and efficient means of limiting risk in reinforcement learning while achieving optimal performance. In particular, its applicability to control problems, pole-balancing tasks, multi-objective reinforcement learning, and simulation-based tasks, makes it a versatile tool for a wide range of tasks. In terms of its limitations, its applicability to tasks with predictable dynamics and its efficiency in some control problems, indicate areas where further research could be directed towards enhancing its performance, possibly through the incorporation of deep learning methods. In this regard, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of a simple maximum entropy method in limiting risk in reinforcement learning, and its comparison with other risk-averse methods in terms of performance and efficiency, provides an attractive option for designers of decision-making systems. In this study, we examine the characteristics of a heat engine working within the Equilume protocol, a dynamic setup maintaining equilibrium via time-varying temperature and chemical potentials. We model the engine's internal chamber as a complex thermodynamic system, balanced between two all-around reservoirs, and derive the phase-space coordinates for its interior. These coordinates enable us to determine the engine's output power, defined as the product of a scaling parameter (λ) and the natural power dimension (ω_dot), demonstrating that wavelength (λ) influences performance. Additionally, we identify an optimal wavelength corresponding to the highest power yield, which we further analyze in terms of its dimensionality across different equilibration periods. Moreover, we investigate the engine's performance during canonical equilibrium simulations and verify that our model's predictions remain valid. Our investigation into the Equilume process also sheds light on the potential of heat engines to achieve exceptional performance beyond the limitations imposed by conventional second-law efficiency bounds. Furthermore, we develop a simplified model to gain insight into the optimal wavelength. Interestingly, the optimal wavelength exhibits asymptotic behavior, approaching the maximum possible value (unity) as the engine size diminishes. Conversely, smaller wavelengths result in sub-unity optimal values. To validate our model's accuracy, we performed three different kinds of error analysis: (i) comparing the exact and perturbative engine outputs, (ii) analyzing the impact of errors in equilibrium conditions on engine performance, and (iii) assessing the stability of our model. The results of this error analysis suggest that the magnitude of wavelength (λ) is a crucial factor in determining the magnitude of errors. Additionally, we performed a detailed stability analysis of our model, examining both perturbative and dynamic stability. In the case of perturbative stability, we explored how different eigenvalues influence the behavior of small disturbances, while for dynamic stability, we investigated the long-term behavior of initial conditions as the engine operates over extended periods, possibly entering a regime characterized by oscillating dynamics. Interestingly, in the limit of small engine sizes, the optimal wavelength approaches the maximum possible value (unity), and the corresponding output power also demonstrates optimal behavior. Furthermore, we developed a simplified model to gain insight into the optimal wavelength. Additionally, we extended our study to a two-dimensional setting, modeling the engine's output power in terms of its dimensionality across different equilibration periods, and interestingly, the results suggest that the optimal wavelength is influenced by the engine's size, and as the engine size diminishes, the optimal wavelength approaches unity. It's demonstrated that these encoding spaces naturally align with certain subsets of the Dyck system, exhibiting similarities in structure and possibly isomorphic to certain subspaces when the alphabet is of a specific size. Additionally, we explore the combinatorial aspects of these encoding maps and calculate the cardinalities of the encoding spaces, also identifying a connection to a specific class of maps and studying its properties. Finally, we discuss potential generalizations of these results to other types of maps. Our analysis ultimately provides a comprehensive characterization of the encoding spaces for any given alphabet size, including a finding that the encoding spaces are isomorphic to the Dyck system under certain conditions. Moreover, the study of encoding maps reveals information about the cardinalities of sets associated with these maps, which are related to the \$(k+1)\\-st\\ power of a set. One such power set has an interesting characterization as the collection of strings that can be formed by concatenating strings from the original set, separated by a fixed delimiter that corresponds to a Dyck word of a specified size. Our analysis reveals that both experimental searches in rare processes and precision measurements in Higgs and top-quark interactions can simultaneously constrain the scales of the model's parameters $B_\mu$ and $\Lambda_v$, thereby facilitating particle physics tests.
